EX 15.134.2 – 租赁激励应如何进行会计处理？
准则参考：IFRS 16 第81段 正文参考：15.134
出租人为促使签订新的或续签的经营租赁协议而向承租人支付的与租赁相关的款项，或出租人报销或承担的承租人成本，均计入租赁付款额。这些款项不被视为计入租赁资产账面价值的初始费用的一部分。相反，应将其从租赁付款额中扣除，并与租赁付款额一并按直线法或其他系统合理的方法进行分摊。
示例1 – 经营租赁激励：免租期
在一份为期10年的租赁协议下，出租人给予一年的免租期，随后九年每年固定租金为C110万。这相当于10年期间每年租金C99万。激励成本应当在租赁期内分摊。因此，每年将在利润表中确认C99万的租金收入。在第1年年末，出租人将确认C99万的应计应收租金，并在随后九年中每年减少C11万。
示例2 – 经营租赁激励：出租人对承租人装修费用的补贴
或者，出租人与承租人约定，一次性预付现金C100万以补贴承租人自身的装修费用，10年租赁期的年固定租金为C110万。这同样相当于无激励情况下每年C100万的租金。因此，租赁期每年将确认C100万的净租金收入。该C100万激励初始确认为应收款项（应计应收租金），并在之后每年向利润表摊销C10万。
应收租赁款属于IFRS 9预期信用损失模型的适用范围。有关减值的更多详情，参见第45章。
FAQ 15.134.3 – 当经营租赁收入的可收回性不确定时，出租人是否应继续确认租赁收入？
准则参考：IFRS 16 第81段 正文参考：15.134
问题 如果出租人评估认为某项经营租赁的部分租金无法收回，出租人是否应继续确认相应的租赁收入？
解答 IFRS 16第81段要求出租人按直线法或其他系统合理的方法将经营租赁的租赁付款额确认为收入。IFRS 16并未规定出租人确认经营租赁收入所必须满足的可收回性标准。因此，出租人可以继续确认经营租赁收入。然而，出租人必须对应收租赁款适用IFRS 9的减值规定。应收租赁款的减值损失应当单独确认为一项费用。
FAQ 15.134.4 – 当行使解约条款且租赁期缩短时，经营租赁出租人应如何对退租补偿金（surrender premiums）进行会计处理？
准则参考：IFRS 16 第81段 正文参考：15.134
出租人与承租人签订了一份租赁期为10年的租赁合同。出租人将该租赁作为经营租赁进行会计处理。该租赁合同包含一项第5年解约条款，若行使该条款，则需支付退租补偿金。在租赁期开始日，出租人认为合理确定不会行使该解约条款，因此确定租赁期为10年。在第3年年末，由于不可预见的情况，承租人正式通知其将在第5年行使该解约条款。
根据IFRS 16第21段，这将导致租赁期发生变动。此外，出租人此前未将退租补偿金付款额计入租赁付款额，但鉴于解约条款的行使，该补偿金现在将构成应予确认的租赁付款额的一部分。
鉴于解约条款现已行使且租赁期缩短，出租人应如何对退租补偿金进行会计处理？
根据IFRS 16第81段，经营租赁的租赁付款额应当按直线法确认为收入；如果其他系统合理的方法更能反映因使用标的资产所产生经济利益的消耗模式，则应采用该其他系统合理的方法。因此，根据第81段的指引，退租补偿金的确认存在两种可能的方法。
一种方法是将退租补偿金与剩余租赁付款额一并，在新的2年剩余租赁期内按直线法采用未来适用法确认。虽然由于退租补偿金和解约条款已包含在原租赁合同中而不构成租赁变更，但直线法与第87段的租赁变更指引一致。根据该指引，经营租赁的变更应当自变更生效日起作为一项新租赁进行会计处理。

另一种方法是计算假如在租赁期开始日即确定租赁期为5年时本应确认的租赁付款总额（包括退租补偿金）。在收到未来行使解约条款通知前已确认的租赁付款额，与假设采用新的较短租赁期计算的修订后租赁付款额之间的任何差额，将确认为累计追补调整（cumulative catch up adjustment）。出租人随后在剩余租赁期内确认剩余的修订后租赁付款额。由于租赁期现已缩短，来自租赁资产的整体利益已加速实现，因此采用追补调整反映了出租人从承租人使用资产中获得利益的修订后模式。
我们认为，上述两种方法均可采用。因此，主体拥有会计政策选择权。所选定的会计政策应当一贯适用，并在重大时予以披露。
FAQ 15.135.1 – 出租人能否将不符合初始直接费用条件的成本予以资本化？
准则参考：IFRS 16 第83、BC150段 正文参考：15.135
问题 出租人签订了一项租赁合同，并向第三方发生了与租赁有形资产相关的费用，例如将其运输至租赁合同指定地点或进行安装的费用。
出租人应如何对这些费用进行会计处理？
解答 这些费用不符合IFRS 16中初始直接费用的定义，因为它们并非为取得租赁而发生的费用。
出租人应首先考虑是否有其他会计准则适用于这些费用（例如，如果这些费用与非租赁组成部分相关，则适用IFRS 15）。
如果这些费用不属于任何其他会计准则的适用范围，IFRS 16并未就如何核算这些费用提供指引。我们认为，出租人可以在以下两种会计政策选择中择一适用：
a) 类比适用IFRS 15
适用IAS 8第11段，IFRS 15中存在类似且相关的问题。如果这些费用在IFRS 15下可以作为合同履约成本予以资本化，则出租人可以将与租赁资产相关的同等费用资本化。有关IFRS 15合同履约成本的指引，参见第11章第278段及以后段落。
IFRS 16并未提供允许将这些费用资本化的指引。考虑到概念框架中费用的定义，这些费用可被视为导致权益减少的负债增加（应付账款），因此在发生时计入费用。
所选定的会计政策应当一贯适用并予以披露。如果该项选择构成关键会计判断，主体应考虑IAS 1的披露要求。详情参见第4章第152段。
FAQ 15.136.1 – 出租人应如何对其自愿豁免的过去租金合同到期应收款项进行会计处理？
准则参考：IFRS 16 第87段，IFRS 9 第3.2.3(a)段 正文参考：15.136
问题 出租人可能同意豁免过去租金合同到期应付的部分款项，而不变更租赁范围或其他条款（例如，在承租人面临财务困难时）。如果此类减免并非合同或法律法规所要求，出租人应如何对应收租赁款的此类豁免进行会计处理？
解答 IFRS 9与IFRS 16对此类自愿豁免已确认金额的处理包含不同指引。因此，我们认为对于经营租赁应收款的此类减免存在会计政策选择，说明如下。
出租人可以将过去租金到期付款额的减少视为应收租赁款的部分消除。IFRS 9第2.1(b)(i)段指出，经营租赁应收款适用IFRS 9的终止确认规定。IFRS 9第3.2.3(a)段确立，当收取金融资产现金流量的合同权利终止时，应当终止确认该金融资产。在此会计处理下，豁免金额将在合同达成减免协议的期间在利润表中确认为损失（即不作为租赁收入的冲减），并相应减少应收租赁款。
或者，在此事实背景下，出租人可以认为满足租赁变更的定义，因为租赁对价发生了变动（即该减免并非原租赁条款的一部分）。因此，出租人可以遵循IFRS 16第87段的指引，该段规定经营租赁的变更应当作为一项新租赁处理，且任何“应计租赁付款额”必须作为新租赁的租赁付款额的一部分。因此，出租人在变更时不会立即改变此前在资产负债表中就合同到期过去租金确认的金额，而是在剩余租赁期内确认较低的租赁收入。
主体应当将其处理方法作为一项会计政策进行选择，并对具有相似特征及处于相似情况下的合同修改一贯适用。主体在选择会计政策时，还应考虑当地监管机构的观点。
请注意，上述会计政策选择仅针对过去租金合同到期应付金额的豁免。自愿豁免尚未到期（因而尚未确认为应收款项）的租赁付款额属于租赁变更。因此，适用IFRS 16第87段，即在豁免付款额时，变更后的租赁应当作为一项新租赁进行会计处理。
FAQ 15.136.2 – 经营租赁发生变更时，初始直接费用应如何进行会计处理？
准则参考：IFRS 16 第87段 正文参考：15.88
问题 当经营租赁的出租人确定租赁付款额的金额或时间变动应当作为租赁变更进行会计处理时，出租人应如何对与该租赁相关的初始直接费用进行会计处理？
解答 IFRS 16第87段针对经营租赁发生变更时出租人的会计处理提供了具体指引。该段规定：“出租人应当自变更生效日起将经营租赁的变更作为一项新租赁进行会计处理，并将与原租赁相关的任何预付或应计租赁付款额作为新租赁的租赁付款额的一部分。”请注意，如果出租人自愿豁免过去租金合同到期应付的金额，则在适用IFRS 9的终止确认指引还是IFRS 16的租赁变更指引之间存在会计政策选择。

在适用IFRS 16的指引时，尽管第87段规定了任何预付或应计租赁付款额的会计处理，但并未规定与租赁相关的任何初始直接费用的处理方法。这可能意味着与原租赁相关的初始直接费用在变更时应予终止确认，且仅有预付或应计租赁付款额可视为与新租赁相关的付款额。然而，IFRS 16要求出租人将租赁变更作为一项新租赁进行会计处理，因此，在变更租赁过程中发生的、符合初始直接费用定义的增量费用可以予以资本化，因为它们属于取得变更后租赁的费用。如果不进行租赁变更，这些增量费用本不会发生。
另一种观点认为，尽管IFRS 16要求出租人将变更作为一项新租赁进行会计处理，但该准则允许将先前确认的预付或应计租赁付款额作为变更后租赁的对价，这表明其考虑了与原租赁之间的联系。基于此，与原租赁相关的任何初始直接费用同样与变更后的租赁相关，因此应当在变更后租赁的剩余租赁期内继续确认并摊销。然而，由于初始直接费用的定义是指初始取得租赁所发生的费用，在变更租赁过程中发生的任何增量费用均应确认为费用。
我们认为，在IFRS 16缺乏具体指引的情况下，上述两种方法均可采用。因此，主体拥有会计政策选择权。所选定的会计政策应当一贯适用，并在重大时予以披露。
EX 15.140.1 – 生产商出租人在融资租赁下出售资产
准则参考：IFRS 16 第71段 正文参考：15.140
主体A生产卡车。其为客户提供直接购买卡车或在融资租赁下租赁卡车两种选择。卡车的制造成本为C25,000。如果直接购买，售价为C30,000（假设为公允价值）。如果客户选择租赁卡车，租期为20年，年租金为C2,809，于每年年初支付。主体A认为该卡车在20年租赁期届满时的余值为C1,000。该类租赁的市场利率为8%。租赁付款额的现值为C29,786，未担保余值的现值为C214。
因此，主体A将按标的资产公允价值（C30,000）与租赁付款额现值（C29,786）两者中的较低者确认销售收入。销售成本等于卡车的账面价值（C25,000）减去余值现值（C214）。因此，在签订租赁合同时，主体A应作如下会计分录：
借 应收租赁款 C29,786 贷 营业收入 C29,786 借 销售成本 C24,786 借 应收租赁款——余值权益 C214 贷 存货 C25,000
主体A将确认C5,000的销售利润（C29,786 − C24,786）。同时，其还将确认C30,000的应收租赁款，即租赁付款额现值加上未担保余值现值（也就是租赁投资净额）。在20年租赁期内，随着出租人将每期租金用于冲减应收款项并按租赁投资净额的固定周期性回报率确认收益，租赁投资净额将摊销至余值C1,000。
EX 15.140.2 – 生产商出租人出售资产且承租人预付定金
准则参考：IFRS 16 第71段 正文参考：15.140

主体A（生产商出租人）于20X8年1月1日签署协议，向主体B（承租人）出租特定设备。主体A承诺于20X9年1月1日向主体B交付设备。主体A将制造该设备，并估计其公允价值为C15,000。该资产的预计建造成本为C10,000。出租人在谈判和安排该租赁时未发生任何初始直接费用。该安排的期限为4年，自设备交付时起算。该资产的预计使用寿命为4年，无余值。承租人有义务在签署合同时一次性预付C5,000，并每年1月1日支付四期年付款额C2,619。首期年付款额于20X9年1月1日到期。
租赁开始日为20X8年1月1日（签署租赁协议之日），租赁期开始日为20X9年1月1日（标的资产可供承租人使用之日）。
对于在租赁开始日但早于租赁期开始日预付的租赁付款额如何进行会计处理，准则并未提供详细指引。我们认为，在租赁开始日，出租人应当将C5,000的预付款确认为一项负债，并在租赁开始日至租赁期开始日（资产达到可使用状态）期间对其进行利息增计。该预付款实质上是承租人在建造期间向出租人提供的预付款或贷款。出租人应当在预付款增计至租赁期开始日期间确认财务费用。
主体A于20X8年1月1日通过比较折现至20X9年1月1日的租赁付款额现值与20X9年1月1日资产的估计公允价值（在本例中，假设余值和初始直接费用均为零）来确定租赁内含利率。假设租赁内含利率为5%，该负债在租赁开始日至租赁期开始日（20X9年1月1日）期间增计至C5,250。增计后的预付款C5,250作为租赁付款额的一部分处理。
在20X9年1月1日租赁期开始日，出租人预计初始确认C5,000的处置利得以及C9,750的应收融资租赁款，即未来租赁付款额折现金额C15,000减去抵销的C5,250负债。
FAQ 15.148.1 – 能否在不详细拆分租金的情况下确定租赁分类？
准则参考：IFRS 16 附录B 第B56段 正文参考：15.148
问题 能否在不详细拆分租金的情况下确定租赁分类？
解答 对建筑物部分进行分类通常比土地部分更为困难。在许多情况下，无需在租赁的土地部分和建筑物部分之间进行详细的租金拆分，即可确定建筑物租赁的分类。
除现值测试外，租赁分类的各项标准均可在不拆分租金的情况下予以考虑。例如，使用寿命相对较短的建筑物（可能是按客户规格建造或用于特定用途的建筑物）很可能作为融资租赁持有。建筑物的长期租赁（通常为99年至999年）也很可能属于融资租赁。
EX 15.148.2 – 采用定性标准进行租赁分类
准则参考：IFRS 16 附录B 第B56段 正文参考：15.148
仅使用IFRS 16中的定性分类标准，也可能确定某项建筑物租赁属于经营租赁。考虑以下租赁：
物业类型： 非专用办公大楼 租赁期： 25年 经济寿命： 50年 初始租金： 市场租金水平 租金重估： 每5年一次，仅向上调整至市场租金水平 购买选择权： 无 余值担保： 无 撤销条款： 无 续租选择权： 承租人可按市场租金将租赁延长5年
很明显，承租人并未享有建筑物所有权相关的几乎全部风险和报酬。租赁期未占资产经济寿命的大部分，承租人对余值没有权益，且租金按市场水平设定。因此，无需进行现值测试，即可合理得出土地租赁和建筑物租赁均属于经营租赁的结论。
FAQ 15.149.1 – 为何按租赁权益的相对公允价值比例在土地和建筑物之间分摊租赁付款额？
准则参考：IFRS 16 附录B 第B56段 正文参考：15.149
问题 为何按租赁权益的相对公允价值比例在土地和建筑物之间分摊租赁付款额？
解答 土地或建筑物的租赁权益公允价值不同于土地或建筑物本身的公允价值。仅参照土地和建筑物的相对公允价值来分摊租赁付款额，无法反映土地通常具有不确定经济寿命且预计在租赁期届满后仍能保持其价值这一事实。相比之下，建筑物的未来经济利益在租赁期内至少会在一定程度上被消耗。因此，合理预期与建筑物相关的租赁付款额将设定在能够使出租人获得初始投资回报并收回租赁期内消耗的建筑物价值的水平。
这就是为什么最低租赁付款额的分摊应当加权以反映其补偿出租人的作用，而不是参照土地和建筑物的相对公允价值。换言之，权重应当反映承租人在土地和建筑物中的租赁权益。
FAQ 15.149.2 – 承租人租赁权益的公允价值如何计算？
准则参考：IFRS 16 附录B 第B56段 正文参考：15.149
问题 承租人租赁权益的公允价值如何计算？
解答 租赁权益的公允价值通过以下公式得出：
租赁权益的公允价值 = 完全所有权权益的公允价值 – 租赁开始日余值权益的现值
就完全所有权建筑物的公允价值而言，由于陈旧过时，其余值按比例可能低于土地；因此，为了使等式平衡，建筑物租赁权益的公允价值按比例将高于土地。这导致租赁付款额的分摊权重倾向于建筑物。
准则并未就如何确定租赁权益的公允价值提供详细指引。尽管如此，仍有多种不同方法可用于进行此项计算。无论采用何种方法，估值输入值很可能保持不变，即：
- 物业在租赁开始日的公允价值。
- 该公允价值在土地和建筑物之间的拆分。
- 物业在租赁期届满时的余值。
无论采用何种方法，均需房地产估值专家提供专业意见。
EX 15.149.3 – 租金分摊
准则参考：IFRS 16 附录B 第B56段 正文参考：15.149
为了拆分租赁付款额，需要对FAQ 15.149.2中讨论的输入值作进一步分析。租金拆分的底层逻辑在于，土地部分不太可能发生折旧，因此，租赁开始日公允价值与租赁期届满时余值之间的任何价值减损，通常衡量了建筑物在租赁期内的价值损失。考虑以下示例：
示例1 – 按租赁权益价值基础分摊租金
物业完全所有权价值： C100m 租赁开始日土地价值： C40m 租赁期： 25年 初始年租金： C6.25m 物业预计余值： C65m（按现行价格） 物业预计实际回报率： 6.0%
如果假设物业在租赁期内的全部价值损失均归属于建筑物，且余值按物业的预计实际回报率折现，则租金可作如下拆分：
土地 建筑物 合计 (Cm) (Cm) (Cm) i 完全所有权价值 40 60 100 ii 余值 40 25 65 iii 余值现值 9 6 15 i – iii 租赁权益价值 31 (36%) 54 (64%) 85 (100%) 租金分摊（% × C6.25m） 2.25 4.00 6.25
示例2 – 按资本价值基础分摊租金
另一种替代方法是评估建筑物在租赁期内的价值损失，然后计算需要将多大比例的租金分摊用于补偿出租人在租赁期内遭受的建筑物价值损失。在下例中，采用6%的比率来确定分摊至摊销的租金金额。
在实务中，房地产估值专家对于分摊租金时应采用何种最恰当的比率可能持有不同观点。例如，国债利率或实际回报率均可能被认为恰当。因此，在确定所采用的比率时，向房地产专家寻求指导十分重要。
土地 建筑物 合计 (Cm) (Cm) (Cm) i 完全所有权价值 40 (40%) 60 (60%) 100 ii 余值 40 25 65 i – ii 摊销额 0 35 35 租金 iii 分摊至摊销的租金（C0.60m） − 0.60 0.60 iv 余额（% × C5.65m） 2.26 3.39 5.65 iii + iv 租金分摊（Cm） 2.26 3.99 6.25
C0.60m为每年年初支付的年租金，当按6%的物业预计实际回报率在25年租赁期内复利计算时，结果为C35m，即完全所有权价值与建筑物余值之间的差额。
FAQ 15.153.1 – 售后租回交易在何种情况下不符合IFRS 15规定的销售条件？
准则参考：IFRS 16 第99段 正文参考：15.153
问题 主体A将一栋剩余使用寿命为30年的建筑物以市场价值C100m出售给银行B。为本例之目的，忽略土地租赁。该主体随后从银行B租回该建筑物，并在未来10年内每年向银行B支付C5m的租金。
在第10年年末，主体A有权以C70m回购该建筑物。
该项交易是否符合售后租回交易的条件？
IFRS 15第B66段规定：“如果主体负有回购资产的义务或享有回购资产的权利（远期合同或买入选择权），则客户未获得对该资产的控制权，因为客户在主导资产的使用以及获得资产几乎全部剩余经济利益方面的能力受到限制。”
在本例中，主体A拥有回购建筑物的选择权，这意味着该交易不符合IFRS 15规定的销售条件，因此不符合售后租回交易的条件。
EX 15.155.1 – 售后租回交易的会计处理（示例）
准则参考：IFRS 16 第100段，IE11（示例24） 正文参考：15.155
卖方兼承租人以现金C2,000,000向非关联买方兼出租人出售一栋建筑物。该建筑物当时的公允价值为C1,800,000；紧接该交易前的账面价值为C1,000,000。
同时，卖方兼承租人与买方兼出租人签订合同，取得该建筑物为期18年的使用权，年付款额为C120,000，于每年年末支付。租赁内含利率为4.5%，由此得出年付款额的现值为C1,459,200。
经评估，向买方兼出租人转移该资产符合IFRS 15下销售的定义。
该项交易应如何进行会计处理？
由于对价（C2,000,000）超过建筑物的公允价值（C1,800,000），该协议包含一项融资交易：
卖方兼承租人按原账面价值（C1,000,000）中与保留的使用权相关的比例初始确认使用权资产。该比例的计算方式为：将租赁付款额现值（C1,459,200）减去租赁付款额中仅属于偿还向卖方兼承租人提供融资的部分（C200,000）[= C1,259,200]，再除以资产的公允价值（C1,800,000）。由此得出使用权资产为C699,555。
销售利得按总利得C800,000（购买价款减去融资部分再减去建筑物账面价值）的一定比例计算，该比例代表实际转移给买方的权利（= 建筑物公允价值C1,800,000减去租赁付款额现值C1,259,200）占建筑物公允价值（C1,800,000）的比率。由此得出利得为C240,355。
FAQ 15.155.2 – 如果售后租回交易的租赁付款额全部为可变付款额，应如何进行初始会计处理？
准则参考：IFRS 16 第100段 正文参考：15.155
问题 如果售后租回交易的租赁付款额全部为可变付款额，应如何进行初始会计处理？

解答 国际财务报告准则解释委员会（“解释委员会”）曾被问及，当租赁包含可变付款额时，卖方兼承租人如何计量租回产生的使用权资产，并据此确定交易日确认的利得或损失金额。解释委员会指出，IFRS 16第100段规定：“如果卖方兼承租人对资产的转移满足IFRS 15关于作为资产销售进行会计处理的规定：(a) 卖方兼承租人应当按资产原账面价值中与卖方兼承租人保留的使用权相关的比例计量租回产生的使用权资产。相应地，卖方兼承租人应当仅确认与转移给买方兼出租人的权利相关的利得或损失金额。”

因此，为计量租回产生的使用权资产，卖方兼承租人需确定转移给买方兼出租人的不动产、厂场和设备（PP&E）中与保留的使用权相关的比例。具体做法是在交易日将通过租回保留的使用权与构成整项不动产、厂场和设备的权利进行比较。IFRS 16并未规定确定该比例的方法。在此可变付款额情景下，卖方兼承租人可以通过比较例如：(a) 预期租赁付款额（包括可变付款额）的现值，与 (b) 交易日不动产、厂场和设备的公允价值，来确定该比例。
卖方兼承租人在交易日确认的利得或损失，是其对租回产生的使用权资产进行计量的结果。由于卖方兼承租人保留的使用权并未因该交易而被重新计量（而是按不动产、厂场和设备原账面价值的一定比例计量），所确认的利得或损失金额仅与转移给买方兼出租人的权利相关。适用IFRS 16第53(i)段，卖方兼承租人应当披露售后租回交易产生的利得或损失。
解释委员会的议程决定说明，即使全部租赁付款额均为可变且不取决于指数或比率，卖方兼承租人仍应在交易日确认一项负债。该负债的初始计量是适用IFRS 16第100(a)段计量使用权资产以及确定售后租回交易利得或损失的结果。
IASB目前正在开展一项关于卖方兼承租人应如何对售后租回交易中产生的租赁负债适用IFRS 16后续计量规定的项目。
FAQ 15.166.1 – 在首次执行日估计增量借款利率时，租赁期应当如何确定？
准则参考：IFRS 16 附录A，IFRS 16 第C8段 正文参考：15.166
问题 在首次执行日估计增量借款利率时，租赁期应当如何确定？
解答 对于此前分类为经营租赁的租赁，采用简化过渡方法的承租人应使用其在首次执行日的增量借款利率。
在确定增量借款利率时，承租人必须考虑的因素之一是租赁期。由此产生的问题是，承租人应当使用原租赁期还是首次执行日的剩余租赁期。
某项物业租赁的租赁期开始日为2001年1月1日（当时租赁期为20年），IFRS 16的采用日为2019年1月1日。在本例中，承租人应当确定2年期（首次执行日的剩余租赁期）还是20年期（原租赁期）的增量借款利率？
IFRS 16的过渡规定并未明确在确定增量借款利率时，租赁期应为原租赁期还是剩余租赁期。我们认为，采用其中任何一种均属恰当，主体拥有会计政策选择权。所选定的会计政策应当一贯适用并予以披露。
如果主体适用IFRS 16第C8(b)(i)段追溯计算使用权资产，其应当使用相同的增量借款利率计算追溯使用权资产和租赁负债。
FAQ 15.167.1 – 在过渡至IFRS 16时，此前分类为经营租赁的租赁所产生的使用权资产的减值要求是什么？
准则参考：IFRS 16 附录C 第C10(b)段 正文参考：15.167
问题 某零售商根据IAS 17分类为经营租赁的租赁合同租赁了90家门店。在采用IFRS 16之前，该零售商决定不再使用其中18家门店进行经营，而是将其转租给第三方。因此，该零售商适用IAS 37的指引评估标的租赁合同是否属于亏损合同，并得出结论认为其中10份租赁合同需要确认亏损合同预计负债。
- 72份合同：未进行评估。
- 10份合同：已进行评估；已确认预计负债。
- 8份合同：已进行评估；未确认预计负债。
在过渡至IFRS 16时，该零售商选择了“简化方法”。
该零售商在首次执行日如何评估每份合同确认的使用权资产是否需要计提减值？每家门店均为IAS 36定义的单独现金产出单元。
在首次执行日，承租人必须评估每份租赁合同确认的使用权资产是否需要计提减值 [IFRS 16 附录C 第C8(c)段]。执行该项测试的方式取决于承租人在过渡前是否已基于IAS 37进行了评估。
主体已基于IAS 37指引进行评估的合同
对于主体已基于IAS 37指引进行评估的合同（本例中为18份合同），IFRS 16第C10(b)段允许其依赖该评估结果。如果主体决定采用该实务权宜之计，则其在首次执行日按紧接首次执行日前已确认的任何亏损合同预计负债金额调整使用权资产。
- 与已确认亏损合同预计负债的10家门店相关的使用权资产，按等于该预计负债账面价值的金额予以扣减。
- 与未确认亏损合同预计负债的8家门店相关的使用权资产不作调整；对其无需执行进一步的减值复核。
如果主体不采用该实务权宜之计，则必须适用IAS 36的指引。因此，其必须评估在首次执行日是否存在发生减值损失的迹象（例如，转租赁租金不同于原租赁租金）。如果存在该迹象，主体必须按照IAS 36的指引计算使用权资产的可收回金额，并在必要时确认减值。如果不存在减值迹象，主体无需计算可收回金额。
主体尚未基于IAS 37指引进行评估的合同
对于尚未基于IAS 37指引进行评估的合同（本例中为72份合同），我们认为主体拥有会计政策选择权。主体可以在过渡至IFRS 16之前执行评估（如IAS 37第66至69段所述），并依赖该评估结果（即按任何亏损合同预计负债的金额调整使用权资产）。或者，主体可以按上述方式适用IAS 36的指引。
请注意：上述示例考虑的是零售门店，其中每项使用权资产同时也是IAS 36定义的现金产出单元。在使用权资产本身并非现金产出单元的情况下，主体仍须照常适用IAS 36，以确定何时需要进行减值复核以及现金产出单元的构成。
FAQ 15.167.2 – 如果主体在过渡时将其IAS 37亏损租赁预计负债纳入使用权资产，未来减值转回的认定成本是多少？
准则参考：IFRS 16 附录C 第C10(b)段 正文参考：15.167
问题 如果主体在过渡时将其IAS 37亏损租赁预计负债纳入使用权资产，未来减值转回的认定成本是多少？
解答 在过渡至IFRS 16时选择“简化方法”的承租人，必须确保此前分类为经营租赁的租赁合同所产生的使用权资产未发生减值。因此，承租人要么在过渡时对使用权资产适用IAS 36，要么依赖其在首次执行日前适用IAS 37对租赁是否构成亏损合同所作的评估（如FAQ 15.167.1所述）。在后一种情况下，承租人按紧接首次执行日前在财务状况表中确认的任何亏损租赁预计负债的金额调整使用权资产。
某零售商根据IAS 17分类为经营租赁的租赁合同租赁了一家门店。该门店是IAS 36定义的单独现金产出单元。在IFRS 16首次执行日之前，承租人适用IAS 37的指引评估了标的租赁合同是否属于亏损合同，并得出结论认为需要确认亏损合同预计负债。紧接首次执行日前，该预计负债的账面价值为C20。
在过渡至IFRS 16时，该零售商选择了“简化方法”，并决定依赖IAS 37的评估结果，而非适用IAS 36的指引。在考虑亏损合同预计负债之前，使用权资产的计量金额为C100；调整后，账面价值为C80。
在首次执行日所作的调整能否在未来期间转回？
IFRS 16并未解决这一问题。承租人对于如何解释过渡时所作的调整拥有会计政策选择权：
- 其可以将使用权资产的初始账面价值（C80）解释为总额C100减去损失准备C20。在此观点下，如果后续期间的减值测试表明使用权资产的价值已经恢复，则该调整在价值恢复的范围内予以转回。按IAS 37下的亏损合同预计负债金额调整使用权资产，仅仅是适用IAS 36指引的一种实务替代方法。使用权资产的后续会计处理不应因是否选择该实务权宜之计而受到影响。
- 或者，承租人可以将使用权资产的初始账面价值（C80）解释为其不可超过的认定成本。在此观点下，无论后续期间基于IAS 36的减值测试是否表明使用权资产的价值已经恢复，该调整均不得转回。
所选定的会计政策必须一贯适用。
FAQ 15.167.3 – 过渡时如何适用低价值资产豁免？
准则参考：IFRS 16 附录C 第C9(a)段 正文参考：15.167
在过渡的“简化方法”下，承租人可以对先前分类为经营租赁的现有租赁合同适用低价值资产豁免 [IFRS 16 附录C 第C9(a)段]。
问题 低价值资产豁免是否也可以适用于根据IAS 17分类为融资租赁的租赁合同？
解答 可以。如果标的资产属于“低价值”（按IFRS 16的定义），承租人无需确认使用权资产和相应的租赁负债。遵循这一原则，承租人在首次执行日可以对先前分类为经营租赁的租赁合同和先前分类为融资租赁的租赁合同均适用低价值资产豁免。
EX 15.167.4 – 过渡时适用实务权宜之计
准则参考：IFRS 16 附录C 第C10段 正文参考：15.167
采用简化过渡方法的承租人在确认此前分类为经营租赁的租赁时，可以选择多项实务权宜之计，包括使用后见之明以及在租赁组成部分和非租赁组成部分之间分摊付款额。

承租人在过渡时被允许使用后见之明（IFRS 16第C10(e)段），准则中给出的示例涉及确定将哪些选择权纳入租赁期。因此，后见之明也可适用于其他判断领域，例如估计拆卸成本。我们认为，后见之明不应适用于不涉及判断或估计的领域。例如，对于付款额随CPI变动的租赁，如果承租人选择追溯计算使用权资产，承租人不能以过渡日的租赁付款额为基础对其进行计量；相反，承租人应当以原租赁付款额以及历次通胀增长为基础进行计算。
在租赁组成部分和非租赁组成部分之间分摊付款额
如果一项租赁包含针对租赁组成部分和非租赁组成部分的付款额，承租人必须适用IFRS 16分摊付款额。在IFRS 16下，租赁组成部分和非租赁组成部分之间的付款额分摊基于租赁期开始日的估计对价和单独售价。我们认为，以首次执行IFRS 16之日（而非租赁期开始日）的估计对价和单独售价为基础分摊付款额是可接受的。
FAQ 15.167.5 – 过渡时如何对融资租赁进行会计处理？
准则参考：IFRS 16 附录C 第C11段 正文参考：15.167
问题 过渡时如何对融资租赁进行会计处理？
解答 采用简化过渡方法且在IAS 17下存在分类为融资租赁的租赁的承租人，在过渡时必须采用紧接首次执行日前租赁资产和租赁负债的账面价值。IFRS 16的计量原则仅在首次执行日之后适用。如果存在计量差异（例如FAQ 15.69.1中讨论的余值担保），任何重新计量均应在紧接首次执行日之后进行，而不作为过渡调整处理（即不计入期初留存收益）。
EX 15.169.1 – 过渡至IFRS 16时转租赁形成的融资租赁的初始确认
准则参考：IFRS 16 附录C 第C15段 正文参考：15.169
在过渡至IFRS 16时，中间承租人采用“简化方法”。其使用IFRS 16第C8(b)(i)段的指引，对在IAS 17下分类为经营租赁的原租赁所产生的使用权资产进行计量。这意味着其计算初始账面价值时视同自租赁期开始日起即已适用IFRS 16，但采用首次执行日的增量借款利率。
在IAS 17下同样分类为经营租赁的转租赁，在首次执行日进行重新评估 [IFRS 16 附录C 第C15段]。基于该重新评估，该转租赁现分类为融资租赁，因此承租人将该转租赁作为在首次执行日签订的一项新融资租赁进行会计处理 [IFRS 16 附录C 第C15(b)段]。其终止确认与原租赁相关的使用权资产，并按等于转租赁投资净额的金额确认一项应收款项。
确认转租赁投资净额是否对损益产生影响？
确认与原租赁相关的使用权资产的影响，在首次执行日列报为对期初留存收益（或其他权益组成部分，视适用情况而定）的调整 [IFRS 16 附录C 第C7段]。然而，准则并未明确说明确认转租赁投资净额的影响是否同样适用此规定。由于两项影响均与首次执行IFRS 16相关，我们认为将两者均列报于留存收益（或其他权益组成部分，视适用情况而定）中是恰当的。
由此产生的会计分录 如下：
借 使用权资产 贷 租赁负债 贷 期初留存收益 借 租赁投资净额 贷 使用权资产 贷 期初留存收益
\ 以上会计分录的目的在于说明一般原则；视具体事实和情况而定，也可能出现留存收益减少的情形。
EX 15.172.1 – 首次执行日之前交易的规定
准则参考：IFRS 16 附录C 第C16、C19段 正文参考：15.172
无论承租人在过渡时采用完全追溯法还是“简化方法”，均有多项过渡规定必须遵守，因为这些是强制性要求而非选择项。例如：
在首次执行日之前签订了售后经营租回交易的主体，必须以与其他任何经营租赁相同的方式对租回进行会计处理（对非市场条款的调整除外）。主体不得选择追溯适用IFRS 16中的售后租回指引。
此前在企业合并中就有利或不利租赁合同确认了资产或负债的主体，在首次执行日必须终止确认该资产或负债，并将其调整至相关的使用权资产。主体不得重新追溯收购会计处理以按企业合并日的公允价值确认使用权资产。

chapter: 16 - Provisions, contingent liabilities and contingent assets (IAS 37)
text: 16.7 The word ‘provision’ could be used to describe amounts that are deducted from assets to arrive at their balance sheet carrying amount. For example, provisions are made for depreciation or amortisation or the impairment of financial or non-financial assets. These are not provisions and are not within the scope of IAS 37. These relate to the measurement of assets, and they are adjustments made to determine the assets’ carrying value.

chapter: 16 - Provisions, contingent liabilities and contingent assets (IAS 37)
text: 16.8 IAS 37 does not specify whether a debit arising when a provision is recognised is treated as an expense or an asset.

text: Provisions versus other liabilities

chapter: 16 - Provisions, contingent liabilities and contingent assets (IAS 37)
text: 16.9 A provision is “a liability of uncertain timing or amount”. Provisions differ from other liabilities in the degree of certainty about the amount or the timing of the payment. So, there is a clear distinction between provisions and other liabilities such as trade payables and accruals.

chapter: 16 - Provisions, contingent liabilities and contingent assets (IAS 37)
text: 16.10 A provision is recognised where all of the following conditions are met:

chapter: 16 - Provisions, contingent liabilities and contingent assets (IAS 37)
text: - An entity has a present obligation (see para 16.11 onwards) as a result of a past event (see para 16.20 onwards).

chapter: 16 - Provisions, contingent liabilities and contingent assets (IAS 37)
text: - It is probable that an outflow of resources embodying economic benefits will be required to settle the obligation (see para 16.23 onwards).

chapter: 16 - Provisions, contingent liabilities and contingent assets (IAS 37)
text: - A reliable estimate can be made of the amount of the obligation (see para 16.25 onwards).

chapter: 16 - Provisions, contingent liabilities and contingent assets (IAS 37)
text: 16.11 A present obligation can arise from a legal agreement (a ‘legal obligation’) or might arise from an entity’s past practice, published policy or current statement (a ‘constructive obligation’).

chapter: 16 - Provisions, contingent liabilities and contingent assets (IAS 37)
text: 16.12 It will usually be straightforward to establish whether a legal obligation exists, because it derives either from a contract (through its explicit or implicit terms), from legislation or from the operation of the law.

chapter: 16 - Provisions, contingent liabilities and contingent assets (IAS 37)
text: 16.13 Proposed legislation moves through various stages before it is finally enacted. A proposed law only creates an obligation for which provision is made when it is virtually certain to be enacted as drafted. This means that an obligation to comply with legislation only arises when that legislation is enacted or virtually certain to be enacted. IAS 37 does not specify a single event to identify when enactment of a law is virtually certain.

chapter: 16 - Provisions, contingent liabilities and contingent assets (IAS 37)
text: 16.16 A constructive obligation might arise where a potentially obligating event has taken place (such as environmental damage), but where no legal obligation exists. The entity could create a constructive obligation by making a public statement that it will rectify the damage. text: Uncertainty as to whether a present obligation exists

chapter: 16 - Provisions, contingent liabilities and contingent assets (IAS 37)
text: 16.17 In rare circumstances, it might not be clear whether a past event results in a present obligation. In these situations, a past event gives rise to a present obligation if, after taking account of all the available evidence, it is more likely than not that a present obligation exists at the balance sheet date.

chapter: 16 - Provisions, contingent liabilities and contingent assets (IAS 37)
text: 16.18 IAS 37 requires that:

chapter: 16 - Provisions, contingent liabilities and contingent assets (IAS 37)
text: - Where it is more likely than not that a present obligation exists at the balance sheet date, the entity should recognise a provision (if the recognition criteria are met).

chapter: 16 - Provisions, contingent liabilities and contingent assets (IAS 37)
text: - Where it is more likely that no present obligation exists at the balance sheet date, the entity should disclose a contingent liability, unless the possibility of an outflow of resources embodying economic benefit is remote, in which case no disclosure is required (see para 16.31).

chapter: 16 - Provisions, contingent liabilities and contingent assets (IAS 37)
text: - It is sometimes unclear whether a present obligation exists in connection with litigation where the events are disputed by the parties. In this situation, it might be necessary for an entity to obtain an expert’s opinion to determine whether a present obligation exists.

chapter: 16 - Provisions, contingent liabilities and contingent assets (IAS 37)
text: 16.19 Further information might become available between the balance sheet date and the date on which an entity’s financial statements are finalised. Where this happens, that information should be taken into account in determining whether or not a present obligation exists at the balance sheet date. A provision should not be made at the period end where the obligating event occurs after the balance sheet date. See chapter 9 para 2 for further gui

text: 16.20 A liability exists only when something has happened in the past (a ‘past event’) to trigger a present obligation. The past event is known in IAS 37 as the ‘obligating event’. An ‘obligating event’ is “an event that creates a legal or constructive obligation that results in an entity having no realistic alternative to settling that obligation”. Many obligating events are obvious; for example, the obligating event giving rise to the need to m

text: 16.21 No obligation arises from a past event if there is a realistic possibility that the entity can avoid settlement. An entity has no realistic alternative to settling an obligation only where:

chapter: 16 - Provisions, contingent liabilities and contingent assets (IAS 37)
text: - the settlement of the obligation can be enforced by law; or

chapter: 16 - Provisions, contingent liabilities and contingent assets (IAS 37)
text: - the event, in the case of a constructive obligation, creates a valid expectation in others that the entity will discharge the obligation.

text: 16.23 Once it has been established that a present obligation exists as a result of a past event, it is necessary to determine whether it will result in a probable outflow of resources embodying economic benefits to settle the obligation. IAS 37 states that “an outflow of resources or other event is regarded as probable if the event is more likely than not to occur …”. No provision is necessary where the outflow is not probable, but a contingent l

chapter: 16 - Provisions, contingent liabilities and contingent assets (IAS 37)
text: 16.24 Obligations arising from a group of similar transactions should be considered together. IAS 37 requires the probability that an outflow of resources will be required in settlement to be determined by considering the class of obligations as a whole. A typical example of this is product warranties.

chapter: 16 - Provisions, contingent liabilities and contingent assets (IAS 37)
text: 16.25 In extremely rare cases, it will not be possible to make a reliable estimate of the obligation. In such cases, the liability is disclosed as a contingent liability. IAS 37 does not provide further guidance on what might be ‘extremely rare cases’.

chapter: 16 - Provisions, contingent liabilities and contingent assets (IAS 37)
text: 16.26 IAS 37 states that, in nearly all cases, an entity will be able to determine a range of possible outcomes and to make an estimate of an obligation that will be sufficiently reliable to use in recognising a provision. Judgement will be needed where the amount is uncertain. A variety of estimation techniques might be used to make the estimate (see para 16.47).

chapter: 16 - Provisions, contingent liabilities and contingent assets (IAS 37)
text: 16.27 Provisions should be based on circumstances at the balance sheet date but adjusted to reflect the current best estimate. The current best estimate will be based on information available up to the date when the financial statements are authorised for issue. If it is no longer probable that an outflow of economic benefits will be required to settle the obligation, the provision should be reversed.

chapter: 16 - Provisions, contingent liabilities and contingent assets (IAS 37)
text: 16.28 A provision should only be used for the expenditures for which it was originally recognised. Where the original provision was charged as an expense, any subsequent reversal should be credited to the same line in the income statement. Changes in provisions that were originally recognised as part of the cost of an asset are dealt with in EX 16.85.7.

text: 16.29 IAS 37 uses the term ‘contingent’ for liabilities and assets that are not recognised because their existence will be confirmed only by the occurrence or non-occurrence of one or more uncertain future events that are not wholly within the entity’s control. The term ‘contingent liability’ is also used for liabilities that do not meet the recognition criteria in IAS 37.

text: 16.40 A provision should be measured at the best estimate of the expenditure required to settle the present obligation at the balance sheet date.

chapter: 16 - Provisions, contingent liabilities and contingent assets (IAS 37)
text: 16.41 This is the amount that an entity would rationally pay to settle the obligation or to transfer it to a third party at the balance sheet date. It will sometimes be impossible to settle or transfer the obligation at the reporting date and, in these cases, entities often provide for the cost of fulfilling the obligation as an estimate of the amount that an entity would rationally pay to settle.

This re-assessment should include the estimated cash flows and the discount rate. A re-assessment should be undertaken at least once every reporting period. The discount rate should be a current rate (rather than a longer-term average) at each reporting date.

text: Expected disposal of assets

chapter: 16 - Provisions, contingent liabilities and contingent assets (IAS 37)
text: 16.52 The measurement of a provision should not take account of any gains from the expected disposal of assets, even if the expected disposal is closely linked to the event giving rise to the provision. For example, a restructuring provision cannot be reduced by an expected gain on disposal of a factory that is being sold as part of the restructuring. The gain is recognised when the factory is sold.

chapter: 16 - Provisions, contingent liabilities and contingent assets (IAS 37)
text: 16.53 Future operating losses do not meet the definition of a liability and the recognition criteria for provisions. This is because future operating losses do not result from a past event (see para 16.20). Therefore, a provision for termination of operations cannot include future operating losses up to the date of closure.

chapter: 16 - Provisions, contingent liabilities and contingent assets (IAS 37)

chapter: 16 - Provisions, contingent liabilities and contingent assets (IAS 37)
text: 16.54 Expected future operating losses are an indication that an impairment review is required in accordance with IAS 36. Such a review would determine whether those assets have suffered an impairment and need to be written down. Anticipated future operating losses might indicate that an entity has an onerous contract. Onerous contracts are covered in detail in paragraph 16.71 onwards.

chapter: 16 - Provisions, contingent liabilities and contingent assets (IAS 37)
text: Restructuring (paras 16.55 - 16.70)

chapter: 16 - Provisions, contingent liabilities and contingent assets (IAS 37)
text: 16.55 IAS 37 explains how to determine when an obligating event has occurred in connection with a restructuring. IAS 37 also applies to provisions for restructuring when there is a discontinued operation. Where a restructuring meets the definition of a discontinued operation in IFRS 5, additional disclosures might be required. Discontinued operations are dealt with in chapter 30 para 39.

chapter: 16 - Provisions, contingent liabilities and contingent assets (IAS 37)
text: 16.56 A ‘restructuring’ is:

chapter: 16 - Provisions, contingent liabilities and contingent assets (IAS 37)
text: “A programme that is planned and controlled by management, and materially changes either: (a) the scope of a business undertaken by an entity; or (b) the manner in which that business is conducted.”

chapter: 16 - Provisions, contingent liabilities and contingent assets (IAS 37)
text: 16.57 IAS 37 gives some examples of situations that fall within the restructuring definition:

chapter: 16 - Provisions, contingent liabilities and contingent assets (IAS 37)
text: - The sale or termination of a line of business.

chapter: 16 - Provisions, contingent liabilities and contingent assets (IAS 37)
text: - The closure of business locations or the relocation of business activities.

chapter: 16 - Provisions, contingent liabilities and contingent assets (IAS 37)
text: - Changes in management structure.

chapter: 16 - Provisions, contingent liabilities and contingent assets (IAS 37)
text: - Fundamental re-organisations that have a material effect on the nature and focus of the entity’s operations.

chapter: 16 - Provisions, contingent liabilities and contingent assets (IAS 37)
text: Applying the recognition criteria

chapter: 16 - Provisions, contingent liabilities and contingent assets (IAS 37)
text: 16.58 A restructuring provision is recognised only when an obligating event has arisen. The obligation for a restructuring is often constructive. A constructive restructuring obligation arises only when both of the conditions below exists:

chapter: 16 - Provisions, contingent liabilities and contingent assets (IAS 37)
text: - A detailed formal plan for the restructuring, which identifies at least:

chapter: 16 - Provisions, contingent liabilities and contingent assets (IAS 37)
text: - the business or part of a business concerned;

chapter: 16 - Provisions, contingent liabilities and contingent assets (IAS 37)
text: - the principal locations affected;

chapter: 16 - Provisions, contingent liabilities and contingent assets (IAS 37)
text: - the location, function and approximate number of employees who will be compensated for terminating their services;

chapter: 16 - Provisions, contingent liabilities and contingent assets (IAS 37)
text: - the expenditures that will be undertaken; and

chapter: 16 - Provisions, contingent liabilities and contingent assets (IAS 37)
text: - when the plan will be implemented.

chapter: 16 - Provisions, contingent liabilities and contingent assets (IAS 37)
text: - A valid expectation, in those affected, that the entity will carry out the restructuring by starting to implement that plan or announcing its main features to those affected by it.

chapter: 16 - Provisions, contingent liabilities and contingent assets (IAS 37)
text: 16.59 Evidence demonstrating that an entity has started to implement a restructuring plan includes:

chapter: 16 - Provisions, contingent liabilities and contingent assets (IAS 37)
text: - Public announcement of the plan’s main features.

chapter: 16 - Provisions, contingent liabilities and contingent assets (IAS 37)
text: 16.60 A constructive obligation arises from a public announcement only when it raises a valid expectation in employees (or their representatives), customers, suppliers or others affected by it in a ‘sufficiently specific manner’ that the entity has no alternative but to discharge its responsibilities.

chapter: 16 - Provisions, contingent liabilities and contingent assets (IAS 37)
text: FAQ 16.60.1 – Is an announcement of a restructuring plan to some of those parties affected by the plan sufficient to recognise a liability for the total expected restructuring provision?

chapter: 16 - Provisions, contingent liabilities and contingent assets (IAS 37)
text: 16.61 The announcement must therefore address the main features of the restructuring plan in a sufficiently specific manner to raise a valid expectation that the entity will carry out the restructuring.

chapter: 16 - Provisions, contingent liabilities and contingent assets (IAS 37)

chapter: 16 - Provisions, contingent liabilities and contingent assets (IAS 37)
text: 16.62 A management or board decision to restructure taken before the balance sheet date does not, in itself, give rise to a constructive obligation.

chapter: 16 - Provisions, contingent liabilities and contingent assets (IAS 37)
text: FAQ 16.62.1 – What are the implications of a management announcement of restructuring after the balance sheet date?

chapter: 16 - Provisions, contingent liabilities and contingent assets (IAS 37)
text: 16.63 A board decision and a formal plan might be all that is necessary to give rise to an obligation in some territories. This might also occur, for example, where the board includes worker representatives and management representatives.

chapter: 16 - Provisions, contingent liabilities and contingent assets (IAS 37)
text: FAQ 16.63.1 – What are the circumstances in which board approval crystallises the obligation?

chapter: 16 - Provisions, contingent liabilities and contingent assets (IAS 37)
text: 16.64 Many entity re-organisations take a number of years to complete. Some or all of the re-organisation might not be an obligation at the first year end following a board decision if the entity is realistically able to change its plans. It is unlikely that the plan will raise a sufficiently valid expectation on the part of others that the entity is committed to restructuring in these circumstances.

chapter: 16 - Provisions, contingent liabilities and contingent assets (IAS 37)
text: FAQ 16.64.1 – Does a restructuring that takes a long time to implement create a constructive obligation?

chapter: 16 - Provisions, contingent liabilities and contingent assets (IAS 37)
text: 16.65 An obligation to sell exists only when there is a binding sale agreement evidencing a commitment to sell part of the business. An entity has an obligation for restructuring related to the sale only when it has found a purchaser and signed an unconditional contract. The unconditional sale agreement must be signed before the year end for an obligation to arise at the year end.

chapter: 16 - Provisions, contingent liabilities and contingent assets (IAS 37)
text: 16.66 It might be necessary to consider the carrying value of the cash-generating unit to which the operations relate in the period between the board decision and the unconditional contract, particularly if management expects a loss on disposal. Impairment reviews are considered in more detail in chapter 24 para 9.

chapter: 16 - Provisions, contingent liabilities and contingent assets (IAS 37)
text: 16.67 The sale of an operation might be a small part of a larger restructuring, in which case a constructive obligation might arise for other aspects of the restructuring plan before a formal sale agreement has been reached.

chapter: 16 - Provisions, contingent liabilities and contingent assets (IAS 37)
text: 16.68 A restructuring provision should include only the direct expenditures arising from the restructuring, which are those that are both:

chapter: 16 - Provisions, contingent liabilities and contingent assets (IAS 37)
text: - necessarily entailed by the restructuring; and

chapter: 16 - Provisions, contingent liabilities and contingent assets (IAS 37)
text: - not associated with the ongoing activities of the entity.

chapter: 16 - Provisions, contingent liabilities and contingent assets (IAS 37)
text: 16.69 Retraining or relocating continuing staff, marketing, or investment in new systems and distribution networks should not be included in a restructuring provision. This is because these costs relate to the future conduct of the business; they do not represent an obligation arising from a past event.

chapter: 16 - Provisions, contingent liabilities and contingent assets (IAS 37)
text: 16.70 Employee termination benefits are often lump-sum payments, but can also include enhancement of pensions and salary until the end of a specified period if the employee renders no further service that provides economic benefits to the entity. Employee termination benefits are dealt with by IAS 19 and considered in detail in chapter 12 para 4.

chapter: 16 - Provisions, contingent liabilities and contingent assets (IAS 37)
text: 16.71 An onerous contract is a contract under which the unavoidable costs of meeting the obligations under the contract exceed the economic benefits expected to be received under it. The present obligation under an onerous contract is recognised and measured as a provision.

chapter: 16 - Provisions, contingent liabilities and contingent assets (IAS 37)

chapter: 16 - Provisions, contingent liabilities and contingent assets (IAS 37)
text: 16.72 ‘Unavoidable costs’ under a contract are defined as being the least net cost of exiting the contract. This will be the lower of the cost to exit or breach the contract and the cost of fulfilling it.

For example, if a levy is triggered as an entity earns revenues in a specific market in the current period, the liability is recognised in the current period as the entity earns those revenues.

chapter: 16 - Provisions, contingent liabilities and contingent assets (IAS 37)
text: Management should reverse the provision and recognise the reversal in the income statement where the expense was charged. chapter: 16 - Provisions, contingent liabilities and contingent assets (IAS 37)

chapter: 16 - Provisions, contingent liabilities and contingent assets (IAS 37)
text: An entity should recognise an obligation (and an expense) before recognising a related reimbursement (for example, insurance recoveries). chapter: 16 - Provisions, contingent liabilities and contingent assets (IAS 37)
text: There is no guidance within IAS 37 about the risks that are specific to the liability.

chapter: 16 - Provisions, contingent liabilities and contingent assets (IAS 37)
text: In March 2011 the IFRS IC issued an agenda decision, which noted that IAS 37 does not state whether own credit risk should be included in the measurement of the provision, but that predominant practice is to exclude it. These suggest that own credit risk should be excluded from the measurement

chapter: 16 - Provisions, contingent liabilities and contingent assets (IAS 37)

text: Reference to standard: IAS 37 para 47 Reference to standing text: 16.49

chapter: 16 - Provisions, contingent liabilities and contingent assets (IAS 37)
text: What factors might impact setting the discount rate?

chapter: 16 - Provisions, contingent liabilities and contingent assets (IAS 37)
text: Judgement should be applied consistently when assessing an appropriate discount rate for provisions under IAS 37. The following principles should be followed:

chapter: 16 - Provisions, contingent liabilities and contingent assets (IAS 37)
text: - Adjusting the discount rate to reflect risks specific to the liability should generally reduce the discount rate from the risk-free rate and lead to an increase in a ‘riskier’ liability.

chapter: 16 - Provisions, contingent liabilities and contingent assets (IAS 37)
text: - Assumptions regarding inflation and the possible impact on future cash flows should be consistent with any inflation assumption implicit in yields underlying the discount rate.

chapter: 16 - Provisions, contingent liabilities and contingent assets (IAS 37)
text: - The starting point and process for determining a discount rate should be consistent from year to year, unless there is a change in circumstances.

chapter: 16 - Provisions, contingent liabilities and contingent assets (IAS 37)
text: - The consistency of the assumptions used should be considered. For example, the yield on high-quality corporate bonds is used to estimate the discount rate for employee benefit obligations. The risk-free rate that is used as the starting point to determine the discount rate for a provision should typically be lower, since IAS 19 does not require a risk-free rate.

chapter: 16 - Provisions, contingent liabilities and contingent assets (IAS 37)
text: - When looking at relatively short-term obligations, consider the materiality of any time value; with low interest rates (whether positive or negative), discounting might not be material.

chapter: 16 - Provisions, contingent liabilities and contingent assets (IAS 37)
text: FAQ 16.50.1 – What discount rate should be used to calculate the borrowing costs that arise from the unwinding of a provision?

chapter: 16 - Provisions, contingent liabilities and contingent assets (IAS 37)
text: Reference to standard: IAS 37 para 60 Reference to standing text: 16.50

chapter: 16 - Provisions, contingent liabilities and contingent assets (IAS 37)
text: The risk-free pre-tax rate reflects the time value of money. Therefore, the same rate should be used to unwind discount and determine the borrowing costs. The discount rate might sometimes be adjusted to remove inflation, when discounting real cash flows, or to reflect risk when risk has not been taken into consideration in the cash flows. How is the discount unwound when the discount rate has been adjusted?

chapter: 16 - Provisions, contingent liabilities and contingent assets (IAS 37)
text: In our opinion, irrespective of the discount rate used to calculate the present value of the provision, the borrowing cost is calculated using the weighted average outstanding liability during the reporting period (before taking account of discounting) and the risk-free pre-tax rate. IAS 37 requires that only the increase in the value of a provision as a result of the passage of time is to be taken to borrowing costs.

chapter: 16 - Provisions, contingent liabilities and contingent assets (IAS 37)
text: Changes in the estimated cash flow and discount rate could also result in changes in the amount of provision as of each reporting date. IAS 37 provides no guidance about changes in the estimated cash flows and discount rates. However, the resulting adjustment is a re-assessment of the provision and the movement should not be charged or credited as a borrowing cost. It should be taken to operating costs.

chapter: 16 - Provisions, contingent liabilities and contingent assets (IAS 37)
text: However, there is an exception for provisions for decommissioning obligations where IFRIC 1 applies. The effect of any changes in estimated cash flows and discount rates should be added to (or deducted from) the related asset, and the resulting carrying value should be depreciated prospectively over its remaining life. Also see EX 16.85.7 for further guidance on decommissioning obligations.

chapter: 16 - Provisions, contingent liabilities and contingent assets (IAS 37)
text: Paragraphs 72 and 73 of IAS 37 explain that a public announcement of a detailed plan to restructure constitutes a constructive obligation only if it is made in such a way and in sufficient detail that it gives rise to valid expectations in other parties that the entity will carry out the restructuring.

However, the principles in IAS 37 related to a restructuring require liabilities to be recognised only where there is a present obligation on the part of the entity. text: FAQ 16.61.1 – Is an announcement of an intention sufficient to recognise a restructuring provision?

chapter: 16 - Provisions, contingent liabilities and contingent assets (IAS 37)
text: Reference to standard: IAS 37 paras 73, 75 Reference to standing text: 16.61

chapter: 16 - Provisions, contingent liabilities and contingent assets (IAS 37)
text: Entity A’s management has prepared a plan for a re-organisation of its operations. The board has approved the plan, which involves closing ten of entity A’s 50 retail outlets. Management will conduct further analysis before deciding which outlets to close. Management has announced its intentions publicly and believes that this has given rise to a valid expectation for those affected. Should a provision for restructuring costs be recognised?

chapter: 16 - Provisions, contingent liabilities and contingent assets (IAS 37)
text: No, a provision for restructuring should not be recognised. A constructive obligation arises only when an entity has both a detailed formal plan for restructuring and makes an announcement of the plan to those affected by it. The plan does not provide sufficient detail (for example, the principal locations affected) that would permit recognition of a constructive obligation.

chapter: 16 - Provisions, contingent liabilities and contingent assets (IAS 37)
text: An entity is planning a head office restructuring. The year end is 31 March 20X1. The entity announced the restructuring, including the functions and the number of employees likely to be affected, before the year end (say, in January 20X1). But there is a 90-day consultation period, so individual employees were not notified by the year end. Can the entity provide for the restructuring costs at 31 March 20X1?

chapter: 16 - Provisions, contingent liabilities and contingent assets (IAS 37)
text: IAS 37 states that a public announcement of a detailed plan to restructure constitutes a constructive obligation to restructure only if it is made in such a way and in sufficient detail (that is, setting out the main features of the plan) that it gives rise to valid expectations in other parties – such as customers, suppliers and employees (or their representatives) – that the entity will carry out the restructuring.

chapter: 16 - Provisions, contingent liabilities and contingent assets (IAS 37)
text: Our view is that it is not necessary for individual employees to have been notified at the year end. The notification of employee representatives could create a constructive obligation. It will be necessary to consider what is involved in the specific consultation. chapter: 16 - Provisions, contingent liabilities and contingent assets (IAS 37)
text: FAQ 16.62.1 – What are the implications of a management announcement of restructuring after the balance sheet date?

chapter: 16 - Provisions, contingent liabilities and contingent assets (IAS 37)
text: Reference to standard: IAS 37 paras 73, 75 Reference to standing text: 16.62

chapter: 16 - Provisions, contingent liabilities and contingent assets (IAS 37)
text: An entity has prepared a formal plan for a re-organisation involving site closures and redundancies. The plan has been approved by the board at the year end, but the entity will not implement or announce the re-organisation until after the year end. What are the implications of a management announcement of restructuring after the balance sheet date?

chapter: 16 - Provisions, contingent liabilities and contingent assets (IAS 37)
text: There is no constructive obligation, even if there is an announcement after the entity’s year end but before its financial statements are approved. The announcement is a non-adjusting post balance sheet event and there was no commitment to restructure at the year end. The entity could change its plans completely after the year end.

chapter: 16 - Provisions, contingent liabilities and contingent assets (IAS 37)
text: A constructive obligation would exist if the entity has raised a valid expectation in those affected by beginning to implement the re-organisation by the end of the year (for example, by scrapping the plant or informing employees and suppliers of the re-organisation), despite the absence of a formal announcement.

chapter: 16 - Provisions, contingent liabilities and contingent assets (IAS 37)
text: What are the circumstances in which board approval crystallises the obligation?

chapter: 16 - Provisions, contingent liabilities and contingent assets (IAS 37)
text: Where employees have been consulted about the restructuring, and the restructuring plan has been developed with their participation, board approval will crystallise an obligation when the decision has been made and it has been communicated to the entity’s employees.

chapter: 16 - Provisions, contingent liabilities and contingent assets (IAS 37)
text: An obligation might also arise from a board decision where negotiations for the sale of part of the business have been agreed with a purchaser, but the contract is subject to board approval, because the agreement will be unconditional once the decision is made.

chapter: 16 - Provisions, contingent liabilities and contingent assets (IAS 37)
text: How should the term ‘economic benefits expected to be received’ be understood?

chapter: 16 - Provisions, contingent liabilities and contingent assets (IAS 37)
text: In our view, the term ‘economic benefits expected to be received’ should usually be construed to include both direct and indirect benefits under the contract.

chapter: 16 - Provisions, contingent liabilities and contingent assets (IAS 37)
text: An entity might, for example, knowingly choose to enter into a contract with a customer to supply goods or services to them at a price lower than cost because the seller is obtaining some indirect benefits as well as the cash consideration from the customer. The benefits that might be obtained over the period of such an arrangement might include building a relationship with potential customers or additional know-how about production of the goods

chapter: 16 - Provisions, contingent liabilities and contingent assets (IAS 37)
text: FAQ 16.72.1 – Is it necessary to include overheads to determine whether a contract is onerous and to measure any resulting provision?

chapter: 16 - Provisions, contingent liabilities and contingent assets (IAS 37)
text: Reference to standard: IAS 37 para 68 Reference to standing text: 16.72

chapter: 16 - Provisions, contingent liabilities and contingent assets (IAS 37)
text: Is it necessary to include overheads to determine whether a contract is onerous and to measure any resulting provision?

chapter: 16 - Provisions, contingent liabilities and contingent assets (IAS 37)
text: Not necessarily. IAS 37 defines an onerous contract as a contract in which the unavoidable costs of meeting the obligations under the contract exceed the economic benefits expected to be received under it. The unavoidable costs under a contract reflect the least net cost of exiting from the contract, which is the lower of the cost of fulfilling the contract and any compensation or penalties arising from failure to fulfil it.

chapter: 16 - Provisions, contingent liabilities and contingent assets (IAS 37)
text: In May 2020, the IASB issued ‘Amendments to IAS 37, Onerous Contracts – Cost of Fulfilling a Contract’, which clarified that the cost of fulfilling a contract comprises the costs that relate directly to a contract, consisting of both the incremental costs of fulfilling that contract, such as direct labour and materials, and an allocation of other costs that relate directly to fulfilling contracts, such as an allocation of the depreciation charge

chapter: 16 - Provisions, contingent liabilities and contingent assets (IAS 37)
text: However, until the amendment is effective, given that the current standard does not include specific guidance on the cost of fulfilling a contract, entities have a policy choice to define the cost of fulfilling a contract as either:

chapter: 16 - Provisions, contingent liabilities and contingent assets (IAS 37)
text: - only the incremental costs required to satisfy the obligation;

chapter: 16 - Provisions, contingent liabilities and contingent assets (IAS 37)
text: - or both the incremental costs as well as an allocation of other costs that relate directly to fulfilling contracts (that is, in line with the amendment described above).

chapter: 16 - Provisions, contingent liabilities and contingent assets (IAS 37)
text: What are assets dedicated to a contract?

chapter: 16 - Provisions, contingent liabilities and contingent assets (IAS 37)
text: In our view, an asset is only dedicated to a contract if there is a contractual requirement to use a specific asset or no other asset can be used.

chapter: 16 - Provisions, contingent liabilities and contingent assets (IAS 37)
text: When there appears to be an onerous contract, assets dedicated to the contract should first be tested for impairment. An onerous contract provision is recognised for any excess of unavoidable costs over expected benefits after the assets have been tested for impairment.

text: How should a provision for long-term purchase contract be assessed?

chapter: 16 - Provisions, contingent liabilities and contingent assets (IAS 37)
text: The examples that follow illustrate when a contract is onerous, whether dedicated assets need to be impaired, and how payments in relation to various contract terms or termination of contracts should be dealt with in the financial statements.

chapter: 16 - Provisions, contingent liabilities and contingent assets (IAS 37)
text: Example 1 – Contract not onerous

chapter: 16 - Provisions, contingent liabilities and contingent assets (IAS 37)
text: An entity has a contract to purchase one million units of gas at 23c per unit, giving a contract price of C230,000. The current market price for a similar contract is 16c per unit, giving a price of C160,000. The gas will be used to generate electricity, which will be sold at a profit.

chapter: 16 - Provisions, contingent liabilities and contingent assets (IAS 37)
text: The economic benefits from the contract include the benefits to the entity of using the gas in its business and, because the electricity will be sold at a profit, the contract is not onerous.

chapter: 16 - Provisions, contingent liabilities and contingent assets (IAS 37)
text: Example 2 – Impairment of assets

chapter: 16 - Provisions, contingent liabilities and contingent assets (IAS 37)
text: The contract’s terms and market prices are the same as in example 1. However, the electricity is sold at a loss, and the entity makes an overall operating loss. All of the gas purchased by the entity is used to generate electricity using dedicated assets. The electricity is sold to a wide range of customers.

chapter: 16 - Provisions, contingent liabilities and contingent assets (IAS 37)
text: The entity first considers whether the assets used to generate electricity are impaired. To the extent that there is still a loss after the assets have been written down, a provision for an onerous contract should be recorded.

chapter: 16 - Provisions, contingent liabilities and contingent assets (IAS 37)
text: Example 3 – Sale to third party at below purchase price

chapter: 16 - Provisions, contingent liabilities and contingent assets (IAS 37)
text: The contract terms and market price are the same as in example 1. However, in this example, the entity sells the gas under contract, which it no longer needs, to a third party for 18c per unit (5c below cost). The entity determines that it would have to pay C55,000 to exit the purchase contract.

chapter: 16 - Provisions, contingent liabilities and contingent assets (IAS 37)
text: The only economic benefit from the purchase contract costing C230,000 are the proceeds from the sales contract, which are C180,000. Therefore, a provision should be made for the onerous element of C50,000, being the lower of the cost of fulfilling the contract and the penalty cost of cancellation (C55,000).

chapter: 16 - Provisions, contingent liabilities and contingent assets (IAS 37)
text: Example 4 – Contract termination costs

chapter: 16 - Provisions, contingent liabilities and contingent assets (IAS 37)
text: In the year ended 31 December 20X1, an entity has a contract with a third party supplier. The entity wishes to terminate this contract in 20X2, even though it will still have two years to run, because it can enter into a cheaper contract with a new supplier. It will incur a charge for terminating the contract.

chapter: 16 - Provisions, contingent liabilities and contingent assets (IAS 37)
text: Does the entity have to provide in 20X1 for the contract that it will be exiting in 20X2?

chapter: 16 - Provisions, contingent liabilities and contingent assets (IAS 37)
text: A provision should be recognised only if the contract is onerous. If the goods received under the supply contract are sold at a profit, the contract is not onerous and provision should not be made in 20X1. The termination cost should be recognised as incurred in 20X2.

chapter: 16 - Provisions, contingent liabilities and contingent assets (IAS 37)

text: IFRIC 6 only addresses sales of historical household equipment; it does not address new waste or historical waste from sources other than private households. Entities will need to determine appropriate accounting policies for other types of waste in accordance with IAS 37’s general requirements and with IAS 8.

text: FAQ 16.77.1 – Are property taxes within the scope of IFRIC 21?

chapter: 16 - Provisions, contingent liabilities and contingent assets (IAS 37)
text: Reference to standard: IFRIC 21 para 2, IFRIC 21 para 4, IFRIC 21 para 5 Reference to standing text: 16.77

chapter: 16 - Provisions, contingent liabilities and contingent assets (IAS 37)
text: Entities often pay property taxes that are collected to fund public services, such as road maintenance.

chapter: 16 - Provisions, contingent liabilities and contingent assets (IAS 37)
text: Are such taxes within the scope of IFRIC 21?

chapter: 16 - Provisions, contingent liabilities and contingent assets (IAS 37)
text: Most property taxes are within the scope of IFRIC 21. The application of the interpretation to such taxes will generally require a detailed analysis of the arrangements for each tax, to determine when the obligation is recognised. Some payments might arise from a contractual agreement with the government, or they might be related to specific services received from the government. Such transactions would be outside the scope of IFRIC 21.

chapter: 16 - Provisions, contingent liabilities and contingent assets (IAS 37)
text: The scope of IFRIC 21 applies to levies not only paid to the government but also ‘imposed by’ the government. Such payments to third parties would therefore be within the scope of the interpretation (for example, a television tax paid by households to the national broadcaster).

text: EX 16.78.2 – Obligating event: generation of revenue

chapter: 16 - Provisions, contingent liabilities and contingent assets (IAS 37)
text: Reference to standard: IFRIC 21 para 8 Reference to standing text: 16.78

chapter: 16 - Provisions, contingent liabilities and contingent assets (IAS 37)
text: An entity reports annually on 31 December. A levy is triggered in full as soon as an entity generates revenue in 20X1. The levy is calculated based on a certain percentage of revenue generated by the entity in 20X0. The entity generated revenue in 20X0 and, in 20X1, starts to generate revenue on 3 January 20X1.

chapter: 16 - Provisions, contingent liabilities and contingent assets (IAS 37)
text: What is the obligating event in this case?

chapter: 16 - Provisions, contingent liabilities and contingent assets (IAS 37)
text: The obligating event, and thus the activity that triggers the payment of the levy, is the first generation of revenue in 20X1. The generation of revenue in 20X0 is not the activity that triggers the payment of the levy and the recognition of the liability. This is necessary, but not sufficient, for recognition. The amount of revenue generated in 20X0 only affects the measurement of the liability.

chapter: 16 - Provisions, contingent liabilities and contingent assets (IAS 37)
text: Legislation requires an entity to pay a levy if it owns property on 31 December. The property tax is 1% of the most recent property valuation, payable by the owner of the property on 31 December. The most recent property valuation is from 30 June of the same year.

chapter: 16 - Provisions, contingent liabilities and contingent assets (IAS 37)
text: When is the liability recognised?

chapter: 16 - Provisions, contingent liabilities and contingent assets (IAS 37)
text: The obligating event is ownership of the property on 31 December. The owner of the property has no present obligation to pay the levy during the year, because it could sell the property before 31 December, or the legislation could change. The liability is therefore recognised on 31 December. The date of the property valuation is not relevant. It is only used to measure the liability.

chapter: 16 - Provisions, contingent liabilities and contingent assets (IAS 37)
text: A levy is triggered if an entity is operating at the end of the annual reporting period. The levy is calculated based on total equity in the entity’s statement of financial position at the end of the annual reporting period. The end of the entity’s annual reporting period is 31 December 20X1.

chapter: 16 - Provisions, contingent liabilities and contingent assets (IAS 37)
text: What is the obligating event that gives rise to a liability to pay the levy?

chapter: 16 - Provisions, contingent liabilities and contingent assets (IAS 37)
text: The obligating event is the entity operating at the end of the annual reporting period. Before that point, the entity has no present obligation to pay a levy, even if it is economically compelled to continue to operate in the future.

chapter: 16 - Provisions, contingent liabilities and contingent assets (IAS 37)
text: Entity C has an annual reporting period that ends on 31 December. A levy is triggered only if entity C operates as a bank at the end of the annual reporting period. The amount of the levy is decided by reference to amounts in entity C’s statement of financial position at the end of the annual reporting period (say, 31 December 20X1).

chapter: 16 - Provisions, contingent liabilities and contingent assets (IAS 37)
text: The liability is recognised on 31 December 20X1, because the obligating event, as identified by the legislation, is to operate as a bank at the end of the annual reporting period. Before the end of the annual reporting period, entity C has no present obligation to pay a levy, even if it is economically compelled to continue to operate as a bank in the future. The activity that triggers the payment of the levy, as identified by the legislation, is

chapter: 16 - Provisions, contingent liabilities and contingent assets (IAS 37)
text: In the interim financial report, the liability is recognised in full in the interim period in which 31 December 20X1 falls, because the liability is recognised in full on 31 December 20X1. The same recognition principles should be applied in the annual financial statements and in the interim financial report.

chapter: 16 - Provisions, contingent liabilities and contingent assets (IAS 37)

At any point in 20X1, entity A has a present obligation to pay a levy on revenues generated to date. Entity A has no present obligation to pay a levy that will arise from generating revenues in the future. In other words, the obligating e

chapter: 16 - Provisions, contingent liabilities and contingent assets (IAS 37)

chapter: 16 - Provisions, contingent liabilities and contingent assets (IAS 37)
text: Legislation requires an entity to pay a levy if it owns property. The obligating event is not specified in the legislation. Entities have a choice of settling the tax either once a year or on a monthly basis. An entity that sells the property during the year would be required to settle the tax for the period up to the sale.

chapter: 16 - Provisions, contingent liabilities and contingent assets (IAS 37)
text: Would monthly recognition be appropriate?

chapter: 16 - Provisions, contingent liabilities and contingent assets (IAS 37)
text: Where the legislation does not specify the obligating event, entities will need to consider a range of factors, including for example payment terms and the impact on the obligation if the property is sold. The consideration of these factors in this case support recognition over time, even though the entity has an option to pay on an annual basis.

chapter: 16 - Provisions, contingent liabilities and contingent assets (IAS 37)

If revenue from the sales of product A exceeds that of product B at the interim date, entity X applies judgement to determine whether there is an obligation at the reporting date which cannot be realistically

chapter: 16 - Provisions, contingent liabilities and contingent assets (IAS 37)
text: A manufacturing entity imports once a year the raw materials used for production. The import is subject to import duties. How should the entity account for these?

chapter: 16 - Provisions, contingent liabilities and contingent assets (IAS 37)
text: The definition of the costs to purchase inventories includes non-refundable import duties. Thus the entity might need to recognise the liability for this levy at the obligating event, which is the date of the import; however, it should recognise the costs as part of the inventory purchased. Subsequently, this forms part of the cost of production and is released as the inventory is sold.

chapter: 16 - Provisions, contingent liabilities and contingent assets (IAS 37)
text: A government imposes a tax every time a property is purchased. How should the buyer account for this levy?

chapter: 16 - Provisions, contingent liabilities and contingent assets (IAS 37)
text: The definition of the purchase price of property, plant and equipment includes non-refundable purchase taxes. IFRIC 21 requires recognition of a liability at the obligating event, which is the date of the transfer of the property. The buyer should recognise the levy as part of the cost of the property, and it should thus recognise the expense over the time during which the property is depreciated.
