text: EX 16.85.1 – Applying the recognition criteria to litigation

chapter: 16 - Provisions, contingent liabilities and contingent assets (IAS 37)
text: Reference to standard: IAS 37 Reference to standing text: 16.85

chapter: 16 - Provisions, contingent liabilities and contingent assets (IAS 37)
text: Litigation is often used to illustrate how to apply certain aspects of IAS 37. The litigation process can be long and the outcome is sometimes unpredictable. Information relating to the litigation cases can be sensitive.

chapter: 16 - Provisions, contingent liabilities and contingent assets (IAS 37)
text: An entity might take legal action against another party or defend an action taken by a third party. Whichever position the entity is in, there will be costs associated with the litigation process (for example, lawyers’ fees and fees for expert witnesses) and finally costs (or proceeds) from either settling the action out of court or arising from the court’s decision. There might also be, for the party losing the action, an insurance claim and pot

chapter: 16 - Provisions, contingent liabilities and contingent assets (IAS 37)
text: The entity will need to consider carefully whether there is a present obligation and a probable outflow for which provision is required. The likelihood of settlement might initially be remote, so a contingent liability is not disclosed. Once an action has been started, the outflow might become possible, requiring disclosure, and then probable, requiring a provision to be recognised. The outcome will not be determined until the final judgment has

chapter: 16 - Provisions, contingent liabilities and contingent assets (IAS 37)
text: Example – Product liability

chapter: 16 - Provisions, contingent liabilities and contingent assets (IAS 37)
text: An entity sells an additive for leaded petrol engines, which allows customers to comply with new emissions requirements. Ten customers have claimed that the canisters were faulty and burst open on use, and the additive has burnt their hands. The entity is insured for such liabilities and does not expect to lose any money, even if the claims succeed.

chapter: 16 - Provisions, contingent liabilities and contingent assets (IAS 37)
text: The entity should first determine whether there is a present obligation. The past event is the sale to the customer of the potentially faulty goods. A present obligation exists if the canisters were faulty. Where the facts are unclear, the entity will determine whether it is probable that there is a present obligation, and this might entail seeking expert advice. In this example, the entity might contend that there is nothing wrong with the canis

chapter: 16 - Provisions, contingent liabilities and contingent assets (IAS 37)
text: Probable outflow of economic benefits

chapter: 16 - Provisions, contingent liabilities and contingent assets (IAS 37)
text: Once it has been established that a present obligation exists, it is then necessary to determine whether the outflow of economic benefits is probable. This judgement is based on whether it is more likely than not that there will be an outflow of economic benefits. It might be necessary to seek an expert’s advice to make these assessments. Further information that becomes available between the balance sheet date and the date on which an entity’s f

chapter: 16 - Provisions, contingent liabilities and contingent assets (IAS 37)
text: When there is a present obligation and an outflow is probable, the next step is to decide whether the entity can estimate the possible outcomes reliably. Again, the entity might need to seek an expert’s advice. IAS 37 mentions that it is only in extremely rare cases that no reliable estimate can be made.

chapter: 16 - Provisions, contingent liabilities and contingent assets (IAS 37)
text: Once it is determined that a provision should be recognised, the next question is measurement. It is helpful here to consider the simple ‘year end’ test. If the entity stopped trading at its year end, how much would it have to pay to settle the obligation? The entity will need to consider the risk and uncertainties associated with the case. This will obviously depend on the possible outcome of the claim. For example, if the entity decided that it

chapter: 16 - Provisions, contingent liabilities and contingent assets (IAS 37)
text: Considerations relating to legal cost

chapter: 16 - Provisions, contingent liabilities and contingent assets (IAS 37)
text: In our view, no liability for legal costs should be recognised until the lawyers have rendered services. Therefore, legal costs cannot be recognised where the provision for the underlying legal claim is not recognised. However, where management determines that a provision should be recognised for the underlying legal claim, it might be appropriate to include an estimate of future direct and incremental legal costs within the provision if a third

chapter: 16 - Provisions, contingent liabilities and contingent assets (IAS 37)
text: A receivable for insurance recovery is recognised where it is virtually certain that it will be received if the entity settles the obligation. If the receipt is not virtually certain, a contingent asset is disclosed. An insurance recovery is typically virtually certain of receipt once it has been accepted by the insurance company.

chapter: 16 - Provisions, contingent liabilities and contingent assets (IAS 37)
text: In the entity’s financial statements, its provision for this litigation and related receivable for insurance recovery might need to be disclosed. In addition to the movement of this provision, a brief description of the nature, expected timing of settlement and indication of the uncertainties needs to be disclosed.

chapter: 16 - Provisions, contingent liabilities and contingent assets (IAS 37)
text: The disclosures required might seriously prejudice the entity’s position in the litigation. In those extremely rare cases, the entity can be exempted from the above disclosure. However, it needs to disclose the general nature of the dispute and the reason why the information has not been disclosed (see FAQ 16.88.1).

chapter: 16 - Provisions, contingent liabilities and contingent assets (IAS 37)
text: EX 16.85.2 – Applying the recognition criteria to warranties

chapter: 16 - Provisions, contingent liabilities and contingent assets (IAS 37)
text: Reference to standard: IAS 37 Reference to standing text: 16.85

chapter: 16 - Provisions, contingent liabilities and contingent assets (IAS 37)
text: A warranty is often provided to customers in conjunction with the sale of goods or services. The nature of the warranty can vary for different entities, industries, products or contracts. The warranty obligation can arise either through the operation of the law (contract or statute) or through an entity’s stated policies or practices (as explained in para 16.11 onwards).

chapter: 16 - Provisions, contingent liabilities and contingent assets (IAS 37)
text: If an item sold proves to have been defective at the time of sale (usually based on evidence coming to light within a standard period), the purchaser might have the right to require the seller to rectify the defect or replace the faulty item. Such a warranty is considered to be an ‘assurance-type warranty’ that relates to the condition of the item sold at the date of sale. It is not usually considered separable from the sale of goods. These warra

chapter: 16 - Provisions, contingent liabilities and contingent assets (IAS 37)
text: A service-type warranty goes further than an assurance-type warranty by providing a customer with services in addition to the assurance that the product will function as expected. Service-type warranties are normally sold separately and are considered as a separable component of the transaction. These warranties are accounted for in accordance with IFRS 15 and are further considered in chapter 11 para 219 onwards.

chapter: 16 - Provisions, contingent liabilities and contingent assets (IAS 37)
text: Provision for an assurance-type warranty is recognised at the time of sale on a portfolio basis. The principles included in the example given in IAS 37 are explained below.

chapter: 16 - Provisions, contingent liabilities and contingent assets (IAS 37)
text: Example 1 – Product repairs or replacement

chapter: 16 - Provisions, contingent liabilities and contingent assets (IAS 37)
text: An entity sells gardening merchandise. It warrants at the time of the sale that it will make good, by repair or replacement, manufacturing defects that become apparent within one year from the date of sale. Its past experience shows that it does receive warranty claims on these products.

chapter: 16 - Provisions, contingent liabilities and contingent assets (IAS 37)
text: A provision should be recognised because:

chapter: 16 - Provisions, contingent liabilities and contingent assets (IAS 37)
text: - A contractual obligation exists.

chapter: 16 - Provisions, contingent liabilities and contingent assets (IAS 37)
text: - The obligating event is the sale of the product.

chapter: 16 - Provisions, contingent liabilities and contingent assets (IAS 37)
text: - The costs of repair do not relate to the entity’s future operations.

chapter: 16 - Provisions, contingent liabilities and contingent assets (IAS 37)
text: - Past experience confirms that it is more likely than not that the obligation will result in an outflow of economic benefits.

chapter: 16 - Provisions, contingent liabilities and contingent assets (IAS 37)
text: - A reliable estimate of the obligation can be made from the entity’s previous claims experience.

chapter: 16 - Provisions, contingent liabilities and contingent assets (IAS 37)
text: The entity would typically use its experience of past claims to estimate the amount of the provision.

chapter: 16 - Provisions, contingent liabilities and contingent assets (IAS 37)
text: Example 2 – Insured warranty obligation

chapter: 16 - Provisions, contingent liabilities and contingent assets (IAS 37)
text: The facts are the same as in example 1, except that the entity makes a payment to a third party insurer, which insures the risk. In the event of a claim by a customer, the entity would claim a corresponding amount from the insurer.

chapter: 16 - Provisions, contingent liabilities and contingent assets (IAS 37)
text: Provision would be made for the warranty for the reasons given in example 1. The existence of the insurance arrangement does not mean that the entity can ignore the warranty obligation. The customer has recourse directly to the entity for the warranty. The entity, in turn, has a claim on the insurer, but this does not remove the entity’s obligation to its customer.

chapter: 16 - Provisions, contingent liabilities and contingent assets (IAS 37)
text: The entity therefore recognises a provision for the warranty obligation. It will also consider whether or not it can recognise a recovery from its insurer. It cannot recognise a separate receivable for such claims, unless it is virtually certain that it will recover in the event that warranty claims are settled. If it is not virtually certain but is probable, the entity should disclose a contingent asset.

chapter: 16 - Provisions, contingent liabilities and contingent assets (IAS 37)
text: An example of how to measure a provision for warranty claims is given in FAQ 16.47.1.

chapter: 16 - Provisions, contingent liabilities and contingent assets (IAS 37)
text: EX 16.85.3 – Applying the recognition criteria to refunds

chapter: 16 - Provisions, contingent liabilities and contingent assets (IAS 37)
text: Reference to standard: IAS 37 Reference to standing text: 16.85

chapter: 16 - Provisions, contingent liabilities and contingent assets (IAS 37)
text: Many entities have refund policies which go beyond the customers’ rights under consumer law. A number of retailers, for example, give cash refunds for products returned, whether or not they are defective, whereas others make cash refunds even where the customer does not have the receipt showing when the goods were purchased.

chapter: 16 - Provisions, contingent liabilities and contingent assets (IAS 37)
text: These policies might have been applied in such a way and for so long that customers expect that they will continue.

chapter: 16 - Provisions, contingent liabilities and contingent assets (IAS 37)
text: IAS 37 includes an example which considers how such refund policies should be dealt with:

chapter: 16 - Provisions, contingent liabilities and contingent assets (IAS 37)
text: Example 1 – Refund obligations based on past practice

chapter: 16 - Provisions, contingent liabilities and contingent assets (IAS 37)
text: A retail entity has a policy of refunding purchases by dissatisfied customers, even where it is under no legal obligation to do so. It has adopted this policy for a number of years, and the policy is well known to its customers.

chapter: 16 - Provisions, contingent liabilities and contingent assets (IAS 37)
text: The entity should recognise a provision because:

chapter: 16 - Provisions, contingent liabilities and contingent assets (IAS 37)
text: - It has a present constructive obligation.

chapter: 16 - Provisions, contingent liabilities and contingent assets (IAS 37)
text: - The obligating event is the sale of the goods, which has raised a valid expectation on the part of its customers from which the entity cannot realistically withdraw.

chapter: 16 - Provisions, contingent liabilities and contingent assets (IAS 37)
text: - The obligation does not relate to costs of future operations.

chapter: 16 - Provisions, contingent liabilities and contingent assets (IAS 37)
text: - Past experience confirms that it is more likely than not that the obligation will result in an outflow of economic benefits.

chapter: 16 - Provisions, contingent liabilities and contingent assets (IAS 37)
text: - A reliable estimate of the obligation can be made on the basis of past refunds.

chapter: 16 - Provisions, contingent liabilities and contingent assets (IAS 37)
text: An entity might sometimes be required to recall faulty goods. The example below considers the implications where goods sold prior to the period end are recalled after the period end.

chapter: 16 - Provisions, contingent liabilities and contingent assets (IAS 37)
text: Example 2 – Product recalls

chapter: 16 - Provisions, contingent liabilities and contingent assets (IAS 37)
text: A retailer has to make a product recall on goods sold before its year end, because the goods have subsequently been found to be faulty. The recall notice was issued after the year end. Costs of the recall can be recovered from the entity’s supplier under the retailer’s supply contract.

chapter: 16 - Provisions, contingent liabilities and contingent assets (IAS 37)
text: Does the retailer need to make a provision at the year end for the recall costs?

chapter: 16 - Provisions, contingent liabilities and contingent assets (IAS 37)
text: Provision for the costs of the recall should be made at the year end. The obligating event was the sale of the faulty goods, and not the recall notice. At the balance sheet date, the entity has an obligation to recall the faulty goods, there is a probable outflow and the obligation can be measured reliably.

chapter: 16 - Provisions, contingent liabilities and contingent assets (IAS 37)
text: How should the retailer account for the recovery from the supplier?

chapter: 16 - Provisions, contingent liabilities and contingent assets (IAS 37)
text: Recovery of the costs from the supplier can only be recorded if it is virtually certain that the costs will be recovered in the event that the recall expenditure is incurred. If it is not virtually certain (for example, if there was some doubt as to the legal enforceability of the recovery or the ability of the supplier to pay), but is probable, the recovery of the costs is disclosed as a contingent asset.

chapter: 16 - Provisions, contingent liabilities and contingent assets (IAS 37)
text: EX 16.85.4 – Applying the recognition criteria to major repairs and maintenance in different situations

chapter: 16 - Provisions, contingent liabilities and contingent assets (IAS 37)
text: Reference to standard: IAS 37 Reference to standing text: 16.85

chapter: 16 - Provisions, contingent liabilities and contingent assets (IAS 37)
text: Often, entities incur major repairs and maintenance to their own assets or leased assets under IFRS 16. Do they need to recognise a provision for such expenses? This is considered in the following examples.

chapter: 16 - Provisions, contingent liabilities and contingent assets (IAS 37)
text: It is highly unlikely that provision would ever be made for repairs and maintenance on owned assets, because it would not meet the recognition criteria in paragraph 14 of IAS 37. Entities have discretion over whether to incur the expenditure. It could avoid the expenditure, for example, by selling the asset. However, when an item of property, plant and equipment (‘PPE’) requires regular replacement or overhaul, the overhaul component should be de

chapter: 16 - Provisions, contingent liabilities and contingent assets (IAS 37)
text: Example 1 – Overhaul of PPE

chapter: 16 - Provisions, contingent liabilities and contingent assets (IAS 37)
text: An entity has a blast furnace, for which the lining needs to be replaced every five years.

chapter: 16 - Provisions, contingent liabilities and contingent assets (IAS 37)
text: No provision can be made for replacement of the furnace lining before the entity incurs the expenditure; until that time, the entity has no present obligation, because it does not have to replace the lining. For example, it could avoid the obligation by shutting the blast furnace. No provision is made before the expenditure is incurred, but the blast furnace lining should be separately identified and depreciated over the period between replacemen

chapter: 16 - Provisions, contingent liabilities and contingent assets (IAS 37)
text: The cost and depreciation attributed to the original blast furnace lining should be removed once the cost of the new blast furnace lining has been capitalised.

chapter: 16 - Provisions, contingent liabilities and contingent assets (IAS 37)
text: Maintenance expenditure in respect of owned assets cannot be provided in advance of being incurred, even if there is an external requirement for maintenance of those assets. This is illustrated in the following example.

chapter: 16 - Provisions, contingent liabilities and contingent assets (IAS 37)
text: Example 2 – Covenants requiring maintenance

chapter: 16 - Provisions, contingent liabilities and contingent assets (IAS 37)
text: An entity has purchased some assets outright and borrowed from a bank to do so. The bank covenants include conditions that the entity should maintain the assets in good condition. Should the entity provide for maintenance on the owned assets because of the maintenance covenant?

chapter: 16 - Provisions, contingent liabilities and contingent assets (IAS 37)
text: Where an owned fixed asset is used as security for a loan, and the covenants require the asset to be maintained, there is no penalty as such in respect of non-maintenance. Of course, if the covenant is broken in any way, the bank could call its loan. The purpose of such a term is to ensure that the bank has sufficient security in case of default.

chapter: 16 - Provisions, contingent liabilities and contingent assets (IAS 37)
text: A failure to maintain an asset used for secured lending might trigger a repayment of the lending, which has already been recognised as a liability. It does not trigger a claim for compensation for the maintenance work. Because the entity can avoid the maintenance by repaying the loan, the entity does not have a present obligation. No provision should be recognised in this situation.

chapter: 16 - Provisions, contingent liabilities and contingent assets (IAS 37)
text: Maintenance requirements can also arise for leased assets and might be required as part of the lease terms.

chapter: 16 - Provisions, contingent liabilities and contingent assets (IAS 37)
text: Example 3 – Overhaul costs for leased assets

chapter: 16 - Provisions, contingent liabilities and contingent assets (IAS 37)
text: An entity leases a ship for 25 years. It has to obtain a certificate of seaworthiness, which entails the entity carrying out significant maintenance and overhaul work in a dry dock every five years. Without such a certificate, the ship cannot operate.

chapter: 16 - Provisions, contingent liabilities and contingent assets (IAS 37)
text: The ship cannot continue to operate without a certificate of seaworthiness, but this in itself does not obligate the entity to carry out the maintenance. It could, for example, decide to lay up the ship and not use it. The entity would consider the terms of the lease to determine whether there is anything that creates a contractual obligation. Where no obligation is created by the lease, there is no present obligation. No provision should be made

chapter: 16 - Provisions, contingent liabilities and contingent assets (IAS 37)
text: EX 16.85.5 – Applying the recognition criteria to lease dilapidations

chapter: 16 - Provisions, contingent liabilities and contingent assets (IAS 37)
text: Reference to standard: IAS 37 Reference to standing text: 16.85

chapter: 16 - Provisions, contingent liabilities and contingent assets (IAS 37)
text: Many property leases include tenant repairing clauses for dilapidations. These clauses typically require the tenant to return the property to the landlord at the end of the tenancy in a specified condition. Should a provision be made for the costs of repairing dilapidations over the tenancy period, or should these costs be expensed when the repairing work is undertaken?

chapter: 16 - Provisions, contingent liabilities and contingent assets (IAS 37)
text: The following example illustrates the issues.

chapter: 16 - Provisions, contingent liabilities and contingent assets (IAS 37)
text: Example – Repairs required under property lease terms

chapter: 16 - Provisions, contingent liabilities and contingent assets (IAS 37)
text: The entity is currently a tenant of a leased property and is due to vacate it in five years’ time. There is a clause in the tenancy agreement relating to work that must be undertaken before the property is vacated. There is also a clause that enables the landlord to recharge the tenant for costs related to repairing the building.

chapter: 16 - Provisions, contingent liabilities and contingent assets (IAS 37)
text: Provision should be made for the estimated costs of the repairs over the period of the tenancy, because:

chapter: 16 - Provisions, contingent liabilities and contingent assets (IAS 37)
text: - The tenant has a present contractual obligation, arising from the lease agreement.

chapter: 16 - Provisions, contingent liabilities and contingent assets (IAS 37)
text: - The obligating event is the wear and tear to the property, which arises over the period of the tenancy.

chapter: 16 - Provisions, contingent liabilities and contingent assets (IAS 37)
text: - The obligation arises from the wear and tear to the property, and is not related to future operating costs.

chapter: 16 - Provisions, contingent liabilities and contingent assets (IAS 37)
text: - It is probable that the obligation will result in an outflow of economic benefits.

chapter: 16 - Provisions, contingent liabilities and contingent assets (IAS 37)
text: - It is possible to make a reliable estimate of the obligation arising from the wear and tear.

chapter: 16 - Provisions, contingent liabilities and contingent assets (IAS 37)
text: - It should be clear from the lease whether or not an obligation exists. A provision should be recognised when any damage is identified.

chapter: 16 - Provisions, contingent liabilities and contingent assets (IAS 37)
text: EX 16.85.6 – Applying the recognition criteria to leasehold improvements

chapter: 16 - Provisions, contingent liabilities and contingent assets (IAS 37)
text: Reference to standard: IAS 37 Reference to standing text: 16.85

chapter: 16 - Provisions, contingent liabilities and contingent assets (IAS 37)
text: Some leases allow the tenant to improve the property by adding, for example, additional partitioning, but include obligations on the lessee to return the property at the end of the lease in its original state. This might entail dismantling the improvements.

chapter: 16 - Provisions, contingent liabilities and contingent assets (IAS 37)
text: Example – Returning property to its condition at lease inception

chapter: 16 - Provisions, contingent liabilities and contingent assets (IAS 37)
text: An entity has entered into a lease for a warehouse. It wishes to use the warehouse for office accommodation. The lease permits the entity to build a mezzanine floor and partition the building for offices at a cost of C1.5 million. The lease is for a period of 15 years and specifies that the property must be returned to the lessor in its original condition. The entity estimates that the present value of the cost of removing the improvements is C50

chapter: 16 - Provisions, contingent liabilities and contingent assets (IAS 37)

The entity has a present obligation under the lease to remove the improvements at the end of the lease term. The obligation arises when the entity completes the improvements, which is the past event. The present value of C500,000 should be recognised when the improvements are completed. The same amount should be recognise

chapter: 16 - Provisions, contingent liabilities and contingent assets (IAS 37)
text: EX 16.85.7 – Applying the recognition criteria to abandonment and decommissioning costs

chapter: 16 - Provisions, contingent liabilities and contingent assets (IAS 37)
text: Reference to standard: IAS 37 Reference to standing text: 16.85

chapter: 16 - Provisions, contingent liabilities and contingent assets (IAS 37)
text: Abandonment is the term used to describe: the plugging and abandonment of wells; the dismantlement of wellheads, production and transportation facilities; and restoration of producing areas in accordance with the licence requirements and the relevant legislation. These activities normally commence at the date when the facility ceases to produce, treat, transport or store saleable quantities of oil or gas.

chapter: 16 - Provisions, contingent liabilities and contingent assets (IAS 37)
text: Similar costs are incurred in other industries, such as: decommissioning costs in the electricity and nuclear industries; abandonment costs in the mining and other extractive industries; clean-up and restoration costs of landfill sites; and environmental clean-up costs in other industries.

chapter: 16 - Provisions, contingent liabilities and contingent assets (IAS 37)
text: Does the liability arise in the future when the asset is constructed or developed gradually over a period?

chapter: 16 - Provisions, contingent liabilities and contingent assets (IAS 37)
text: The creation of the asset typically results in a present obligation to incur abandonment and decommissioning costs.

chapter: 16 - Provisions, contingent liabilities and contingent assets (IAS 37)
text: IAS 37 includes an example of how the rules apply, and this example is explained below.

chapter: 16 - Provisions, contingent liabilities and contingent assets (IAS 37)
text: Example 1 – Decommissioning oil rigs and repairing environmental damage

chapter: 16 - Provisions, contingent liabilities and contingent assets (IAS 37)
text: An entity operates an oil field in the North Sea. Its operating licence requires it to remove the oil rig at the end of its production life and to restore the seabed. 90% of the costs of undertaking this work arise from the installation of the rig. A further 10% of the costs arise through the extraction of oil. The rig has been constructed at the balance sheet date, but no oil has been extracted.

chapter: 16 - Provisions, contingent liabilities and contingent assets (IAS 37)
text: A provision should be made for 90% of the costs of abandoning the rig, because:

chapter: 16 - Provisions, contingent liabilities and contingent assets (IAS 37)
text: - A present legal obligation exists because of the operating licence.

chapter: 16 - Provisions, contingent liabilities and contingent assets (IAS 37)
text: - The obligating event is installing the rig, which has caused the damage.

chapter: 16 - Provisions, contingent liabilities and contingent assets (IAS 37)
text: - The costs do not relate to the entity’s future operations; even if the rig is no longer operated after the balance sheet date, the costs would still have to be incurred.

chapter: 16 - Provisions, contingent liabilities and contingent assets (IAS 37)
text: - The obligation will result in an outflow of economic benefits.

chapter: 16 - Provisions, contingent liabilities and contingent assets (IAS 37)
text: - It is possible to make a reliable estimate of the costs.

chapter: 16 - Provisions, contingent liabilities and contingent assets (IAS 37)
text: The costs are treated as part of the cost of the oil rig to be depreciated over the production life of the rig.

chapter: 16 - Provisions, contingent liabilities and contingent assets (IAS 37)
text: There is no obligation to rectify the damage that will be caused by the extraction of the oil, until that oil is extracted. Provision for these costs will be recognised as the damage is caused (that is, as the oil is extracted).

text: How should subsequent remeasurement of the provision be accounted for?

text: Example 2 – How would a change in provisions affect the related assets from the decommissioning obligation?

chapter: 16 - Provisions, contingent liabilities and contingent assets (IAS 37)
text: An entity has constructed a nuclear facility for C100 million. It expects that the plant will run for the next 30 years. It has estimated, using existing technology, that the cost of decommissioning the plant will be C200 million following the end of plant operation and C100 million in 50 years’ time in today’s currency. For simplicity of this example, it has been assumed that the obligation arises on day 1 and decommissioning cost will take plac

After payment of C200 million, the obligation will be C41,460,000 at the end of year 30, which is the end of the useful life of the facility. In years 31 to 50, the discount for the provision is unwound at the risk-free rate as a borrowing cost until the obligation crystallises at the end of year 50. This means that the entity wi

chapter: 16 - Provisions, contingent liabilities and contingent assets (IAS 37)
text: Several assumptions are required to estimate the decommissioning cost. These assumptions will be reassessed each period until the asset is decommissioned. Management will consider, for example, developments in decommissioning technology.

chapter: 16 - Provisions, contingent liabilities and contingent assets (IAS 37)
text: Although there is no specific guidance in IAS 37, IFRIC 1 requires changes in the estimated cost of decommissioning or changes in the discount rate to be added to or deducted from the cost of the asset and to be depreciated prospectively over its remaining useful life. This method is consistent with the treatment of similar changes to estimates in IAS 16. See chapter 22 para 27 for further guidance on IFRIC 1.

chapter: 16 - Provisions, contingent liabilities and contingent assets (IAS 37)
text: Any amount deducted from the cost of the asset must not exceed the asset’s carrying amount. Any excess should be recognised immediately in the income statement. Management will need to consider whether any increase in the asset might be recoverable, in which case an impairment test will be performed.

chapter: 16 - Provisions, contingent liabilities and contingent assets (IAS 37)
text: Assume the facts (including discount rate) are the same as in example 2. At the end of year 10, the obligation is C100,120,000. The carrying value of the asset is C109,650,000 (accumulated amortisation of C54,820,000 having been charged, of which C21,490,000 relates to the decommissioning element of the asset). Researchers have found a new way of decommissioning. It is believed that this new method, which is far safer and less labour intensive, w

chapter: 16 - Provisions, contingent liabilities and contingent assets (IAS 37)
text: The net present value of the obligation should be reduced from C100,120,000 to C83,280,000 (representing the present value of C175 million in 30 years’ time and C50 million in 45 years’ time at a discount rate of 4.5%). The double entry is:

chapter: 16 - Provisions, contingent liabilities and contingent assets (IAS 37)
text: Whether the asset is held at cost or revalued once the asset has reached the end of its useful life, all changes to the estimated liability should be recognised in profit or loss in the period of the change.

chapter: 16 - Provisions, contingent liabilities and contingent assets (IAS 37)
text: EX 16.85.8 – Applying the recognition criteria to environmental liabilities

chapter: 16 - Provisions, contingent liabilities and contingent assets (IAS 37)
text: Reference to standard: IAS 37 Reference to standing text: 16.85

chapter: 16 - Provisions, contingent liabilities and contingent assets (IAS 37)
text: Environmental damage can occur in a number of ways, including contamination of land, pollution of rivers and waterways, emission of harmful gases into the atmosphere (see EX 16.85.9), and excavating holes and drilling in the ground. Some aspects of environmental damage are controlled by legislation, whereas others are not.

chapter: 16 - Provisions, contingent liabilities and contingent assets (IAS 37)
text: A present obligation can arise either from legislation (where damage that is controlled by legislation is caused) or from a constructive obligation (where an entity makes a statement that it will rectify damage or creates an obligation through an established practice of rectifying the damage).

chapter: 16 - Provisions, contingent liabilities and contingent assets (IAS 37)
text: Some obligating events can occur over a period of time (for example, where damage is caused by the extraction of oil and gas). This is in addition to the obligating event that might arise when an oil rig is first built.

chapter: 16 - Provisions, contingent liabilities and contingent assets (IAS 37)
text: IAS 37 covers these issues in a number of examples, which are explored below.

chapter: 16 - Provisions, contingent liabilities and contingent assets (IAS 37)
text: Example 1 – Environmental legislation due to be enacted

chapter: 16 - Provisions, contingent liabilities and contingent assets (IAS 37)
text: An oil company causes contamination, which it will clean up only when compelled to do so by law. No legislation currently exists that requires remediation but, at the entity’s year end, it is virtually certain that a draft law requiring clean-up will be enacted.

chapter: 16 - Provisions, contingent liabilities and contingent assets (IAS 37)
text: The entity should recognise a provision, because:

chapter: 16 - Provisions, contingent liabilities and contingent assets (IAS 37)
text: - There is a legal obligation, as it is virtually certain that the legislation will be enacted. [IAS 37 para 22].

chapter: 16 - Provisions, contingent liabilities and contingent assets (IAS 37)
text: - The obligating event is the contamination of the land.

chapter: 16 - Provisions, contingent liabilities and contingent assets (IAS 37)
text: - The related costs do not form part of the entity’s future operations.

chapter: 16 - Provisions, contingent liabilities and contingent assets (IAS 37)
text: - It is more likely than not that the obligation will result in an outflow of economic benefits.

chapter: 16 - Provisions, contingent liabilities and contingent assets (IAS 37)
text: - It will be possible to make a reliable estimate of the obligation.

chapter: 16 - Provisions, contingent liabilities and contingent assets (IAS 37)
text: If, at the balance sheet date, the draft legislation was not virtually certain to be enacted, no provision would be made, but the potential change in the law would be disclosed.

chapter: 16 - Provisions, contingent liabilities and contingent assets (IAS 37)
text: Example 2 – Published environmental policy

chapter: 16 - Provisions, contingent liabilities and contingent assets (IAS 37)
text: The facts are similar to example 1, except that there is no planned environmental legislation, but the entity has a published environmental policy under which it undertakes to clean up all contamination that it causes. The entity has a record of honouring its published policy.

chapter: 16 - Provisions, contingent liabilities and contingent assets (IAS 37)
text: The entity should recognise a provision, because:

chapter: 16 - Provisions, contingent liabilities and contingent assets (IAS 37)
text: - It has a present constructive obligation that arises from its commitment to the public at large by the publication of its environmental policies. It has raised a valid expectation that it will incur clean-up costs from which it cannot realistically withdraw.

chapter: 16 - Provisions, contingent liabilities and contingent assets (IAS 37)
text: - The obligating event is the contamination of the land.

chapter: 16 - Provisions, contingent liabilities and contingent assets (IAS 37)
text: - The related costs do not form part of the entity’s future operations.

chapter: 16 - Provisions, contingent liabilities and contingent assets (IAS 37)
text: - It is more likely than not that the obligation will result in an outflow of economic benefits.

chapter: 16 - Provisions, contingent liabilities and contingent assets (IAS 37)
text: - It will be possible to make a reliable estimate of the obligation.

chapter: 16 - Provisions, contingent liabilities and contingent assets (IAS 37)
text: Example 3 – Legislation in respect of future activity

chapter: 16 - Provisions, contingent liabilities and contingent assets (IAS 37)
text: A new law has been passed that requires smoke filters (that will not be capitalised by the entity) to be fitted to factories by the middle of the entity’s next year. The entity has not yet fitted the smoke filters.

chapter: 16 - Provisions, contingent liabilities and contingent assets (IAS 37)
text: The legislation has not yet come into operation, so there is no present legal obligation for the entity to fit the filters. The entity’s management has done nothing to suggest that a constructive obligation exists. Consequently, no provision should be made.

chapter: 16 - Provisions, contingent liabilities and contingent assets (IAS 37)
text: Example 4 – Legislation in force

chapter: 16 - Provisions, contingent liabilities and contingent assets (IAS 37)
text: The facts are the same as in example 3, except that the entity is now in the subsequent year and the law is effective, but the entity still has not fitted the filters.

chapter: 16 - Provisions, contingent liabilities and contingent assets (IAS 37)
text: The entity should not make a provision for the cost of fitting the filters (assuming that the smoke filters will not be capitalised). Even though it might appear that there is a present obligation, as the law compelling the filters to be fitted is now operational, no obligation arises for the cost of fitting the filters, because no obligating event has taken place (that is, the filters have not yet been fitted). However, a provision might still b

chapter: 16 - Provisions, contingent liabilities and contingent assets (IAS 37)
text: - There is present obligation for the penalties that the entity will incur for not complying with the legislation.

chapter: 16 - Provisions, contingent liabilities and contingent assets (IAS 37)
text: - The obligating event is the failure to comply with the law.

chapter: 16 - Provisions, contingent liabilities and contingent assets (IAS 37)
text: - The fines do not relate to future operations.

chapter: 16 - Provisions, contingent liabilities and contingent assets (IAS 37)
text: - It is more likely than not that the obligation will result in an outflow of economic benefits, based on an assessment of factors such as the stringency of the enforcement regime.

chapter: 16 - Provisions, contingent liabilities and contingent assets (IAS 37)
text: - It is possible to make a reliable estimate of the fines, based on factors such as whether the rates have been published.

chapter: 16 - Provisions, contingent liabilities and contingent assets (IAS 37)
text: Example 5 – Legislation in force in respect of past contamination

chapter: 16 - Provisions, contingent liabilities and contingent assets (IAS 37)
text: Health and safety legislation has been introduced that requires asbestos to be removed from all buildings. Where its existence is known, asbestos removal is required, whether the property is in use or operations have ceased. The legislation is effective from 31 December 20X2. Entity A owns a 20-year-old factory and has confirmed that it contains asbestos. The estimated cost of removing the asbestos is C70,000, plus a further C30,000 in lost profi

chapter: 16 - Provisions, contingent liabilities and contingent assets (IAS 37)
text: The health and safety legislation has been enacted, and so there is a requirement to remove the asbestos. The obligating (past) event is the contamination caused by the presence of the asbestos. The legal requirement to remove it creates an obligation. So, entity A should recognise a provision for C70,000, being the direct cost of removing the asbestos.

chapter: 16 - Provisions, contingent liabilities and contingent assets (IAS 37)
text: No provision should be made for the operating losses that will be incurred during the period of asbestos removal, because there is no obligation to incur these losses.

chapter: 16 - Provisions, contingent liabilities and contingent assets (IAS 37)
text: The existence of signed contracts does not affect the conclusion of whether to provide for the costs. The contracts are executory contracts, so no liability to the contractor arises until the contractor performs work under the contract.

chapter: 16 - Provisions, contingent liabilities and contingent assets (IAS 37)
text: The introduction of the new law does not create the obligating event on its own. It is the combination of the past contamination and the new law that creates the obligation to remove the asbestos. This can be contrasted with the smoke filters (in example 4 above), where there is no past contamination, and so the obligation created when the legislation comes into force is only for penalties and fines.

chapter: 16 - Provisions, contingent liabilities and contingent assets (IAS 37)
text: EX 16.85.9 – Detailed discussion of applying the recognition criteria to emissions obligations

chapter: 16 - Provisions, contingent liabilities and contingent assets (IAS 37)
text: Reference to standard: IAS 37 Reference to standing text: 16.85

chapter: 16 - Provisions, contingent liabilities and contingent assets (IAS 37)
text: Many jurisdictions have introduced cap and trade schemes to encourage a reduction in greenhouse gas emissions. The schemes generally involve the allocation of a limited number of allowances at the start of a compliance period and require entities to have sufficient allowances at the end of the compliance period to cover the volume of emissions made. Some schemes permit entities to purchase additional allowances (on top of their free allocation) o

chapter: 16 - Provisions, contingent liabilities and contingent assets (IAS 37)
text: The emission of greenhouse gases creates an obligation to deliver allowances. Entities recognise a liability (and related expense) in respect of this obligation to the extent of emissions made as at the balance sheet date. There are a number of accounting models that can be used for accounting for participation in these schemes. The liability’s measurement will depend on the accounting model used.

chapter: 16 - Provisions, contingent liabilities and contingent assets (IAS 37)
text: One model is the IFRIC 3 model, which dealt with the accounting for a ‘cap and trade’ emissions rights scheme. It required entities to account for the emissions allowances that they received from governments as intangible assets, recorded initially at fair value. chapter: 16 - Provisions, contingent liabilities and contingent assets (IAS 37)

However, in our view whenever emission rights are assets held for sale in the ordinary course of business, they fall under the definition of inventories and must be measured at the lower of cost or net realisable value in accordance with IAS 2. If the requirements for broker-traders apply to the entity, the emission rights are measured at fair v

chapter: 16 - Provisions, contingent liabilities and contingent assets (IAS 37)

Emissions allowances recognised as an asset should be tested for impairment where there are indicators of impairment, in accordance with the requirements of IAS 36, which is dealt with in chapter 24 para 9.

chapter: 16 - Provisions, contingent liabilities and contingent assets (IAS 37)

However, to the extent that the entity has entered into a forward contract to buy allowances at a fixed price on a future date, it is permissible to provide at the forward contracted rate (rather than the market rate), because this is the bes

text: Using the forward rate is not appropriate where the entity trades in these emission allowance. Once the entity commences trading, these instruments fall outside the ‘own use exemption’ in 2.4 of IFRS 9. The forward contracts will be within IFRS 9’s scope and are required to be measured at fair value.

chapter: 16 - Provisions, contingent liabilities and contingent assets (IAS 37)
text: Any provision based on the market rate could alternatively be based on a forward rate, provided the entity meets the ‘own use exemption’ in IFRS 9 with respect to its emissions allowances forward contracts.

chapter: 16 - Provisions, contingent liabilities and contingent assets (IAS 37)
text: The accounting policy chosen for emissions obligations (which should be consistently applied) will depend on the overall accounting model that is being used for emissions (including allowances).

chapter: 16 - Provisions, contingent liabilities and contingent assets (IAS 37)
text: Entities should make clear in their accounting policy note which approach is applied.

chapter: 16 - Provisions, contingent liabilities and contingent assets (IAS 37)
text: The ‘full market value’ approach (that is, the method set out in IFRIC 3) is illustrated in the following example.

chapter: 16 - Provisions, contingent liabilities and contingent assets (IAS 37)
text: Example – Emissions accounting

chapter: 16 - Provisions, contingent liabilities and contingent assets (IAS 37)
text: An entity participates in a ‘cap and trade’ scheme for emissions rights; on 1 January 20X6, it is allocated, free of charge, allowances to emit 10,000 tonnes of carbon dioxide during the calendar year 20X6, which is also its financial accounting period. The market price of an allowance (equivalent to one tonne of carbon dioxide) at 1 January 20X6 is C10, giving a fair value of C100,000.

chapter: 16 - Provisions, contingent liabilities and contingent assets (IAS 37)
text: At 30 June 20X6, the entity has emitted 6,000 tonnes of carbon dioxide and expects its emissions for the full year to be 12,500 tonnes. The market price for allowances has risen to C11 (per tonne).

chapter: 16 - Provisions, contingent liabilities and contingent assets (IAS 37)
text: At the year end, the entity has emitted the expected 12,500 tonnes and the market price of allowances is C12 (per tonne). How should the entity account for the scheme under the method set out in IFRIC 3 (the ‘full market value’ approach), assuming that the entity uses the revaluation model in IAS 38 to measure the intangible asset at fair value after its initial recognition?

chapter: 16 - Provisions, contingent liabilities and contingent assets (IAS 37)
text: The entity would record the initial receipt of allowances at the fair value of C100,000, setting up an intangible asset for this amount and recording a government grant as deferred income for the same amount.

chapter: 16 - Provisions, contingent liabilities and contingent assets (IAS 37)
text: At 30 June 20X6, the entity would record a liability for the emissions to date of C66,000 (6,000 tonnes at C11 per tonne). The intangible asset of C100,000 is revalued to C110,000 (10,000 tonnes at C11 per tonne). The revaluation surplus of C10,000 on the intangible asset is reported in other comprehensive income. There is diversity in practice with respect to how an entity recognises the deferred income related to the government grant:

chapter: 16 - Provisions, contingent liabilities and contingent assets (IAS 37)
text: - One approach is the deferred income is released in the proportion that emissions to date bear to total emissions expected for the compliance period – that is, C100,000 × 6,000/12,500 = C48,000. This approach considers the matching principle in IAS 20 to be applied to the compliance period as a whole. The profit or loss to 30 June 20X6, therefore, reflects deferred income released of C48,000 less the accrued emissions liability expense of C66,00

chapter: 16 - Provisions, contingent liabilities and contingent assets (IAS 37)
text: - Another approach would be to release the deferred income per allowance as the allowances are used - that is, C100,000 × 6,000/10,000 = C60,000. This approach recognises the fact that 60% of the allowances (that is, 60% of the government grant) has been used by the end of the interim reporting period. The profit or loss to 30 June 20X6, therefore, reflects deferred income released of C60,000 less the accrued emissions liability expense of C66,00

chapter: 16 - Provisions, contingent liabilities and contingent assets (IAS 37)
text: At 31 December 20X6 (and ignoring the 30 June 20X6 entries), the entity records a liability for emissions of C150,000 (12,500 tonnes at C12 per tonne). The asset is revalued to C120,000 (10,000 tonnes at C12 per tonne). All of the deferred income of C100,000 is released.

chapter: 16 - Provisions, contingent liabilities and contingent assets (IAS 37)
text: The effect on profit or loss for the full year is to record a liability of C150,000 (based on the market price of allowances at the balance sheet date) in respect of the emissions obligation and to release deferred income of C100,000. The revaluation surplus of C20,000 is reported in other comprehensive income. There is a net charge to profit or loss of C50,000. Taken together with the revaluation surplus in other comprehensive income of C20,000,

chapter: 16 - Provisions, contingent liabilities and contingent assets (IAS 37)
text: If the cost model in IAS 38 had been used for the intangible asset, and the asset had been measured after its initial recognition at cost less amortisation and/or impairment (cost being fair value on initial recognition for this purpose), there would be no revaluation surplus of C20,000 at the year end and the intangible asset would be stated at C100,000. Because part of the liability of C150,000 would be settled by using allowances stated at C10

chapter: 16 - Provisions, contingent liabilities and contingent assets (IAS 37)
text: Entities using the ‘cost of settlement’ approach only measure the obligation at the current (that is, balance sheet date) market price of allowances to the extent that emissions made to date exceed the volume of allowances held. If emissions do not exceed allowances held, there is no obligation to purchase additional allowances and therefore no liability. In the example above, the allowances would be initially recognised at nil cost and the liabi

chapter: 16 - Provisions, contingent liabilities and contingent assets (IAS 37)
text: There is an additional consideration for entities using the ‘cost of settlement’ approach, because the measurement of the obligation for which allowances are held will depend on whether the carrying amount of allowances is allocated to the obligation on a FIFO or on a weighted average basis. This is a particular issue where a balance sheet date is not the end of a compliance period – for example, at an interim balance sheet date (where the financ

chapter: 16 - Provisions, contingent liabilities and contingent assets (IAS 37)
text: Entities using the FIFO method measure the obligation at the carrying amount per unit of emissions, up to the number of allowances (if any) held at the balance sheet date and at the expected cost (that is, the market price at the balance sheet date) per unit for the shortfall (if any) at the balance sheet date.

chapter: 16 - Provisions, contingent liabilities and contingent assets (IAS 37)
text: Entities using the weighted average method measure the obligation using the weighted average cost per unit of emissions expected to be incurred for the compliance period as a whole. To do this, the entity determines the expected total emissions for the compliance period and compares this with the number of allowance units granted by the government (and/or purchased) and still held by the entity for that compliance period, to determine the expecte

chapter: 16 - Provisions, contingent liabilities and contingent assets (IAS 37)
text: The weighted average method is consistent with the approach to measuring items at an interim date (listed in paras B1 to B23 of IAS 34), such as tax, bonuses and volume rebates. The principle under this approach is that, where an entity has an obligation whose effective rateable measurement is determined by reference to a full period’s activities, measurement is made on the basis of the volume of activity giving rise to the obligation up to the i

text: EX 16.85.10 – Applying the recognition criteria to self-insurance

chapter: 16 - Provisions, contingent liabilities and contingent assets (IAS 37)
text: Reference to standard: IAS 37 Reference to standing text: 16.85

chapter: 16 - Provisions, contingent liabilities and contingent assets (IAS 37)
text: An entity might take out insurance to cover potential future losses. The cost is accounted for, based on the nature of the insurance premium. An entity might decide to self-insure rather than take out an insurance contract with a third party.

chapter: 16 - Provisions, contingent liabilities and contingent assets (IAS 37)
text: An entity that self-insures some of its risks makes provision for claims in respect of events that occurred before the balance sheet date, even if those claims are reported after the year end. The entity should take into account any additional evidence that comes to light after the balance sheet date, to determine which obligating events have occurred by the balance sheet date. The entity also makes provision for an estimate of expected claims th

chapter: 16 - Provisions, contingent liabilities and contingent assets (IAS 37)
text: Example 1 – Self-insurance

chapter: 16 - Provisions, contingent liabilities and contingent assets (IAS 37)
text: An entity that operates a chain of retail outlets decides not to insure itself with a third party for the risk of minor accidents to customers. Instead, it self-insures. Its past experience suggests that it will pay C200,000 on average per annum in respect of such accidents.

chapter: 16 - Provisions, contingent liabilities and contingent assets (IAS 37)
text: An obligation to another party does not arise until an accident occurs. Therefore, if no accidents have occurred at the year end, there is no present obligation and no provision should be made.

chapter: 16 - Provisions, contingent liabilities and contingent assets (IAS 37)
text: Where an accident has happened, the retailer might not know of its occurrence, but should still be making a provision. The retailer should estimate (probably actuarially) the level of accidents that have occurred but which have not yet been reported (that is, IBNR claims by customers) and make a provision for its estimate of the obligation.

chapter: 16 - Provisions, contingent liabilities and contingent assets (IAS 37)
text: During the period between the entity’s year end and the date on which its financial statements are finalised, a number of IBNR claims might have surfaced, so that a better estimate for these claims can be made.

chapter: 16 - Provisions, contingent liabilities and contingent assets (IAS 37)
text: - The entity has a legal obligation, which its past experience shows is likely to have arisen by the balance sheet date.

text: 环境损害已在期末之前发生，但目前尚无现行法律要求清理，且主体也未采取任何产生推定义务的行为。然而，一项要求主体修复该损害的新法律将在期末后不久通过。该新法规将产生一项由过去事项引起的现时义务（因为污染已经发生）。在资产负债表日是否需要计提任何准备？

chapter: 16 - Provisions, contingent liabilities and contingent assets (IAS 37)
text: 管理层应当在资产负债表日判断是否几乎确定该新法律将按草案颁布。如果该法规几乎确定将颁布，则存在导致义务发生的事项和现时义务。但是，如果颁布并非几乎确定，则不存在义务，因为尽管潜在的导致义务发生的事项已经发生（即土地污染），但尚不存在可依法强制执行的义务。

chapter: 16 - Provisions, contingent liabilities and contingent assets (IAS 37)
text: 当无法可靠评估是否存在现时义务时，管理层应如何进行会计处理？

chapter: 16 - Provisions, contingent liabilities and contingent assets (IAS 37)
text: 导致义务发生的事项是过去的污染行为，而非未来调查的结果，且在调查完成之前管理层无法确定导致义务发生的事项是否已经发生。IAS 37 第15段指出，在极少数情况下，不清楚是否存在现时义务。在这些情况下，如果考虑所有可获得的证据后，在资产负债表日存在现时义务的可能性大于不存在的可能性，则认为过去事项产生了现时义务。因此，管理层在评估是否存在现时义务时，应考虑所有可获得的证据，包括资产负债表日后获得的证据。管理层得出结论认为，现有证据不支持存在现时义务的结论，因此不确认负债。管理层应当就一旦过去污染被证实可能被处以的潜在处罚和罚款，披露一项或有负债。

chapter: 16 - Provisions, contingent liabilities and contingent assets (IAS 37)
text: 在资产负债表日后至财务报表批准报出日之间获得的关于导致义务发生的事项是否存在的任何新证据，在评估资产负债表日是否存在现时义务时，均属于调整事项。

chapter: 16 - Provisions, contingent liabilities and contingent assets (IAS 37)
text: 如果主体在资产负债表日有义务开展调查（无论调查结果如何），且该调查不会带来其他经济利益，则主体应当在资产负债表日就此类成本确认一项负债。

chapter: 16 - Provisions, contingent liabilities and contingent assets (IAS 37)
text: 例如，某航空公司可能根据当地法规被要求定期对其所有飞机进行发动机大修。如果不完成大修，该航空公司就无法续签执照并继续运营每架飞机。这并不构成现时义务，因为在大修实施之前尚未发生导致义务发生的事项。该航空公司可以通过出售飞机或以其他方式停止使用飞机来避免大修成本。

chapter: 16 - Provisions, contingent liabilities and contingent assets (IAS 37)
text: 20X1年期间，某食品制造商的15名客户出现严重食物中毒，据称是由该主体销售的产品所致。作为预防措施，管理层将该产品从超市货架上撤回。在20X1年底前，有人对该主体提起了损害赔偿诉讼。20X1年12月31日，该主体的律师向管理层提供意见称，该制造商被要求支付赔偿的可能性大于不被要求的可能性。管理层在20X1年12月31日的资产负债表中确认了损害赔偿准备。

chapter: 16 - Provisions, contingent liabilities and contingent assets (IAS 37)
text: 20X2年12月31日，该主体的律师向管理层提供意见称，由于一项类似案件作出了有利裁决，如今被要求支付赔偿的可能性微乎其微。这一评估变动在财务报表中应如何反映？

chapter: 16 - Provisions, contingent liabilities and contingent assets (IAS 37)
text: 管理层应当转回该准备，并在原计入费用的利润表项目中确认该转回。管理层还应当将该诉讼作为或有负债予以披露，除非经济利益流出的可能性极小。披露内容应当说明评估变动的原因以及转回的金额。

chapter: 16 - Provisions, contingent liabilities and contingent assets (IAS 37)
text: 应付款项、准备、披露的或有事项和可能性极小的或有事项处于一个连续的光谱上，在某项义务的存续期间，履行该义务导致经济利益流出的概率可能会在这四个类别之间移动。在一个极端，如果履行义务导致经济利益流出的可能性极小，则无需披露。当经济利益流出的可能性超过极小但低于很可能时，披露为或有负债。如果变得很可能导致经济利益流出，则确认一项准备。当负债的金额和时间变得确定时，该义务列报为“贸易或其他应付款项”或金融负债。

chapter: 16 - Provisions, contingent liabilities and contingent assets (IAS 37)
text: 在一个极端，当主体开始通过法律程序提出索赔时，流入的概率可能较低。经济利益流入并非很可能，且不要求披露或有资产。

chapter: 16 - Provisions, contingent liabilities and contingent assets (IAS 37)
text: 随后在判决作出之前，该索赔可能会变得很可能胜诉。在判决作出前案件结果就达到几乎确定的情况极为罕见。因此不确认该资产，但披露一项或有资产。

chapter: 16 - Provisions, contingent liabilities and contingent assets (IAS 37)
text: 在另一个极端，当主体在法院获得有利判决且案件最终了结而获得裁决赔偿，从而使流入几乎确定时，该资产不再属于或有资产，应当予以确认并同时确认利得。

chapter: 16 - Provisions, contingent liabilities and contingent assets (IAS 37)
text: 如果法院判决可以上诉，主体需要考虑判决的具体情况、适用法律和上诉程序，以确定流入是否几乎确定：

chapter: 16 - Provisions, contingent liabilities and contingent assets (IAS 37)
text: - 上诉可能表明该判决并非终局性的，因此或有资产仍然存在（例如，因上诉程序而无法依法强制执行的裁决可能表明该判决并非终局性的）。

chapter: 16 - Provisions, contingent liabilities and contingent assets (IAS 37)
text: - 上诉也可能是一项独立的法律程序，在此情况下，管理层需要评估流入是否几乎确定。

chapter: 16 - Provisions, contingent liabilities and contingent assets (IAS 37)
text: - 如果收到不受限制的现金裁决款项且主体控制该现金，通常会导致确认一项利得。然而，主体还需要评估上诉成功的可能性。如果上诉成功的可能性大于不成功的可能性，则应当就预期需要退还的金额计提准备。

chapter: 16 - Provisions, contingent liabilities and contingent assets (IAS 37)
text: 在资产负债表日后至财务报表批准日之间作出的对主体有利的判决，通常属于非调整事项。关于非调整的资产负债表日后事项的进一步指引，参见第9章第9段。

chapter: 16 - Provisions, contingent liabilities and contingent assets (IAS 37)
text: FAQ 16.36.2 – 与所得税以外的税项相关的保证金应如何进行会计处理？

chapter: 16 - Provisions, contingent liabilities and contingent assets (IAS 37)
text: 准则索引：IAS 37 第10、32、33段 正文索引：16.36

chapter: 16 - Provisions, contingent liabilities and contingent assets (IAS 37)
text: 与所得税以外的税项相关的保证金应如何进行会计处理？

chapter: 16 - Provisions, contingent liabilities and contingent assets (IAS 37)
text: IAS 37 中没有关于主体就所得税以外的税项（因此不属于 IAS 12 范围）所缴纳的保证金进行会计处理的指引。

chapter: 16 - Provisions, contingent liabilities and contingent assets (IAS 37)
text: 例如，某主体与税务机关就该主体是否需要缴纳一项非所得税税项存在争议。当该主体考虑所有可获得的证据后，认为该争议以有利于主体解决的可能性大于不利于主体的可能性。基于上述证据，该主体适用 IAS 37，披露一项或有负债而不确认负债。为避免可能的罚款，该主体还将争议金额作为保证金存入税务机关。当争议解决时，税务机关将被要求要么向主体退还该税务保证金（如果争议以有利于主体解决），要么使用该保证金清偿主体的负债（如果争议以有利于税务机关解决）。

chapter: 16 - Provisions, contingent liabilities and contingent assets (IAS 37)
text: 2019年1月，国际财务报告准则解释委员会（IFRS IC）发布了一项议程决定，指出向税务机关缴纳的此类保证金赋予了主体获取未来经济利益的权利——要么通过收到现金退款，要么通过用该款项清偿税务负债。因此，该权利不是 IAS 37 所定义的或有资产，因为它是主体的一项资产，而非潜在资产。税务保证金的性质（无论是自愿缴纳还是强制要求）不影响主体的权利，因此也不影响存在一项资产的结论。

chapter: 16 - Provisions, contingent liabilities and contingent assets (IAS 37)
text: 作为 IFRS IC 议程决定的一部分，委员会指出没有任何准则专门适用于该资产。因此，主体需要适用 IAS 8，并运用判断为该资产制定和采用会计政策。该议程决定指出，税务保证金的会计处理可能与货币性资产的会计处理相似或相关。如果是这种情况，主体需要参考与货币性资产相关的要求。

chapter: 16 - Provisions, contingent liabilities and contingent assets (IAS 37)
text: FAQ 16.37.1 – 准备及相关补偿应如何确认？

chapter: 16 - Provisions, contingent liabilities and contingent assets (IAS 37)
text: 准则索引：IAS 37 第53段 正文索引：16.37

chapter: 16 - Provisions, contingent liabilities and contingent assets (IAS 37)
text: 准备及相关补偿应如何确认？

chapter: 16 - Provisions, contingent liabilities and contingent assets (IAS 37)
text: 主体应当在确认相关补偿（例如保险赔款）之前先确认义务（和费用）。这是因为主体必须为很可能的流出计提准备，而获得补偿的权利仅在主体履行该义务时几乎确定能够收回赔款的情况下才能确认。

chapter: 16 - Provisions, contingent liabilities and contingent assets (IAS 37)
text: FAQ 16.37.2 – 资产负债表日后事项对保险赔款确认有何影响？

chapter: 16 - Provisions, contingent liabilities and contingent assets (IAS 37)
text: 准则索引：IAS 37 第53段 正文索引：16.37

chapter: 16 - Provisions, contingent liabilities and contingent assets (IAS 37)
text: 资产负债表日后事项对保险赔款确认有何影响？

chapter: 16 - Provisions, contingent liabilities and contingent assets (IAS 37)
text: 在资产负债表日，可能不清楚是否存在某项义务（及相关补偿资产）。在资产负债表日后获得、且证实主体在资产负债表日存在现时义务的证据属于调整事项，因此应当确认负债。如果在年末几乎确定主体在履行该义务时将收到补偿，则也应确认一项补偿资产。

chapter: 16 - Provisions, contingent liabilities and contingent assets (IAS 37)
text: 例如，年末针对某主体的法律诉讼正在进行中，且流出很可能发生。该主体同时正在与其保险公司协商补偿事宜。保险公司已同意如果主体败诉将予以赔付，尽管在达成和解之前金额尚不确定。管理层得出结论认为信用风险微不足道。

chapter: 16 - Provisions, contingent liabilities and contingent assets (IAS 37)
text: 应当就该补偿确认一项资产，因为在资产负债表日几乎确定主体在履行该义务时将收到补偿。[IAS 37 第53段]。年末后的和解证实了该负债及相关补偿资产的存在和金额。补偿资产不得超过相关负债。

chapter: 16 - Provisions, contingent liabilities and contingent assets (IAS 37)
text: 针对义务计提的准备和针对预期赔款确认的应收款在资产负债表中以总额列报，但在利润表中可以抵销后以净额列报。利润表中的这种列报方式更好地反映了交易的实质，并符合 IAS 1 的指引。[IAS 1 第34(b)段]。

chapter: 16 - Provisions, contingent liabilities and contingent assets (IAS 37)
text: FAQ 16.46.1 – 未来技术变革有何影响？

chapter: 16 - Provisions, contingent liabilities and contingent assets (IAS 37)
text: 准则索引：IAS 37 第48段 正文索引：16.46

chapter: 16 - Provisions, contingent liabilities and contingent assets (IAS 37)
text: 准备的计量需要作出判断，有时可能难以预测未来发展（例如技术变革）的影响。当为将在多年内发生的修复工作计提准备时，通常会遇到这种情况。根据 IAS 37，所确认的金额（包括准备以及如确认资产时的资产）应当反映“具备技术资格的客观观察者在考虑关于清理时将可获得技术的所有可获得证据后作出的合理预期”。例如，适当包括“因应用现有技术的经验增加而预期的成本降低，或将现有技术应用于比以往更大或更复杂的清理作业的预期成本”。[IAS 37 第49段]。除非有充分的客观证据支持，否则主体不能预期全新技术的开发。

chapter: 16 - Provisions, contingent liabilities and contingent assets (IAS 37)
text: 在确定所考虑的技术变革是否恰当时需要极其谨慎。如果有充分证据表明此类情况很可能发生，则预期对现有方法进行一定程度的改进、调整和成本降低是合理的。

chapter: 16 - Provisions, contingent liabilities and contingent assets (IAS 37)
text: FAQ 16.47.2 – 期望值法在什么情况下可能不适用？

chapter: 16 - Provisions, contingent liabilities and contingent assets (IAS 37)
text: 准则索引：IAS 37 第39段 正文索引：16.47

chapter: 16 - Provisions, contingent liabilities and contingent assets (IAS 37)
text: 期望值法在什么情况下可能不适用？

chapter: 16 - Provisions, contingent liabilities and contingent assets (IAS 37)
text: 在某些情况下，特别是存在二元结果时，最可能金额比概率加权估计能得出更好的结果。例如，某主体有一项未决诉讼。如果败诉，将支付 C100万；如果胜诉，则无需支付任何款项。在资产负债表日，该主体估计败诉的可能性为 70%。期望值法得出的准备为 C700,000。然而，该金额可能没有意义，因为它既不是主体预期支付的金额，也不是主体可能支付的金额。采用最可能金额 C100万 更为恰当。

chapter: 16 - Provisions, contingent liabilities and contingent assets (IAS 37)
text: FAQ 16.47.3 – 最可能结果法在什么情况下可能不适用？

chapter: 16 - Provisions, contingent liabilities and contingent assets (IAS 37)
text: 准则索引：IAS 37 第39段 正文索引：16.47

chapter: 16 - Provisions, contingent liabilities and contingent assets (IAS 37)
text: 最可能结果法在什么情况下可能不适用？

chapter: 16 - Provisions, contingent liabilities and contingent assets (IAS 37)
text: 最可能结果可能为单一义务的负债提供最佳估计，但并非总是如此。如果其他可能结果大多高于或大多低于最可能结果，则最佳估计将是更高或更低的金额。例如，某主体必须修复其为客户建造的工厂中的一项故障，该主体可能得出结论认为最可能的结果是首次尝试维修即告成功，但如果存在很大可能需要开展进一步工作，则可能需要计提更大金额的准备。

chapter: 16 - Provisions, contingent liabilities and contingent assets (IAS 37)
text: FAQ 16.47.4 – 两种估计方法如何反映风险？

chapter: 16 - Provisions, contingent liabilities and contingent assets (IAS 37)
text: 两种估计方法如何反映风险？

chapter: 16 - Provisions, contingent liabilities and contingent assets (IAS 37)
text: 期望值法通过考虑潜在结果将风险纳入估计现金流量中。采用期望值法时，通常不应在折现率中再包含风险。然而，当采用最可能结果法时，结果变动的风险通常反映在折现率中。

text: IAS 37 提及折现时应考虑：

chapter: 16 - Provisions, contingent liabilities and contingent assets (IAS 37)
text: - 针对“负债特有风险”可能作出的调整。[IAS 37 第47段]。

chapter: 16 - Provisions, contingent liabilities and contingent assets (IAS 37)
text: 尽管 IAS 37 未明确规定反映货币时间价值的折现率，但我们认为税前无风险利率是恰当且通常采用的利率。与义务产生币种及期限相匹配的政府债券“收益率”（而非票面利率），是匹配负债到期期限的税前无风险利率的良好替代指标。当义务通过单笔付款清偿时，这相对直接，因为政府债券在到期时有单笔本金偿还。当准备由不同期间发生的一系列现金流量组成时，可能需要调整折现率以反映现金流量的不同时间分布。

chapter: 16 - Provisions, contingent liabilities and contingent assets (IAS 37)
text: FAQ 16.49.2至FAQ 16.49.6更详细地讨论了与确定折现率相关的部分问题。

text: FAQ 16.49.2 – 负折现率是否反映时间价值？

text: 准则索引：IAS 37 第47段 正文索引：16.49

chapter: 16 - Provisions, contingent liabilities and contingent assets (IAS 37)
text: 负折现率是否反映时间价值？

chapter: 16 - Provisions, contingent liabilities and contingent assets (IAS 37)
text: IAS 37 并未明确折现率是否可以为负。

chapter: 16 - Provisions, contingent liabilities and contingent assets (IAS 37)
text: IAS 37 第46段指出，报告日后不久发生的现金流出比随后发生的同等金额的现金流出负担更重。这暗示时间价值不能为负。国际财务报告准则解释委员会（IFRS IC）在2015年9月的一项议程决定中指出，负利息费用可以列报为财务费用以外的费用，这表明负利息反映了时间价值以外的因素。这与 IFRS 9 第B4.1.7A段一致，该段指出利息可以为负，并举例说明：“金融资产的持有人明示或默示地为将其资金存放特定期间而付费（且该费用超过了持有人因货币时间价值、信用风险以及其他基本借贷风险和成本而收到的对价）”。

chapter: 16 - Provisions, contingent liabilities and contingent assets (IAS 37)
text: 然而，这些陈述同样适用于正折现率。

chapter: 16 - Provisions, contingent liabilities and contingent assets (IAS 37)
text: IAS 37 第37段表明，准备按照报告期末清偿现时义务所需的金额计量。当利率为负时，第三方会要求支付大于预期未来成本的金额，以弥补该付款的价值损失。这意味着应当使用负折现率。但是，IAS 37 第36段暗示了一种履约成本模型，在该模型下，准备按主体未来的成本计量，而不使用负折现率。

chapter: 16 - Provisions, contingent liabilities and contingent assets (IAS 37)
text: 相关指引并不明确，实务做法也不一致。IAS 37 并未禁止使用负折现率。

text: 折现率如何反映负债特有的风险？

chapter: 16 - Provisions, contingent liabilities and contingent assets (IAS 37)
text: 管理层对 A 型号产品质量保证准备采用与 B 型号产品质量保证准备相同的折现率进行折现，可能并不恰当。这些准备针对不同产品产生的质量保证义务。不同产品可能具有不同风险，因此，除非已在总现金流量估计中另行反映，否则即使两项准备均属于产品质量保证义务，采用不同的折现率也可能是恰当的。例如，鉴于 A 型号吸尘器采用的技术较旧，与 B 型号相比，A 型号吸尘器的质量保证在现金流量方面可能具有更高的变动风险。

chapter: 16 - Provisions, contingent liabilities and contingent assets (IAS 37)
text: FAQ 16.49.4 – 通货膨胀如何影响折现率？

chapter: 16 - Provisions, contingent liabilities and contingent assets (IAS 37)
text: 准则索引：IAS 37 第47段 正文索引：16.49

chapter: 16 - Provisions, contingent liabilities and contingent assets (IAS 37)
text: 通货膨胀如何影响折现率？

chapter: 16 - Provisions, contingent liabilities and contingent assets (IAS 37)
text: 以预期未来价格（即包含通货膨胀）表示的现金流出，应当使用包含通货膨胀的“名义”折现率进行折现。按当前价格估计的现金流量，应当使用不含通货膨胀影响的“实际”折现率（例如，经调整以剔除通货膨胀影响的政府债券利率）进行折现。在正常的通货膨胀环境下，实际折现率低于名义折现率。使用名义利率对经价格变动调整后的现金流量进行折现所得出的净现值，应当与使用实际利率对未经通货膨胀调整的现金流量进行折现所得出的净现值相同。以下示例说明了这一点。

chapter: 16 - Provisions, contingent liabilities and contingent assets (IAS 37)
text: 某主体估计，其需要在未来三年每年年末支付 C1,000（按当前价格计）以清偿某项义务。通货膨胀将使这些现金流量增加至下表所示的金额。该主体确定名义折现率（即包含通货膨胀）为 4.5%。对现金流量进行折现得出的净现值为 C2,887。通过使用称为迭代法的估计过程，可以计算出需应用于不含通货膨胀的现金流量以得出相同现值的折现率（即实际利率）。

chapter: 16 - Provisions, contingent liabilities and contingent assets (IAS 37)
text: 净现值 现金流量 第1年 第2年 第3年 C C C C 反映每年2.5%通货膨胀的现金流量 基于4.5%名义折现率的净现值 2,887 1,025 1,051 1,077 不含通货膨胀的现金流量 基于1.95%实际折现率的净现值 2,887 1,000 1,000 1,000

chapter: 16 - Provisions, contingent liabilities and contingent assets (IAS 37)
text: 该示例表明等效的实际利率为 1.95%。使用 4.5% 的名义折现率（包含通货膨胀）对不含通货膨胀的现金流量（即每年 C1,000）进行折现是不恰当的，因为这会低估净现值。

chapter: 16 - Provisions, contingent liabilities and contingent assets (IAS 37)
text: FAQ 16.49.5 – 是否应考虑自身信用风险？

chapter: 16 - Provisions, contingent liabilities and contingent assets (IAS 37)
text: 准则索引：IAS 37 第47段 正文索引：16.49

chapter: 16 - Provisions, contingent liabilities and contingent assets (IAS 37)
text: 是否应考虑自身信用风险？

chapter: 16 - Provisions, contingent liabilities and contingent assets (IAS 37)
text: IAS 37 中没有关于负债特有风险的具体指引。

chapter: 16 - Provisions, contingent liabilities and contingent assets (IAS 37)
text: 2011年3月，国际财务报告准则解释委员会（IFRS IC）发布了一项议程决定，指出 IAS 37 未说明准备的计量中是否应包含自身信用风险，但主流实务是将其排除在外。该决定还指出，自身信用风险“在实务中通常被视为主体的风险，而非负债特有的风险”。

chapter: 16 - Provisions, contingent liabilities and contingent assets (IAS 37)
text: IAS 19 确实考虑了自身信用风险，其在第84段指出“折现率不反映主体债权人所承担的主体特定信用风险”。IAS 19 第BC134段指出：“此外，折现率不应反映主体自身的信用评级，否则信用评级较低的主体反而会确认较小的负债。”这些规定表明，准备的计量中应当排除自身信用风险。

chapter: 16 - Provisions, contingent liabilities and contingent assets (IAS 37)
text: 这与我们的观点一致，即准备语境下的风险反映的是清偿或履行义务所需资源的不确定性，通常不包括主体自身的信用风险。

chapter: 16 - Provisions, contingent liabilities and contingent assets (IAS 37)
text: FAQ 16.49.6 – 哪些因素可能影响折现率的设定？

chapter: 16 - Provisions, contingent liabilities and contingent assets (IAS 37)
text: 准则索引：IAS 37 第47段 正文索引：16.49

chapter: 16 - Provisions, contingent liabilities and contingent assets (IAS 37)
text: 哪些因素可能影响折现率的设定？

chapter: 16 - Provisions, contingent liabilities and contingent assets (IAS 37)
text: 在评估 IAS 37 下准备的恰当折现率时，应当一贯地运用判断，并遵循以下原则：

chapter: 16 - Provisions, contingent liabilities and contingent assets (IAS 37)
text: - 为反映负债特有风险而调整折现率，通常应当在无风险利率的基础上调低折现率，从而导致“风险较高”的负债金额增加。

chapter: 16 - Provisions, contingent liabilities and contingent assets (IAS 37)
text: - 关于通货膨胀及其对未来现金流量可能影响的假设，应当与折现率所基于的收益率中隐含的任何通货膨胀假设保持一致。

chapter: 16 - Provisions, contingent liabilities and contingent assets (IAS 37)
text: - 除非情况发生变化，确定折现率的起点和流程应当在各年度之间保持一致。

chapter: 16 - Provisions, contingent liabilities and contingent assets (IAS 37)
text: - 应当考虑所采用假设的一致性。例如，高质量公司债券的收益率用于估计雇员福利义务的折现率。用作确定准备折现率起点的无风险利率通常应当更低，因为 IAS 19 并不要求采用无风险利率。

chapter: 16 - Provisions, contingent liabilities and contingent assets (IAS 37)
text: - 在考察相对短期的义务时，应考虑时间价值的重要性；在低利率（无论正负）环境下，折现的影响可能并不重大。

chapter: 16 - Provisions, contingent liabilities and contingent assets (IAS 37)
text: FAQ 16.50.1 – 应使用什么折现率来计算因准备折现的转回而产生的借款费用？

chapter: 16 - Provisions, contingent liabilities and contingent assets (IAS 37)
text: 准则索引：IAS 37 第60段 正文索引：16.50

chapter: 16 - Provisions, contingent liabilities and contingent assets (IAS 37)
text: 税前无风险利率反映了货币时间价值。因此，应当使用相同利率进行折现的转回并确定借款费用。在折现实际现金流量时，折现率有时可能会被调整以剔除通货膨胀，或在现金流量未考虑风险时被调整以反映风险。当折现率已经过调整时，应如何进行折现的转回？

chapter: 16 - Provisions, contingent liabilities and contingent assets (IAS 37)
text: 我们认为，无论采用何种折现率计算准备的现值，借款费用均应使用报告期间的加权平均未清偿负债（未考虑折现前）和税前无风险利率进行计算。IAS 37 要求仅将因时间推移导致的准备价值增加计入借款费用。

chapter: 16 - Provisions, contingent liabilities and contingent assets (IAS 37)
text: FAQ 16.51.1 – 因估计现金流量和折现率变动导致的准备重估应如何进行会计处理？

chapter: 16 - Provisions, contingent liabilities and contingent assets (IAS 37)
text: 准则索引：IAS 37 第59段 正文索引：16.51

chapter: 16 - Provisions, contingent liabilities and contingent assets (IAS 37)
text: 因估计现金流量和折现率变动导致的准备重估应如何进行会计处理？

chapter: 16 - Provisions, contingent liabilities and contingent assets (IAS 37)
text: 估计现金流量和折现率的变动也可能导致每个报告日准备金额的变动。IAS 37 未就估计现金流量和折现率的变动提供指引。然而，由此产生的调整是对准备的重新评估，该变动不应计入（借记或贷记）借款费用，而应当计入经营成本。

chapter: 16 - Provisions, contingent liabilities and contingent assets (IAS 37)
text: 不过，对于适用 IFRIC 1 的弃置义务准备存在例外情况。估计现金流量和折现率的任何变动影响应当加计到（或扣减自）相关资产，并对其调整后的账面价值在剩余使用寿命内采用未来适用法计提折旧。关于弃置义务的进一步指引，另请参见EX 16.85.7。

chapter: 16 - Provisions, contingent liabilities and contingent assets (IAS 37)
text: FAQ 16.51.2 – 折现率变动会产生什么影响？

chapter: 16 - Provisions, contingent liabilities and contingent assets (IAS 37)
text: 准则索引：IAS 37 第59段 正文索引：16.51

chapter: 16 - Provisions, contingent liabilities and contingent assets (IAS 37)
text: 折现率变动会产生什么影响？

chapter: 16 - Provisions, contingent liabilities and contingent assets (IAS 37)
text: 以下示例说明了折现率变动的影响。

chapter: 16 - Provisions, contingent liabilities and contingent assets (IAS 37)
text: 某主体有一项在第5年末到期的 C1,000 的义务。基于 4.5% 的税前无风险利率，该义务的现值为 C802。在第3年末，折现率为 4%。第3年期初的现值（采用 4.5% 的折现率）为 C876，第3年期末的现值（采用 4% 的折现率）为 C925。

chapter: 16 - Provisions, contingent liabilities and contingent assets (IAS 37)
text: 净现值 以下各年末的准备 第1年 第2年 第3年 第4年 第5年 C C C C C C 原无风险利率 4.50% 802 839 876 916 957 1,000 修订后无风险利率 4.00% 925 962 1,000 第3年准备的变动分析如下： 第3年期初余额 876 借款费用（C876 × 4.5% 1 ） 39 轧差金额（计入经营成本） 10 第3年期末余额 925

chapter: 16 - Provisions, contingent liabilities and contingent assets (IAS 37)
text: 1 在本示例中，我们假设折现率在年末下降。如果折现率在年度内逐步变动，采用加权平均折现率也可能是恰当的。

chapter: 16 - Provisions, contingent liabilities and contingent assets (IAS 37)
text: 本示例讨论的是采用无风险利率对估计现金流量进行折现以计算准备现值的情形。但是，主体也可能采用实际利率或经风险调整的利率进行折现。即使如此，仍应使用无风险利率进行折现的转回，因为 IAS 37 要求财务费用仅反映货币时间价值。

chapter: 16 - Provisions, contingent liabilities and contingent assets (IAS 37)
text: FAQ 16.53.1 – 处置组的未来经营亏损能否确认为准备？

chapter: 16 - Provisions, contingent liabilities and contingent assets (IAS 37)
text: 准则索引：IAS 37 第63段 正文索引：16.53

chapter: 16 - Provisions, contingent liabilities and contingent assets (IAS 37)
text: 某主体生产并销售家具。20X7年第一季度末，该主体董事会批准并宣布了一项出售其厨房事业部的正式计划。管理层预计在下一财年（20X8年）第一季度出售该事业部。20X7年末，由于该事业部符合 IFRS 5 划分为持有待售的条件，将被披露为持有待售处置组。预计在资产负债表日至预期处置日期间，厨房事业部的经营亏损约为 C250,000。管理层能否将这些经营亏损计入重组准备？

chapter: 16 - Provisions, contingent liabilities and contingent assets (IAS 37)
text: 管理层不应为未来经营亏损确认准备，即使这些亏损与处置组相关。

chapter: 16 - Provisions, contingent liabilities and contingent assets (IAS 37)
text: 尽管 IFRS 5 要求处置组按照账面价值与公允价值减去出售费用后的净额两者中的较低者计量（这可能需要按照 IAS 36 确认减值），但 IFRS 5 并未提供确认准备的指引。IAS 37 中的确认和计量原则仍然适用于准备。

chapter: 16 - Provisions, contingent liabilities and contingent assets (IAS 37)
text: 一旦董事会制定并宣布了重组计划，主体即应确认重组准备。这可能与处置组划分为持有待售同时发生。但是，经营亏损不应计入该准备。未来经营亏损不符合负债的定义。

chapter: 16 - Provisions, contingent liabilities and contingent assets (IAS 37)
text: FAQ 16.60.1 – 仅向受重组计划影响的部分方宣布重组计划，是否足以确认全部预期重组准备的负债？

chapter: 16 - Provisions, contingent liabilities and contingent assets (IAS 37)
text: 准则索引：IAS 37 第73、75段；IAS 19 第165段 正文索引：16.60

chapter: 16 - Provisions, contingent liabilities and contingent assets (IAS 37)
text: 仅向受重组计划影响的部分方宣布重组计划，是否足以确认全部预期重组准备的负债？

chapter: 16 - Provisions, contingent liabilities and contingent assets (IAS 37)
text: A主体的管理层制定了一项业务改组计划。2020年，董事会批准了该计划，涉及关闭A主体位于指定购物中心的30家零售门店中的10家。取消或不再续签与拟关闭地点相关的租赁合同的意向已在2020年通知了出租人。A主体并未向受影响地点的员工表明任何有关其未来雇佣的计划。2020年未发布任何公开声明，且向受影响员工宣布该计划（即管理层计划解雇拟关闭零售门店的所有员工）发生在2021年。

chapter: 16 - Provisions, contingent liabilities and contingent assets (IAS 37)
text: A主体已经处理了其对租赁会计的影响，现拟评估其是否可以在2020年12月31日为其他重组成本（特别是与受影响员工相关的裁员费用）计提准备。

chapter: 16 - Provisions, contingent liabilities and contingent assets (IAS 37)
text: IAS 37 第72段和第73段解释称，只有当详细重组计划的公开宣布以足够详细的方式作出，从而在其他方中形成主体将实施重组的合理预期时，该公开宣布才构成推定义务。

chapter: 16 - Provisions, contingent liabilities and contingent assets (IAS 37)
text: IAS 37 未就“其他方”的解释提供进一步指引。然而，IAS 37 中与重组相关的原则要求，仅在主体存在现时义务时才确认负债。因此，如果主体存在除重组之外能够避免潜在流出的替代行动，则不确认负债。IAS 37 示例5B 证明了这一点，该示例说明在确认重组准备之前需要同时与员工和客户沟通。IAS 37 第79段还解释称，重组计划的不同方面可能会在不同时点产生推定义务并进行会计处理。

chapter: 16 - Provisions, contingent liabilities and contingent assets (IAS 37)
text: 支付给员工的辞退付款属于 IAS 19 的范围。在此情形下，尚未向员工发出任何要约。根据 IAS 19 第165(b)段，A主体应当在确认属于 IAS 37 范围的重组成本时，确认辞退福利的负债和费用。

chapter: 16 - Provisions, contingent liabilities and contingent assets (IAS 37)
text: 如果受影响的员工群体在报告期末尚未收到任何沟通通知，则在2020年12月31日不存在针对员工的与重组相关的推定义务。

chapter: 16 - Provisions, contingent liabilities and contingent assets (IAS 37)
text: FAQ 16.61.1 – 宣布重组意向是否足以确认重组准备？

chapter: 16 - Provisions, contingent liabilities and contingent assets (IAS 37)
text: 准则索引：IAS 37 第73、75段 正文索引：16.61

chapter: 16 - Provisions, contingent liabilities and contingent assets (IAS 37)
text: A主体的管理层制定了一项业务改组计划。董事会已批准该计划，涉及关闭A主体50家零售门店中的10家。管理层在决定关闭哪些门店之前将进行进一步分析。管理层已公开宣布其意向，并认为这已在受影响方中形成了合理预期。是否应当确认重组成本准备？

chapter: 16 - Provisions, contingent liabilities and contingent assets (IAS 37)
text: 否，不应确认重组准备。仅当主体同时拥有详细、正式的重组计划并向受其影响的各方宣布该计划时，才产生推定义务。该计划未提供足够的细节（例如受影响的主要地点），不足以允许确认推定义务。

chapter: 16 - Provisions, contingent liabilities and contingent assets (IAS 37)
text: FAQ 16.61.2 – 确认重组准备是否必须通知到每一名受影响的员工？

chapter: 16 - Provisions, contingent liabilities and contingent assets (IAS 37)
text: 准则索引：IAS 37 第73、75段 正文索引：16.61

chapter: 16 - Provisions, contingent liabilities and contingent assets (IAS 37)
text: 某主体计划进行总部重组，年末为 20X1年3月31日。该主体在年末之前（例如 20X1年1月）宣布了该重组，包括可能受影响的职能部门和员工人数。但由于存在90天的协商期，截至年末尚未通知到每一名受影响的员工。该主体能否在 20X1年3月31日为重组成本计提准备？

chapter: 16 - Provisions, contingent liabilities and contingent assets (IAS 37)
text: IAS 37 指出，只有当详细重组计划的公开宣布以足够详细的方式（即列明计划的主要特征）作出，从而在其他方（例如客户、供应商以及员工或其代表）中形成主体将实施重组的合理预期时，该公开宣布才构成重组的推定义务。

chapter: 16 - Provisions, contingent liabilities and contingent assets (IAS 37)
text: 我们认为，年末时并不需要已通知到每一名员工。通知员工代表即可产生推定义务。需要考虑具体协商所涉及的内容。例如，如果谈判仅涉及具体条款，而非可能改变主体（已详细宣布的）计划的事项，则该宣布将产生推定义务。

chapter: 16 - Provisions, contingent liabilities and contingent assets (IAS 37)
text: FAQ 16.62.1 – 管理层在资产负债表日后宣布重组有何影响？

chapter: 16 - Provisions, contingent liabilities and contingent assets (IAS 37)
text: 准则索引：IAS 37 第73、75段 正文索引：16.62

chapter: 16 - Provisions, contingent liabilities and contingent assets (IAS 37)
text: 某主体制定了一项涉及关闭场地和裁员的正式改组计划。该计划在年末已获董事会批准，但主体直至年末之后才实施或宣布该改组。管理层在资产负债表日后宣布重组有何影响？

chapter: 16 - Provisions, contingent liabilities and contingent assets (IAS 37)
text: 即使在主体年末之后、财务报表批准之前作出了宣布，也不存在推定义务。该宣布属于非调整的资产负债表日后事项，在年末时主体并未作出重组承诺。主体在年末之后仍可能完全改变其计划。

chapter: 16 - Provisions, contingent liabilities and contingent assets (IAS 37)
text: 尽管缺乏正式宣布，但如果主体在年末前已通过开始实施改组（例如报废厂房，或向员工和供应商通报改组情况）而在受影响方中形成了合理预期，则会存在推定义务。

chapter: 16 - Provisions, contingent liabilities and contingent assets (IAS 37)
text: FAQ 16.63.1 – 在哪些情况下董事会批准会确立义务？

chapter: 16 - Provisions, contingent liabilities and contingent assets (IAS 37)
text: 准则索引：IAS 37 第73、75段 正文索引：16.63

chapter: 16 - Provisions, contingent liabilities and contingent assets (IAS 37)
text: 在哪些情况下董事会批准会确立义务？

chapter: 16 - Provisions, contingent liabilities and contingent assets (IAS 37)
text: 不一定。IAS 37 将亏损合同定义为履行合同义务不可避免的成本超过预期从该合同中获得的经济利益的合同。合同下的不可避免的成本反映了退出合同的最低净成本，即履行该合同的成本与未能履行该合同而产生的任何补偿或违约金两者中的较低者。

chapter: 16 - Provisions, contingent liabilities and contingent assets (IAS 37)

text: WEEE 指令规定，历史家用设备的废弃物管理成本应当由在各成员国适用法规所规定期间（“计量期间”）内参与市场的该类设备生产商承担。WEEE 指令规定，各成员国应当建立相应机制，使生产商按比例分摊成本（例如，按各类设备各自的市场份额比例）。

chapter: 16 - Provisions, contingent liabilities and contingent assets (IAS 37)
text: WEEE 指令本身不能对个别生产商施加任何法定义务；它仅对政府/国家施加将其转化为当地法律的义务。因此，与该指令相关的具体要求因国而异。例如，如果当地法律未将处置 WEEE 的义务施加于生产商，主体在 WEEE 指令下可能不承担义务，但需要考虑是否存在其他法定义务或推定义务。在其他司法管辖区，当地法律可能将处置 WEEE 的义务施加于生产商，但可能为每家生产商提供加入集体方案（并可能将其义务转移给该集体方案）的机会，或者可能要求生产商在退出市场时支付某些退出费用。在这些情况下，当商品投放市场时，可能需要计提准备。是否应当确认义务取决于当地法律的具体要求。
