EX 22.77.1 – 重估减少的处理
准则参考：IAS 16 第40段 正文参考：22.77
某项不动产、厂场和设备的成本为C100，按直线法在10年内计提折旧，残值为零。第1年末，该资产重估为C135。重估利得C45（C135 − C90，即C100减去折旧C10）计入其他综合收益（OCI）并在权益中累计。
第2年末，该资产的价值降至C50。在扣除当年折旧C15（C135 / 9）后，产生重估损失C70（C120 − C50）。
根据IAS 16，C70的重估损失应首先冲减储备中重估盈余项下就同一资产持有的先前盈余。该金额为C45，因此C45的重估损失冲减储备中的重估盈余，其余C25计入利润表。
C 第2年初账面价值 135 当年折旧 (15) 第2年末重估前的账面价值 120 冲减重估盈余的价值减少 (45) 75 计入利润表的价值减少 (25) 第2年末账面价值（重估金额） 50
本准则允许随着相关资产的使用及盈余的实现，将重估盈余结转至留存收益。盈余可随着相关资产的折旧而实现。在本例中，第2年将实现C5的盈余（当年折旧C15减去按历史成本金额计提的折旧C10）。如果该金额已结转至留存收益，则重估盈余上的剩余余额仅为C40。此时，C70的重估损失中仅能冲减重估盈余C40，而C30将计入利润表。
此外，在确定可供冲减的重估盈余余额时，还应考虑可能已计入重估盈余的递延所得税。
EX 22.80.1 – 复原义务与土地成本的折旧
准则参考：IAS 16 第52段 正文参考：22.80
垃圾填埋场在不再使用时需要进行复原。复原场地的义务成本应在向场地倾倒垃圾的期间内计提折旧。该场地本身对垃圾填埋场运营方而言具有有限使用寿命，其残值将远低于其原始成本。土地成本也应在该场地的使用寿命内折旧至其残值。
EX 22.83.1 – 某些资产不计提折旧的情况
准则参考：IAS 16 第52段 正文参考：22.83
一个颇具挑战性的问题是，对某些资产不计提年度折旧费用是否恰当。该问题最常出现在建筑物方面。当建筑物的残值超过其账面价值时，不记录折旧费用可能是恰当的。
一家公司于20X6年以C100万的成本购买了一处物业。该物业的预计总物理寿命为50年。然而，该公司认为很可能在20年后出售该物业。根据20X6年价格，20年后的估计残值为（a）C100万，或（b）C900,000。残值等于或接近原始成本的情况十分罕见，因为这假定20年后的潜在买方愿意为一处20年房龄的物业支付与新物业相近的金额。
在情形（a）中，公司认为基于资产负债表日现行价格的残值将等于成本。因此不存在可折旧金额，折旧正确地为零。
在情形（b）中，公司认为基于资产负债表日现行价格的残值将为C900,000；因此可折旧金额为C100,000。年度折旧（按直线法）将为C5,000（(1,000,000 − 900,000) / 20）。
EX 22.83.2 – 当重置支出等于年度折旧费用时的折旧
准则参考：IAS 16 第52段 正文参考：22.83
某主体经营多家酒店。酒店设备（如床上用品和餐具）的总账面价值年复一年保持稳定。所有设备每隔几年就会更换一次，以确保维持高标准。管理层推行了滚动更换计划，使得重置资产的成本每年保持在稳定水平。
管理层希望减少行政管理工作，提议不再对酒店设备计提折旧，而是每年将重置成本费用化。
主体应当将使用寿命超过一年的所有资产予以资本化，并在其使用寿命内计提折旧。出于效率考虑，管理层可以将成组的类似资产作为单项资产予以资本化，然后如同单项资产一样计算这些资产的折旧。
拟议的将年内购买的所有重置资产费用化、且不对已资本化资产计提折旧的政策是不恰当的。
EX 22.84.1 – 折旧资本化计入另一项资产的成本
准则参考：IAS 16 第49段 正文参考：22.84
一家矿业公司为挖掘新矿山而购置了土方设备。因此，该设备的折旧是挖掘该矿山的直接归属成本。该设备的折旧费用应当作为矿山成本的一部分予以资本化。用于开发活动的设备的折旧可根据IAS 38计入无形资产的成本。
EX 22.84.2 – 计入另一项资产生产成本的折旧费用
准则参考：IAS 16 第49段 正文参考：22.84
A主体为汽车行业制造汽车零部件，并在其生产过程中使用部分自制模具工具。A主体的客户（汽车制造商）不断推出新车型或重新设计现有车型。因此，A主体必须不断开发新工具用于其生产过程。
这些工具的成本予以资本化，并在三年（即工具的预计使用寿命）内计提折旧。
A主体拥有一座厂房，所有生产均在该厂房内进行。该厂房的10%用于开发和制造工具。该建筑物采用直线法计提折旧。
主体应将厂房折旧费用的10%计入工具的成本，并予以资本化和计提折旧。厂房的折旧费用构成生产工具成本的一部分。
EX 22.87.1 – 土地的可折旧组成部分
准则参考：IAS 16 第58段 正文参考：22.87

土地资产的账面价值可能包括场地拆卸、移除和复原成本。复原成本组成部分应在从该土地获取经济利益的期间内计提折旧。土地本身在某些情况下可能具有有限使用寿命，在此情况下应在该使用寿命内计提折旧。一个例子是需要复原的垃圾填埋场。复原场地的义务成本可以在向场地倾倒垃圾的期间内计提折旧。场地本身对垃圾填埋场运营方而言可能具有有限使用寿命，其残值可能远低于原始成本。土地成本也应在该场地的使用寿命内折旧至其残值。
EX 22.89.1 – 资产达到预定可使用状态时开始计提折旧
准则参考：IAS 16 第57段 正文参考：22.89
B主体自建了一台自用机器。建造工作于20X6年11月1日完成，但主体直到20X7年3月1日才开始使用该机器。
主体应自机器达到预定可使用状态之日（即20X6年11月1日）起开始计提折旧。机器在达到预定可使用状态后有一段时间未被使用，这一事实在考虑何时开始计提折旧时不具有相关性。
EX 22.89.2 – 资产处于使用中时的折旧
准则参考：IAS 16 第57段 正文参考：22.89

C主体于20X1年6月以C10,000万（C100m）的原始成本购置了一座厂房，预计使用寿命为20年，残值为零。20X6年6月，由于产品需求下滑，账面净值为C7,500万（C75m）的该厂房被关闭。C主体根据已制定的出售计划，确定该厂房符合IFRS 5划分为持有待售的标准。20X6年确认了C5,000万（C50m）的减值费用，将厂房减记至公允价值减去出售费用后的净额C2,500万（C25m），并停止计提折旧。然而，20X6年12月，需求意外上升并超过了当前产能。管理层决定放弃出售计划并重新启用该厂房。预计未来现金流量足以证明转回原C5,000万（C50m）的全部减值是合理的。重新启用预计耗时六个月，至20X7年6月完成。
主体将转回先前的减值C5,000万（C50m），并扣除20X6年6月至20X7年6月资产闲置期间本应计提的折旧C500万（C5m）。厂房的账面净值C7,000万（C70m，即C25m + C50m − C5m）将在其剩余14年的预计使用寿命内计提折旧。
EX 22.89.3 – 折旧期间
准则参考：IAS 16 第43段 正文参考：22.89
A主体正在考虑采用一项政策：对当年资本化的不动产、厂场和设备在次年才开始计提折旧，但在资产处置当年计提全年折旧。这是否可以接受？
有形固定资产的可折旧金额应在其使用寿命内系统地分摊。折旧方法应反映主体预期消耗该资产未来经济利益的方式。“使用寿命”是指主体预期可使用该资产的期间。折旧应在资产购置并可供使用时立即开始。A主体应在使用期间内对资产计提折旧。
EX 22.89.4 – 租赁改良支出的使用寿命
准则参考：IAS 16 第56(d)、57段 正文参考：22.89
A主体签订了一份为期九年的租赁协议，并拥有再续租六年的权利。在租赁期开始日，A主体并未合理确定将行使续租选择权，因此确定租赁期为九年。A主体将进行重大租赁改良以符合其品牌标准。这些租赁改良的预计使用寿命为10年。
IAS 16第56(d)段规定，在确定资产的使用寿命时，应考虑对资产使用的法律或类似限制，例如相关租赁的到期日。因此，通常预期租赁改良的使用寿命（即折旧期间）与IFRS 16下的租赁期相同。但是，在某些情况下，租赁改良的使用寿命可能超过经评估的租赁期（例如，管理层将在租赁期满时拆除并重新部署该租赁改良）。

2019年11月发布的国际财务报告准则解释委员会（IFRS IC）议程决定探讨了任何相关的不可移除租赁改良的使用寿命是否受限于应用IFRS 16确定的租赁期这一问题。IFRIC议程决定确认，报告主体在确定不可移除租赁改良的使用寿命时应适用IAS 16第56至57段。如果相关租赁的租赁期短于这些租赁改良的经济寿命，报告主体应考虑其是否预期在租赁期之后继续使用该租赁改良；如果不是，则根据IAS 16第57段，不可移除租赁改良的使用寿命应被视为与租赁期相同。委员会指出，应用IAS 16第56至57段，对于主体仅在使用租赁标的资产期间方能使用并从中获益的租赁改良，主体通常会得出这一结论。
有关该议程决定就租赁期与租赁改良使用寿命之间相互作用所提供的指引，参见第15.37段。
FAQ 22.92.1 – 如果资产处于闲置状态，主体可以停止计提折旧吗？
准则参考：IAS 16 第55段 正文参考：22.92
不可以，当资产处于闲置状态时，折旧并不停止[IAS 16 第55段]。如果某项资产按直线法计提折旧，在其闲置期间仍将继续计提折旧。如果某项资产采用工作量法计提折旧，则在没有生产时，折旧费用可以为零。
EX 22.94.1 – 折旧方法
准则参考：IAS 16 第62段 正文参考：22.94
直线法是实务中最常用的方法，因为参照时间期间评估使用寿命可能更容易。然而，使用量可能是更可靠的计量形式。成本或重估金额减去估计残值后在使用寿命内分摊，从而在资产的使用寿命内系统地计入每个会计期间。

除直线法外，还有多种不同的折旧确定方法。这些方法可能基于使用量分摊可折旧金额（如工作量法），或旨在资产使用早期计提较高的折旧金额。常见方法包括余额递减法、工作量法、年数总和法和数字总和法。当资产在其使用寿命早期消耗经济利益更快时，采用加速折旧法是恰当的。资产可能会变得不那么可靠且更容易发生故障、生产高质量产品的能力下降或技术在逐渐落后。资产产出价格下跌是需要考虑的一个因素，但其本身并不要求必须采用加速折旧法。本示例将讨论其中若干种方法。
余额递减法 ：该方法旨在资产使用早期计提较高的折旧金额，具体如下（本例假设无残值）：
C 成本 125 折旧费用（20%） 25 第1年末账面价值 100 折旧费用（100的20%） 20 第2年末账面价值 80 折旧费用（80的20%） 16 第3年末账面价值 64
逆向余额递减法： 逆向余额递减法并非常用的折旧方法。它会导致折旧费用随时间推移而增加。当资产主要通过耗用被消耗，且初期产量处于较低水平但随时间逐步攀升时，该方法可能是恰当的。然而，此类情况较为罕见，采用工作量法计提折旧可能更为恰当，因为它反映了资产经济利益的消耗情况。
年数总和法（数字总和法） ：该方法在效果上与余额递减法相似，尽管计算机制不同。如果某项资产预计可使用（例如）12个期间（年、月等），则将数字1至12相加（合计78）；第1期计提12/78，下一期计提11/78，依此类推。
工作量法（或产量法）： 该方法将折旧与资产的估计使用量或产出挂钩。每小时使用量或每单位产出的折旧率通过将可折旧金额除以资产的估计总服务能力（按小时或单位计量）得出。当资产的使用量在各期间差异很大时，有时会采用该方法，以更好地计量经济利益的消耗。常采用这种方式计提折旧的资产类型示例包括：按小时计费率的航空发动机；以及按产量计提的垃圾填埋场和自然资源。
示例——基于工作量法计提的折旧
一台机器的成本为C100,000，预计残值为C10,000。该机器的预计总使用时间为500,000小时。因此，每小时使用量的折旧率为C0.18（(C100,000 − C10,000) 除以 500,000）。
示例——基于估计使用量计提的折旧
购置一处垃圾填埋场发生C500万的成本。该垃圾填埋场拥有200万立方米的空间。适用于该场地成本的折旧率计算为每使用1立方米空间C2.5。第一年使用了200,000立方米，按每立方米C2.5计提的折旧为C500,000。
EX 22.94.2 – 主体可以变更为采用“工作量法”计算折旧吗？
A主体拥有并运营一家地方航空公司。飞机发动机在必须更换之前可飞行5,000个飞行小时。该主体计划在更换前充分利用发动机固有的5,000个小时。飞机每年的飞行里程保持一致。A主体确定按飞行小时（工作量法）对发动机计提折旧最恰当地反映了经济利益的消耗方式。然而，由于每年的飞行小时数基本一致，A主体采用直线法折旧作为飞行小时的替代方法。
在某一季度，由于实施了旅行限制，A主体的机队停飞。目前尚不清楚这些限制何时解除。A主体在季度末重新评估折旧方法，并确定直线法现在不再是工作量法的合理替代方法。此外，A主体确定直线法不再反映资产所包含经济利益的消耗。因此，管理层将其折旧方法变更为工作量法，并遵循IAS 8中关于会计估计变更的要求。
一旦封锁结束，A主体不太可能就这些资产将其折旧方法改回直线法。这是因为工作量法将继续反映发动机所包含经济利益的预期消耗方式。
B主体拥有并运营一家地方航空公司。飞机发动机在必须更换之前可飞行5,000个飞行小时，这足以覆盖七年的飞行航线。然而，该主体的政策是无论飞行小时数多少，每五年更换一次发动机。因此，B主体确定发动机的经济利益受时间限制，直线法折旧是最恰当的折旧方法。
在某一季度，由于实施了旅行限制，B主体的机队停飞。目前尚不清楚这些限制何时解除。遵循其每五年更换一次发动机的政策，B主体仍认为发动机的使用寿命为五年。鉴于B主体已确定发动机的经济利益受时间限制，变更为工作量法计提折旧是不恰当的。B主体应在飞机停飞期间继续计提折旧。

政府实施了封锁措施，因此承租人C无法开业其租赁门店。此外，进入该门店受到极大限制，承租人C不被允许在门店内进行任何翻新工作，也不被允许将该门店用作线上销售的仓库；但承租人C的商品仍存放在该场所内。承租人C在租赁期内按直线法对其使用权资产计提折旧，因为该方法最密切地反映了租赁资产所包含的未来经济利益的预期消耗方式；对于该使用权资产，主要的限制因素是承租人在租赁期内享有使用标的资产的合同权利的时间期限。
在封锁期间，承租人C停止对该资产计提折旧或变更其折旧方法都是不恰当的。这是因为在直线法折旧下，资产闲置时折旧并不停止[IAS 16 第55段]。
EX 22.98.1 – 确定恰当的折旧方法
准则参考：IAS 16 第56段 正文参考：22.98
B主体制造工业化学品，并在生产过程中使用混合机。混合机的产量年复一年保持稳定，且该机器可用于生产不同产品。然而，维护成本逐年增加，而且每隔五年就会推出新一代机器（较现有机器有重大改进）。
管理层应根据产量确定折旧方法。由于产量年复一年保持稳定，直线法折旧可能是基于使用量方法的合理替代方法。
在确定混合机的使用寿命时，应考虑维护成本或技术陈旧过时等因素。
EX 22.99.1 – 重估资产的折旧基础
准则参考：IAS 16 第48段 正文参考：22.99
本准则未规定应以何种资产价值作为计算年度折旧费用的基础。年度平均值可能是最佳计量方式，但在实务中，只要在每个期间一贯使用，期初余额或期末余额均可使用。在确定当年的折旧费用时，最常用的是期初余额加上后续新增资产的成本。这避免了重新计算年初已计提并已用于（例如）中期报告的折旧。然而，如果年末重估导致价值发生重大变动，则可能会产生问题。
EX 22.100.1 – 使用寿命估计的变更
准则参考：IAS 16 第51段 正文参考：22.100

A主体于20X0年1月1日以C100,000购买了一项资产，该资产的预计使用寿命为10年，残值为零。该主体一直采用直线法按每年C10,000计提折旧。20X4年1月1日，当该资产的账面净值为C60,000时，董事们复核了预计使用寿命，并认为该资产可能还能再使用四年，从而将总使用寿命修订为八年。该主体应修订年度折旧计提额，将未摊销成本（即C60,000）在修订后的剩余四年使用寿命内分摊。因此，未来四年应按每年C15,000计提折旧。
或者，假设使用寿命仍为10年，该主体可能决定自20X4年1月1日起，采用年数总和法（数字总和法）计算将比直线法更公允地列报。如果是这样，由于该资产仍有六年的剩余使用寿命，20X4年的折旧费用将为C17,143（即C60,000 × 6 / (6 + 5 + 4 + 3 + 2 + 1)）。
EX 22.100.2 – 购入固定资产使用寿命的缩短
准则参考：IAS 16 第51段 正文参考：22.100
A主体在年内进行了一项收购。被收购主体拥有一套大型计算机系统，收购方现在打算在几年后将其更换。该计算机设备的公允价值在收购日已确定，而决定更换它属于收购后事项。管理层希望立即计提额外折旧，并将其列报为与该收购相关的特殊项目。这是否恰当？
更换计算机系统的决定属于收购后决策。它不影响在购买对价分摊中所分配的公允价值。即使在作出该决定后，也不会立即产生减值，因为现金产出单元的未来现金流量能够支持其资产的账面价值。然而，由于已决定在几年后报废该设备，其账面价值现在应在修订后较短的使用寿命内计提折旧。残值和使用寿命至少必须在每个财务年度终了进行复核。如果任一项被修订，该变更应作为会计估计变更采用未来适用法进行会计处理。
FAQ 22.100.3 – 气候相关因素如何影响资产的使用寿命和残值？
准则参考：IAS 16 第51段 正文参考：22.100
由于气候变化（无论是自然气候事件还是政府行动的结果），可能需要重新评估厂场和设备的使用寿命和残值。例如，消费者行为的变化或碳排放相关法规的出台，可能会影响IAS 16范围内多项资产的使用寿命和/或残值。气候影响可能导致资产提前陈旧过时、对其使用施加法律限制，或导致资产无法使用。以下示例说明了气候变化的可能影响。
全球邮轮航运公司ABC plc.正在考虑环保法规变化对其业务的影响。相当数量的港口已经禁止较旧及高排放的邮轮入港，且该公司预计未来此类港口的数量将会增加。事实上，该公司预计欧洲和北美等整个地区将在未来十年内禁止使用船用重油的邮轮进入其港口。
为了继续在这些地区开展业务，该公司被迫在未来十年内以污染更低的船舶替换现有船队。
由于即将出台的法规和船队替换计划，该公司可能需要缩短其船舶的使用寿命并降低其残值，因为该公司预计较旧及高排放船舶在二手市场上的价格将会下跌。
在重新评估厂场和设备的使用寿命和残值时，主体可能会考虑气候相关因素，例如：
- 行业法规的（潜在）变化；
- 公司、同行群体及整个行业作出的排放承诺；
- 消费者行为的（潜在）变化；
- 技术的（潜在）变化（例如新能源的使用）；以及
- 厂场和设备在其使用寿命结束时的役龄，以及它们对其他公司是否仍可能具有经济利益。
主体还应考虑资产使用寿命或残值的变化是否导致该资产所属现金产出单元出现减值迹象（参见IAS 36 第12段）。
资产使用寿命和/或残值的变更属于会计估计变更，需要按照IAS 16和IAS 8的要求采用未来适用法处理。会计估计变更需要按照IAS 8第39段予以披露。披露内容应包括作出变更的原因以及会计估计变更的性质和金额（参见第3.30段及后续段落）。
如果存在重大估计不确定性，主体应按照IAS 1第125段和第129段披露重新评估使用寿命/残值所依据假设的性质详情，包括估计不确定性的来源和敏感性分析（参见第4.155段及后续段落）。
EX 22.101.1 – 修订资产的残值
准则参考：IAS 16 第54段 正文参考：22.101
20X1年1月1日，一家财务年度截止日为12月31日的主体以C1,000购买了一项资产，预计使用寿命为六年。该资产在购置日的估计残值为C100，截至第2年末该估计未发生变化。由于技术的突破性进步，残值有所下降；截至20X3年10月31日，估计残值为C81。经开展减值评估，未发现减值。
在就修订后的残值作出任何调整之前，20X3年10月31日的账面价值为C575（即34个月内每月计提折旧C12.50）。从账面价值中扣除修订后的残值后，剩余C494（即C575 − C81）将在剩余三年零两个月的使用寿命内计提折旧。因此，20X3年最后两个月的折旧为C26，20X3年末的账面价值为C549。
当对残值作出新估计时，这可能会对当年及未来年度的折旧费用产生影响[IAS 8 第38段]。如果重新估计并非由特定事件驱动而是在年末进行的（这是最低要求），则需要运用判断以确定年内是否存在残值发生变化的更早时点。
在某个时点，修订后的残值可能会超过账面价值。在这种情况下，折旧费用调整为零，且任何超出部分不予转回。如果在处置时销售收入超过当时的账面价值，则可能确认处置利得。
EX 22.104.1 – 投保资产重置产生的利得
准则参考：IAS 16 第65段 正文参考：22.104
A主体账面列示的厂房和机器设备价值为C200,000。这些厂房和机器设备在火灾中被毁。这些资产投保了“以新换旧”险，保险公司用成本为C200万的新机器予以替换。替换机器由保险公司采购，主体并未收到C200万的现金赔偿。
A主体在终止确认厂房和机器设备的账面价值时将损失计入利润表。一旦收款基本确定，A主体应按照IAS 37在利润表中单独确认一项应收款项以及由保险赔偿产生的利得。该应收款项应按保险人将提供的资产的公允价值计量。
EX 22.105.1 – 保险赔偿的不确定性
准则参考：IAS 16 第65段 正文参考：22.105
一项资产在火灾中被毁并已提出保险索赔。对于该资产的损失是否在保险单承保范围内存在不确定性。该补偿属于一项或有资产。然而，如果保险公司接受索赔并同意支付赔偿，则该资产不再是或有资产，该补偿应计入利润表。

Objective and scope (paras 23.1- 23.20)
23.1 This chapter addresses the IFRS requirements for investment property as follows:
- Classification as an investment property.
- Initial recognition and measurement.
- Subsequent measurement.
23.2 Property in the scope of IAS 16, ‘Property, plant and equipment’, is covered in chapter 22 para 6.

23.3 Properties that meet the definition of investment property are in the scope of IAS 40. The scope is wide and does not only apply to investment property entities. Investment property held by entities whose main activity is something other than investment holding and management is still in the scope of IAS 40.

23.4 Investment property is land or a building which an entity owns or leases with the intention of earning rent or holding for capital appreciation. A building which is held for use in the production or supply of goods or for administrative purposes is not an investment property and is in the scope of IAS 16 (see chapter 22 para 6). Properties constructed and sold in the ordinary course of business are in the scope of IAS 2, ‘Inventory’ (see cha
EX 23.4.1 – Land used for production or supply of goods or services EX 23.4.2 – Land used to earn rentals
23.5 IAS 40 does not include:
- Biological assets related to agricultural activity, which are dealt with by IAS 41.
- Mineral rights and mineral reserves, such as oil, natural gas and similar non-regenerative assets.

23.6 Investment property acquired under a lease is recognised and initially measured based on the guidance in IFRS 16 ‘Leases’ (see chapter 15 para 56). IAS 40 applies to all aspects of subsequent measurement for investment property acquired under a lease.
23.7 A right-of-use asset relating to property which is held to earn rentals and/or for capital appreciation is an investment property in the scope of IAS 40.
[The next paragraph is 23.9.]

23.9 Management should assess whether its acquisition of an investment property meets the definition of a business in IFRS 3. Acquisition of a business is accounted for in accordance with IFRS 3 (see chapter 29 para 6).
Classification as an investment property
23.10 Investment property includes:
- Land held for long-term appreciation in value, rather than for short-term sale in the ordinary course of business.
- Land whose future use has not yet been determined.
- A building owned or held under a lease and leased out under an operating lease.
- A building that is vacant, but held to be leased out under an operating lease.
- Property that is being constructed or developed for future use as investment property.
EX 23.10.1 – Land with undetermined use
23.11 Investment property excludes:
- Property intended for sale in the ordinary course of business or for development and resale.
- Owner-occupied property, including property held for such use or for redevelopment prior to such use.
- Property that is leased to another entity under a finance lease.

23.12 Owner-occupied property is property held by the owner, or a right-of-use asset relating to property held by a lessee, for use in the production or supply of goods or services or for administrative purposes.

23.13 Owner-occupied property is used in conjunction with the other assets of the entity, such as plant and machinery and inventory. It does not generate cash flows independently of the other assets of the entity. By contrast, investment property is held to earn rentals and for capital appreciation. It generates cash flows independently of the other assets of the entity.

23.14 The purchase of a property that is to be demolished immediately (or shortly after acquisition) and redeveloped for resale is not treated as an investment property. The property was not acquired for its rental potential or for a capital gain on its disposal.

23.15 A property could be partly owner-occupied and partly held for rental income or capital appreciation. For example, an entity might own a four-storey block and use the bottom two storeys for its administrative function, whilst renting out the upper two floors. If the entity could sell floors separately or lease them out on a finance lease, it should treat the lower half of the property as owner-occupied property (IAS 16) and the upper half as
EX 23.15.1 – Accounting for multi-purpose properties

23.16 An entity can provide ancillary services, such as maintenance and security, to the third party occupants of a property owned by the entity. Services that are an insignificant element of the whole arrangement do not affect the classification of the property as an investment property.
23.17 An owner-managed hotel is regarded as an owner-occupied property rather than an investment property. The property is being used to a significant extent for the supply of goods and services.
EX 23.17.1 – Judgement involved in ancillary services
23.18 Entities should disclose the criteria used in assessing whether something is investment property or owner-occupied property where this involves judgement.

23.19 One group entity might lease property to another entity in the same group. The property is not treated as investment property in the consolidated financial statements. The property is owner-occupied from the group’s point of view. The property will be treated as investment property in the separate financial statements of the entity that leases the property out to the other entity.
EX 23.19.1 – Property occupied by a subsidiary

23.20 Property owned or held under a finance lease by a group entity and occupied by an associate or a joint venture is accounted for as investment property in the consolidated financial statements. The property is not owner-occupied from the group’s perspective, because associates and joint ventures are not considered part of the group for consolidation purposes.

Recognition (paras 23.21-23.44)

23.21 Investment property is recognised when it is probable that the future economic benefits associated with the property will flow to the entity and the cost of the property to the entity can be reliably measured.

23.22 Judgement is required when determining the unit of account; that is how individual items are identified and the extent to which items are aggregated. These judgements might include whether individual items are aggregated or whether large items should be recognised as separate components.

23.23 Land and buildings elements of a property are considered separately for the purpose of lease classification in IFRS 16. If the lessee’s interests in both land and buildings are classified as investment property and the fair value model is adopted, they are treated together as one unit of account.
[IFRS 16 App B para B55].

23.24 Disaggregation or componentisation is the separation of an asset into its significant components. Each component of an investment property with a cost that is significant in relation to the total cost of the property is identified and treated separately. These components might include lifts or an air-conditioning system that have a shorter useful life than the rest of the property. The components are considered separately for the purposes o

23.25 The costs of day-to-day servicing and maintenance of a property are not recognised as an asset, because they do not add to the future economic benefits of the item. These costs maintain the asset’s potential to deliver the future economic benefits that were expected when the asset was originally acquired. Day-to-day servicing costs include costs of labour and consumables and could include the cost of small replacement parts.
23.26 Initial measurement will depend on whether the property is owned or held under a lease.
23.27 Owned investment property is measured initially at cost plus transaction costs.

23.28 ‘Cost’ is defined as “the amount of cash or cash equivalents paid or the fair value of other consideration given to acquire an asset at the time of its acquisition or construction or, where applicable, the amount attributed to that asset when initially recognised in accordance with the specific requirements of other IFRS, for example, IFRS 2”.

23.29 Cost is the purchase price, including directly attributable expenditure. Directly attributable expenditure includes transaction costs, such as legal fees and property transfer taxes. If the asset is being constructed, it will also include borrowing costs.

23.30 Directly attributable costs can be capitalised only until the investment property is “capable of operating in the manner intended by management”. If investment property is purchased or constructed and can operate in that manner immediately, but is not brought into use immediately, further costs incurred cannot be capitalised. 23.40 An investment property might be acquired in exchange for another non-monetary asset or assets or for a combination of non-monetary and monetary assets. The cost of such an acquired investment property is measured at fair value of the consideration given, unless:
- the exchange transaction has no commercial substance; or
- the fair value of the asset received and the asset given up cannot be reliably measured.
This applies even if an entity cannot immediately derecognise the asset given up. If the acquired item is not measured at fair value, it is measured at the carrying amount of the asset given up.

23.41 A transaction has commercial substance if the entity’s future cash flows are expected to change as a result of the transaction. Exchange transactions will have a business purpose, and an exchange of assets that are not identical is likely to result in a change in the entity’s cash flows. If the expected difference in the cash flows is significant, the exchange has commercial substance (see chapter 22 para 37).

23.42 Commercial substance will often be clear without the entity having to perform detailed calculations. If the entity is in the same position as it was before the transaction and no significant change has taken place in its net assets, no gain or loss is recognised on the transaction, and the cost of the new asset is the carrying amount of the asset given up.
23.43 The fair value of the asset received might provide evidence of an impairment in the asset given up. The asset given up is written down, and this value is assigned to the new asset.

23.44 The fair value of the asset given up is used to measure the cost of the asset received where both the fair value of the asset given up and the fair value of the asset received can be measured with equal reliability. If the fair value of the asset received can be measured more reliably, that value is used.

The leases are intended to increase the possibility of selling the property, rather than to earn rental income on a continuing basis, and the property is not held for capital appreciation. EX 23.72.2 – Transfer of inventory (2)
Reference to standard: IAS 40 para 57(d) Reference to standing text: 23.72
Renting until market activity improves

Entity B, a property developer with a history of developing properties for sale immediately after completion, constructs a residential property for sale. However, as property prices are at a multi-year low and there are few buyers/transactions in the market, entity B decides to rent out the property until market activity improves. How should entity B account for the property?

Entity B needs to carefully assess whether the property should continue to be classified as inventory or be transferred to investment properties in accordance with paragraph 57(d) of IAS 40. The property should continue to be classified as inventory if this is consistent with entity B’s strategy for this property. However, it should be transferred to investment property if there is a change in management’s intention to hold the property for futur

Determining the correct classification of such a property requires judgement. The inception of a lease with third parties, in itself, does not automatically require reclassification as investment property, although it might be indicative of a change in management’s intention.

The property can, therefore, continue to be classified as inventory to the extent that it is available for immediate sale in its present condition, at a current market price, in the ordinary course of business. Factors to consider include:
- Is the property actively marketed for sale?
- Is the property available for sale at a price that is reasonable relative to its current market value?
- Does a market exist for properties with sitting tenants, with longer lease terms, such that the property is in a condition to be sold immediately?

- Where there is no market for properties with sitting tenants, are the terms of any leases less than the length of the period that other similar properties take to be sold in the ordinary course of business under current market conditions?

If the entity is unwilling to sell the property at the current depressed market price, it is likely that the property’s intended use has changed to meet the definition of an investment property – that is, held to earn rental income and for capital appreciation. Factors to consider are:
- Has the board decided to postpone the sale of the property until the market price recovers?
- Is there a change in the business plan that takes into account the rental income earned and the necessary future maintenance expenses?
- Has this change in business plan been publicly announced?
- Is the property no longer actively marketed for sale?
- Is there currently no active market for similar properties?
- Is the property available for sale only at a price that is not reasonable relative to its current market value?

23.1 本章阐述国际财务报告准则（IFRS）对投资性房地产的以下要求：
23.2 属于《国际会计准则第16号——不动产、厂场和设备》（IAS 16）范围内的房地产，在第22章第6段中予以阐述。
23.3 符合投资性房地产定义的房地产均属于 IAS 40 的范围。该范围非常广泛，并不仅适用于投资性房地产主体。主营业务并非投资持有和管理的主体所持有的投资性房地产，同样属于 IAS 40 的范围。

23.4 投资性房地产是指主体拥有或租赁的、旨在赚取租金或持有以备资本增值的土地或建筑物。为用于生产或提供商品或行政管理目的而持有的建筑物不属于投资性房地产，而属于 IAS 16 的范围（参见第22章第6段）。在正常经营过程中建造并出售的房地产属于《国际会计准则第2号——存货》（IAS 2）的范围（参见第25章第2段）。符合分类为持有待售条件（或包含在分类为持有待售的处置组中）的投资性房地产，按照 IFRS 5 进行计量（参见第30章第10段）。
EX 23.4.1 – 用于生产或提供商品或服务的土地
EX 23.4.2 – 用于赚取租金的土地
23.5 IAS 40 不包括：
与农业活动相关的生物资产，由 IAS 41 规范。
矿产权和矿产储量，如石油、天然气及类似的非再生性资产。
23.6 通过租赁取得的投资性房地产，根据《国际财务报告准则第16号——租赁》（IFRS 16）的指引进行确认和初始计量（参见第15章第56段）。IAS 40 适用于通过租赁取得的投资性房地产后续计量的所有方面。
23.7 与为赚取租金和/或资本增值而持有的房地产相关的使用权资产，属于 IAS 40 范围内的投资性房地产。
23.9 管理层应评估其对投资性房地产的收购是否符合 IFRS 3 中业务的定义。业务收购应按照 IFRS 3 进行会计处理（参见第29章第6段）。
\[IAS 40 第14A段\]。
23.10 投资性房地产包括：
为长期资本增值而持有的土地，而非为在正常经营过程中短期出售而持有的土地。
尚未确定未来用途的土地。
自有或通过租赁持有并以经营租赁方式租出的建筑物。
空置但持有以备以经营租赁方式租出的建筑物。
正在建造或开发以备未来作为投资性房地产使用的房地产。
EX 23.10.1 – 尚未确定未来用途的土地
23.11 投资性房地产不包括：
拟在正常经营过程中出售或开发后转售的房地产。
自用房地产，包括为自用目的而持有的房地产，或在自用前拟进行重新开发的房地产。
以融资租赁方式租给其他主体的房地产。
23.12 自用房地产是指由所有者持有的、或由承租人作为使用权资产持有的、用于生产或提供商品或服务或用于行政管理目的的房地产。
23.13 自用房地产与主体的其他资产（如厂场、机器设备和存货）共同使用，无法独立于主体的其他资产产生现金流量。相比之下，投资性房地产是为赚取租金和资本增值而持有的，能够独立于主体的其他资产产生现金流量。
23.14 购入后拟立即（或短期内）拆除并重新开发以备转售的房地产，不作为投资性房地产处理。该房地产并非为获取租金潜力或处置时的资本利得而购入。

23.15 一项房地产可能部分自用，部分用于赚取租金收入或资本增值。例如，某主体可能拥有一栋四层建筑，将下面两层用于行政管理职能，同时将上面两层出租。如果该主体能够将各楼层单独出售或以融资租赁方式单独出租，则应将房地产的下半部分作为自用房地产（IAS 16）处理，将上半部分作为投资性房地产（IAS 40）处理。如果各部分不能单独出售或以融资租赁方式单独出租，则整栋建筑物应整体作为投资性房地产或整体作为自用房地产处理。如果自用部分不重大，则整栋建筑物可以分类为投资性房地产。
EX 23.15.1 – 多用途房地产的会计处理
23.16 主体可以向其所拥有房地产的第三方占用人提供附带服务，例如维护和安保服务。如果在整个安排中这些服务属于不重大的组成部分，则不影响该房地产分类为投资性房地产。
23.17 由所有者自行管理的酒店被视为自用房地产，而非投资性房地产，因为该房地产在很大程度上用于提供商品和服务。
EX 23.17.1 – 附带服务涉及的判断
23.18 在判断某项资产属于投资性房地产还是自用房地产涉及重大判断的情况下，主体应披露作出该判断所采用的标准。
23.19 同一集团内的一个主体可能会将房地产出租给同一集团内的另一主体。该房地产在合并财务报表中不作为投资性房地产处理。从集团的角度来看，该房地产属于自用房地产。而在将该房地产出租给另一主体的主体的单独财务报表中，该房地产将作为投资性房地产处理。
EX 23.19.1 – 由子公司占用的房地产
23.20 由集团内某主体拥有或以融资租赁方式持有、并由联营企业或合营企业占用的房地产，在合并财务报表中应作为投资性房地产进行会计处理。从集团的角度来看，该房地产不属于自用房地产，因为就合并目的而言，联营企业和合营企业不被视为集团的组成部分。
\[IFRS 10 附录A\]。
23.21 当与投资性房地产相关的未来经济利益很可能流入主体，且该房地产的成本能够可靠计量时，应确认投资性房地产。
23.22 在确定计量单元（即如何识别单项资产以及各项资产的汇总程度）时需要运用判断。这些判断可能包括是否将单项资产汇总，或者是否应将大型项目确认为单独的组成部分。
23.23 就 IFRS 16 中的租赁分类而言，房地产中的土地和建筑物要素应分开考虑。如果承租人在土地和建筑物中的权益均分类为投资性房地产并采用公允价值模式，则两者作为一个整体计量单元处理。
\[IFRS 16 附录B 第B55段\]。
23.24 拆分或组成部分划分是指将一项资产拆分为其重大组成部分。投资性房地产中成本相对于该房地产总成本而言重大的每一组成部分，均应单独识别和处理。这些组成部分可能包括使用寿命短于房地产其余部分的电梯或空调系统。如果主体采用成本模式，在确定折旧年限和折旧方法时应对这些组成部分单独考虑。
23.25 房地产的日常维修和保养成本不确认为资产，因为它们不会增加该项目的未来经济利益。这些成本仅用于维持该资产在最初取得时预期能够带来的未来经济利益的潜力。日常维修成本包括人工成本和易耗品成本，也可能包括小型替换部件的成本。
23.26 初始计量取决于该房地产是自有的还是通过租赁持有的。
23.27 自有投资性房地产应按成本加上交易费用进行初始计量。
23.28 “成本”定义为“在购置或建造资产时为取得该资产而支付的现金或现金等价物金额或付出的其他对价的公允价值，或在适用情况下，按照其他国际财务报告准则（例如 IFRS 2）的具体规定在初始确认时归属于该资产的金额”。
23.29 成本是指购买价款，包括可直接归属的支出。可直接归属的支出包括交易费用，例如法律费用和房产转让税。如果该资产正在建造中，成本还将包括借款费用。
23.30 可直接归属的成本只能在投资性房地产“能够以管理层预期的方式运行”之前予以资本化。如果购入或建造的投资性房地产已能够立即以该方式运行，但尚未立即投入使用，则后续发生的成本不能资本化。该原则与 IAS 16 中确定资本化计入不动产、厂场和设备（PPE）成本的原则相似（参见第22章第20段）。
FAQ 23.30.1 – 自行建造的投资性房地产应在何时停止成本资本化？
EX 23.30.2 – 使资产达到预定可使用状态的后续成本
23.31 可资本化的成本不包括：
开办费，除非其对于使房地产达到能够以管理层预期的方式运行所必需的状态是必要的。
在投资性房地产达到计划出租率之前发生的经营亏损。
在建造或开发该房地产过程中发生的非正常数量的材料、人工或其他资源浪费，因为这些浪费不会带来经济利益。
EX 23.31.1 – 不予计入的成本
23.32 为促使承租人签订租赁合同而向其提供的激励不属于建造成本；它们是与承租人就使用租赁资产所约定净对价的组成部分。出租人将激励成本作为总租赁付款额的抵减项，并按照 IFRS 16 进行确认。参见第15章第134段。
EX 15.134.2 – 租赁激励应如何进行会计处理？
23.34 投资性房地产的成本为该资产确认日的等价现金价格。投资性房地产可能在延期付款条件下购入。在此类情况下，其成本为折现后的金额。折现金额与总付款额之间的差额在信用期内作为应付利息处理，除非其符合 IAS 23 的规定在建造期间予以资本化（参见第22章第34段）。
23.35 主体可能会购入一项房地产（土地和建筑物），目的是在购入后立即（或在不久的将来）拆除该建筑物并建造新建筑物取而代之。关于该建筑物的购入和拆除成本的详细讨论，参见第22章第21段。
EX 23.35.1 – 拆除成本
租赁房地产——承租人视角
23.36 承租人作为使用权资产持有的投资性房地产，根据 IFRS 16 进行初始确认（参见第15章第70段）。
23.37 如果通过租赁持有的房地产权益分类为投资性房地产并按公允价值进行会计处理，则被计量的是该租赁权益（即使用权资产），而非标的房地产本身。
\[IAS 40 第40A段\]。
23.40 投资性房地产可能通过以一项或多项其他非货币性资产，或非货币性资产与货币性资产的组合进行交换而取得。此类取得的投资性房地产的成本应按所付出对价的公允价值计量，除非：
该交换交易不具有商业实质；或
换入资产和换出资产的公允价值均无法可靠计量。
即使主体无法立即终止确认换出资产，本规定同样适用。如果换入项目不按公允价值计量，则按换出资产的账面价值计量。
23.41 如果主体的未来现金流量预期将因该交易而发生变化，则该交易具有商业实质。交换交易通常具有商业目的，且非相同资产的交换很可能导致主体的现金流量发生变化。如果预期现金流量的差异是重大的，则该交换具有商业实质（参见第22章第37段）。
23.42 商业实质通常无需主体进行详细计算即可明确判断。如果主体在交易后的处境与交易前相同，且其净资产未发生重大变化，则不就该交易确认利得或损失，新资产的成本为换出资产的账面价值。
23.43 换入资产的公允价值可能提供换出资产已发生减值的证据。此时应减记换出资产，并将该减记后的价值分配给新资产。
23.44 如果换出资产的公允价值与换入资产的公允价值能够以同等可靠性计量，则使用换出资产的公允价值计量换入资产的成本。如果换入资产的公允价值能够更可靠地计量，则使用换入资产的公允价值。
初始确认后发生的成本（第23.45–23.81段）
23.45 一旦投资性房地产达到管理层预期可使用状态，成本确认即停止。主体可能会在日后就该资产发生进一步成本。后续成本仅在满足资产确认条件时才予以资本化。所有其他后续成本在发生当期确认为费用。
EX 23.45.1 – 后续支出
23.46 一项资产可能由若干不同的重大组成部分构成。每一组成部分在计提折旧时应单独处理，并在其各自的使用寿命内计提折旧。如果使用寿命和消耗模式相似，可以将这些组成部分合并计提折旧。当某一重大组成部分被替换或修复时，应终止确认旧组成部分；如果新组成部分的成本可收回，则将其资本化。
23.47 替换组成部分的成本如果满足确认条件，应确认为资产。被替换部件的账面价值应予以终止确认，同时消除被替换部件的成本和累计折旧。如果无法确定被替换部件或组成部分的成本和折旧，则替换成本可作为被替换部件成本的合理替代值。
EX 23.47.1 – 采用成本模式确认的投资性房地产的资本性改良支出
23.48 如果投资性房地产按公允价值计量，则不太可能对各组成部分进行单独识别和会计处理。任何组成部分的价值减损都将反映在公允价值计量中。
23.49 采用 IFRS 16 的主体可以选择公允价值模式或成本模式作为其会计政策。一旦选定，该政策应适用于主体的所有投资性房地产（第23.50段所述情况除外）。
FAQ 23.49.1 – 成本模式下公允价值的披露
23.50 对于所有支持特定负债的投资性房地产——只要该负债支付的回报直接与包括该投资性房地产在内的特定资产的公允价值或回报挂钩——主体可以统一选择公允价值模式或成本模式，而不受其对所有其他投资性房地产所选会计政策的影响。
\[IAS 40 第32A段\]。
FAQ 23.50.1 – 支持特定负债的投资性房地产
23.51 在 IAS 40 下采用成本模式的主体，仍然可以对其自用房地产采用重估模式，因为自用房地产是按照 IAS 16 进行会计处理的。
\[IAS 40 附录B 第B51段\]。
23.52 已采用公允价值模式的主体通常不应在日后变更为成本模式，因为这种变更不太可能提供可靠且更相关的信息。
23.53 鼓励但不要求主体聘请具有相关专业资格、且对所估值房地产的地理位置和类别具有近期经验的独立评估师进行估值。
FAQ 23.49.1 – 成本模式下公允价值的披露
23.54 采用成本模式的主体应按成本减去累计折旧和任何累计减值损失后的金额列示投资性房地产。这与 IAS 16 中的成本模式一致（参见第22章第65段）。
23.55 成本模式下的投资性房地产，如果其账面价值超过其可收回金额，则已发生减值。
23.56 公允价值按照 IFRS 13 确定。公允价值是指“市场参与者在计量日发生的有序交易中，出售一项资产所能收到或者转移一项负债所需支付的价格”（参见第5章第2段）。
\[IFRS 13 第9段\]。\[IAS 40 附录B 第B53段\]。
23.57 公允价值反映当前租赁的租金收入以及市场参与者基于当前状况对未来租金收入作出的其他假设。当前租赁协议可能规定每五年按通货膨胀率加上固定百分比进行一次调租。基于官方预测的通货膨胀率估计未来租金是合理的。
23.58 准则存在一项可推翻的推定，即公允价值能够持续可靠地计量。以下情况不适用公允价值计量要求：
正在建造中的投资性房地产，其公允价值目前无法可靠计量，但主体预期在建造过程中的较晚时点或建造完成时能够可靠计量其公允价值；以及
在极少数情况下且仅在初始确认时，公允价值无法持续可靠计量的投资性房地产。
EX 23.58.1 – 公允价值无法可靠计量
FAQ 23.58.2 – 在不确定环境下确定投资性房地产的公允价值
23.59 一旦主体能够可靠计量在建投资性房地产的公允价值，或建造完成，主体应按公允价值计量该房地产。在此之前，该房地产应按照 IAS 16 下的成本模式进行计量。
\[IAS 40 第53A段\]。
23.60 将租赁资产从初始确认金额（成本）后续重新计量至公允价值，不应产生初始利得或损失。取得日的公允价值扣除预期租赁负债后通常为零。但是，如果重新计量至公允价值发生在不同时点，则可能产生利得或损失。在初始确认后，确定公允价值的基础除了租赁付款额和折现率外，还会考虑其他因素。这种情况可能发生在初始确认之后才选择采用公允价值模式的情形下。
23.61 当且仅当可比房地产交易市场不活跃，且无法获得公允价值的替代可靠计量（例如基于折现现金流量预测的计量）时，投资性房地产的公允价值才无法持续可靠计量。例如，当近期没有交易或可获得的价格，或者判断表明在某项市场交易中卖方被迫以低于市场金额的价格出售房地产时，该市场即被视为不活跃。
23.62 在极少数情况下，某项房地产合理公允价值计量的区间可能非常大，以致于从该区间内选择任何单一公允价值计量均无助于决策。在此情况下，公允价值可能无法持续可靠计量，此时应采用成本模式。
23.63 如果主体此前已按公允价值计量某项投资性房地产，则即使可比市场交易变得不再频繁或市场价格变得不那么容易获得，主体也必须继续按公允价值对其进行计量。
23.64 将租赁资产从初始确认金额（成本）后续重新计量至公允价值，不应产生初始利得或损失。取得日的公允价值扣除预期租赁负债后通常为零。但是，如果重新计量至公允价值发生在不同时点，则可能产生利得或损失。在初始确认后，确定公允价值的基础除了租赁付款额和折现率外，还会考虑其他因素。这种情况可能发生在初始确认之后才选择采用公允价值模式的情形下。
23.65 如果写字楼以精装带家具的方式出租，家具通常包含在公允价值中。包含在投资性房地产公允价值中的家具不单独计提折旧。在每个估值日对整个房地产公允价值进行的调整都将考虑家具的状况。如果家具在资产负债表上单独确认，则不包含在房地产的公允价值中，并在其使用寿命内计提折旧。
23.66 预付或应计经营租赁收入不包括在相关投资性房地产的公允价值中。预付或应计经营租赁收入属于单独的资产或负债。
23.67 出租人为促使承租人签订租赁合同而支付给承租人的激励，初始确认为一项资产，并在租赁期内作为租赁付款额的抵减项处理（参见第15章第134段）。房地产的公允价值以净租金（扣除激励后）为基础确定。公允价值不反映出租人通过提供激励而实质上补贴的那部分毛租金。
EX 23.67.1 – 租赁激励
23.68 通过租赁持有的房地产的公允价值既反映预期现金流入，也反映预期现金流出。后者可能包括应付或有租金以及固定租赁付款额。为了得出房地产的公允价值，需要将租赁负债加回至估值金额中。租赁负债在资产负债表上确认为一项负债。实质上，这是对资产和租赁负债进行的“总额列示”（gross-up）。

23.69 主体可能认为与某项投资性房地产相关的未来付款额的现值将超过其当前估计的未来现金收款的现值。一个常见的问题是：主体租入了一项房地产，而该租赁项下的未来付款额及其他所需付款额的现值，超过了主体合理预期从未来租金收入及其他所得中获得的现值。主体首先需要就租赁负债进行会计处理，然后需要对差额（缺口）进行评估。如果该差额小于资产的账面价值，则减记该资产。如果在极少数情况下该差额超过账面价值，则将该资产减记至零。随后，主体适用 IAS 37 确认一项亏损合同的预计负债。该预计负债的金额同样参照 IAS 37 计量（参见第16章第71段）。
23.70 因重估至公允价值而产生的利得和损失，在其发生的当期计入损益（利润表）。
23.71 仅当房地产的用途发生变更时，主体才应将房地产转入或转出投资性房地产。用途变更必须有确凿证据；仅仅是管理层意图的改变，不足以构成用途变更的证据。
EX 23.71.1 – 关于投资性房地产转换的修订
23.72 用途变更的示例包括：

转出类别 转入类别 何时转换？ 成本模式下的投资性房地产 公允价值模式下的投资性房地产 投资性房地产 不动产、厂场和设备（PPE） 在开始自用或以自用为目的开始开发时，将投资性房地产转换为自用房地产。\[IAS 40 第57(a)段\]。 按账面价值进行转换。不确认利得或损失。 转换日的公允价值成为按照 IAS 16 进行后续会计处理的认定成本。 不动产、厂场和设备（PPE） 投资性房地产 在自用结束时，将自用房地产转换为投资性房地产。\[IAS 40 第57(c)段\]。 按账面价值进行转换。不确认利得或损失。 截至转换日适用 IAS 16。在转换日按公允价值计量该房地产，任何重估利得或损失均按照 IAS 16 作为重估处理。 投资性房地产 存货 在以出售为目的开始开发之日，将投资性房地产转换为存货。\[IAS 40 第57(b)段\]。 按账面价值进行转换。不确认利得或损失。 转换日的公允价值成为按照 IAS 2 进行后续会计处理的认定成本。 存货 投资性房地产 当作为存货持有的房地
23.73 以下情况不发生转换：
未经开发即出售的投资性房地产
如果一项投资性房地产拟未经开发即予以处置，则其用途并未发生变更。该房地产不转换为存货，而是继续保留在投资性房地产中，直至处置或以其他方式终止确认。\[IAS 40 第58段\]。
为继续作为投资性房地产使用而开发的投资性房地产
为继续作为未来投资性房地产使用而进行开发的投资性房地产，同样继续保留在投资性房地产中，不转换为存货或自用房地产。其用途并未发生变更。\[IAS 40 第58段\]。
EX 23.73.1 – 转换的时点
23.74 投资性房地产在处置时，或者在永久退出使用且预计不能从其处置中产生未来经济利益时，应予以终止确认。
23.75 处置可能通过出售进行，在此情况下，处置日按照 IFRS 15（IAS 18）的原则确定；或者通过签订融资租赁或售后租回交易进行，在此情况下，处置日适用 IFRS 16 确定。关于 IFRS 15 参见第11章第153段，关于 IFRS 16 参见第15章第118段和第152段。
23.76 对于因难以持续获取可靠公允价值而采用成本模式计量的房地产（尽管主体对其他投资性房地产的常规政策是采用公允价值模式），其计入损益（利润表）的处置利得或损失应单独披露。
23.77 投资性房地产处置或报废的利得或损失，按处置净收益（扣除直接处置费用后）与处置日账面价值（无论是成本模式还是公允价值模式下）之间的差额计算。该利得或损失计入损益（利润表），除非 IFRS 16 对售后租回交易另有规定。
FAQ 23.77.1 – IAS 1 单独披露要求
23.78 出售投资性房地产的应收延期对价应折现至现值以得出等价现金价格，该金额即为销售所得。该金额与应收金额之间的差额作为利息收入处理，并采用实际利率法在直至实际收款的期间内予以确认。
23.79 主体应适用 IAS 37 对处置后保留的负债或或有负债进行确认、计量和披露。\[IAS 40 第71段\]。此类或有负债的示例可能包括：同意补偿买方可能产生的任何税务负债、弥补环境损害的任何潜在责任，或弥补租户拖欠应付租金的损失。在确定卖方是否已转移该房地产所有权上的几乎全部风险和报酬、从而确认销售是否已发生时，也应考虑此类负债和或有负债。
23.80 因投资性房地产发生减值、损失或其他处置而来自第三方的补偿，在成为应收款项时计入损益（利润表）。
23.81 资产的减值或损失、与该减值或损失相关的索赔要求，以及随后购买或建造替换资产，属于独立的经济事项，应分别进行会计处理。就确认和披露而言，不得合并这些独立经济事项的影响。因此，应按以下方式进行会计处理：
减值按照 IAS 36 进行确认。
报废或处置按照第23.74–23.79段所述进行会计处理。
来自第三方的补偿在成为应收款项时计入损益（利润表）。
修复资产以及购买或建造替换资产的成本，按照 IAS 40 的确认和计量规则确定并确认为投资性房地产。
EX 23.81.1 – 来自第三方的补偿
23.82 准则要求披露公允价值调整产生的净利得或损失，但未规定其在利润表中的列报方式。但是，这些利得或损失应与租金收入和直接经营费用分开列示，因为后者要求单独披露。
FAQ 23.82.1 – 公允价值利得和损失的列报
23.83 IFRS 16 规定了租金收入的会计处理。关于 IFRS 16，请参见第15章第134段。
23.84 租金收入通常作为总收入的一部分列报。IFRS 16 要求披露当期确认的或有租金，以及前五年每年应收的经营租赁付款额和五年以上应收的经营租赁付款额总额。出租人还必须披露定性和定量信息以评估租赁的影响；这可能包括出租人租赁安排的性质以及其如何管理租赁资产的余值风险。
23.85 投资性房地产在资产负债表表内非流动资产项下作为单独的行项目列报。
23.86 该准则对所有投资性房地产规定了广泛的披露要求。对于租赁房地产，IFRS 16 中还包含额外的披露要求。
23.87 对投资性房地产采用公允价值模式的主体，除需遵守 IAS 40 要求的披露外，还需遵守 IFRS 13 的披露要求（参见第5章第142段）。
EX 23.4.1 – 用于生产或提供商品或服务的土地
准则参考：IAS 40 第5段
某主体购入一块用于农业耕作的土地。该土地将用于种植甘蔗、棉花和玉米等各类农作物。该主体的商业计划是持续开展农业活动若干年，以实现两个战略目标：第一，产生现金流量为投资提供资金；第二，证明该土地用于农业目的的可行性。
该土地在用于农业目的期间分类为不动产、厂场和设备（PPE）。仅当满足 IAS 40 中的转换条件时，才将其转换为投资性房地产、存货或持有待售的非流动资产。
EX 23.4.2 – 用于赚取租金的土地
准则参考：IAS 40 第5段
主体 A 购入一块拟用于建造购物中心的空地。开工前需要取得的许可和行政审批预计耗时最长可达 18 个月。在取得所需审批之前的期间内，主体 A 将该土地用于农业活动。
该土地的农业用途可视为附属于建造购物中心这一主要目标。自初始确认起将该土地分类为投资性房地产可能是恰当的。
EX 23.10.1 – 尚未确定未来用途的土地
准则参考：IAS 40 第8(b)段
主体 A 是一家工业产品供应商。20X3 年，主体 A 在某大城市郊区购入了一块土地。该区域主要为低成本公共住房，公共交通设施非常有限。政府计划在五年后将该区域开发为工业园区，如果政府推进该计划，该土地预计将大幅增值。主体 A 的管理层尚未决定如何处置该房地产。管理层应如何对尚未确定未来用途而持有的房地产进行分类？
管理层应将该房地产分类为投资性房地产。尽管管理层尚未确定工业园区开发后该房地产的用途，但在中期内该土地是为资本增值而持有的。如果主体尚未确定将土地用作自用房地产还是在正常经营过程中短期出售，则该土地视为为资本增值而持有。
EX 23.15.1 – 多用途房地产的会计处理
准则参考：IAS 40 第10段
主体 A 拥有一座酒店度假村，其中包括位于独立建筑物内的赌场。
除赌场外，主体 A 经营酒店度假村内的酒店及其他设施；该赌场可以单独出售或以融资租赁方式出租。该赌场将出租给独立的运营商。主体 A 不再参与赌场的任何事务。如果没有酒店及其他设施的存在，赌场运营商将不愿意经营该赌场。
管理层应将酒店及其他设施分类为不动产、厂场和设备（PPE），并将赌场分类为投资性房地产。该赌场可以单独出售或以融资租赁方式出租。
如果该赌场不能单独出售或以融资租赁方式单独出租，则整个房地产将作为自用房地产处理。
EX 23.17.1 – 附带服务涉及的判断
准则参考：IAS 40 第12、13段

判断附带服务是否重大以至于该房地产不符合投资性房地产的条件可能会非常困难——例如，某家酒店的管理职能和服务提供并非由所有者执行，而是由所有者根据管理合同将这些职责转移给第三方执行。此类合同差异很大：在一种极端情况下，所有者在实质上可能是一名被动投资者；而在另一种极端情况下，所有者可能只是外包了某些职能，但仍保留了因酒店经营引起的现金流量变动的重大风险敞口。在前一种情况下，该酒店可能作为投资性房地产处理；而在后一种情况下，则作为自用房地产处理。
EX 23.19.1 – 由子公司占用的房地产
准则参考：IAS 40 第15段
主体 A 拥有一家酒店。主体 B（主体 A 的同系子公司）管理着一家连锁酒店，并就经营该连锁酒店收取管理费，但主体 A 拥有的这家酒店除外。主体 A 拥有的该酒店以每月 C2m 的租金出租给主体 B，租期五年。经营主体 A 酒店产生的任何利润或亏损均由主体 B 承担。主体 A 拥有的该酒店预计剩余使用寿命为 40 年。
在合并财务报表中，该酒店分类为不动产、厂场和设备（PPE）。从集团的角度来看，该房地产既由集团拥有又由集团管理，因此被确认为用于提供商品或服务的自用房地产。
在主体 A 的单独财务报表中，该房地产分类为投资性房地产；而主体 B 应在其单独财务报表中将该交易确认为一项租赁安排。
准则参考：IAS 40 第20段

主体 D 近期购入了一项房地产。该主体的内部法务律师花费了大量时间起草购买协议并与卖方律师就法律条款进行谈判。主体 D 的管理层估计该律师年薪、社会保障及福利待遇中可归属的份额为 C70,000，并拟将其资本化计入该房地产的成本。内部法务律师的雇佣相关成本不能资本化，因为这些成本属于与“一般及行政管理费用”相关的内部成本，并非可直接归属于购买该房地产的支出。即使主体 D 未购入该房地产，这些成本也同样会发生。与购入投资性房地产相关的外部法律费用可以作为投资性房地产成本的一部分予以资本化，但不能确认为一项单独的资产。
准则参考：IAS 40 第20段
主体 A 收购了一个大型投资性房地产组合，该收购通过贷款融资完成。作为该安排的一部分，该主体必须偿还其现有借款，并因此发生了提前还款违约金。这些解约成本不能作为房地产成本的一部分予以资本化，因为它们并非使投资性房地产达到预定可使用状态的可直接归属成本。
FAQ 23.30.1 – 自行建造的投资性房地产应在何时停止成本资本化？
准则参考：IAS 23 第23段
成本资本化在建造完成时停止。“当资产的实体建造完成时，即使日常行政管理工作可能仍在继续，该资产通常也已达到预定可使用或可销售状态……”\[IAS 23 第23段\]。对于在建造完成后因出租投资性房地产而发生的成本，应考虑 IFRS 16 中的指引，以确定其是否符合初始直接费用的定义并应予以资本化。进一步指引参见第15章第74段。
EX 23.30.2 – 使资产达到预定可使用状态的后续成本
准则参考：IAS 16 第16段

一栋建筑物于 3 月 31 日完成实体建造，但当地卫生与安全监管机构直到 6 月 30 日才批准该房地产投入使用。对于该类型和该地点的建筑物而言，取得卫生与安全审批延迟三个月属于正常情况。主体 M 在此期间发生了 C400,000 的安保费用。在预期延迟期间内发生的安保费用应予以资本化。取得监管批准的法定要求意味着，尽管该建筑物在 3 月 31 日已达到实体上的预定可使用状态，但仍无法投入其预定用途。
EX 23.31.1 – 不予计入的成本
准则参考：IAS 40 第23段
主体 M 开发用于出租的写字楼。在某栋建筑物竣工后，主体 M 发生了在建筑物达到合理出租率之前必须发生的费用（如安保费、水电费和营销费用）。从建筑物竣工到获得合理数量租户之间的通常时间约为三个月。这些成本在发生时予以费用化，因为它们与维护建筑物和吸引租户有关，并非使资产达到可运行状态所必需的支出。
EX 23.35.1 – 拆除成本
准则参考：IAS 16 第17(b)段
主体 A 以 C100m 的总对价购入一块带有废弃建筑物的土地。该建筑物在购入后即被拆除，并将在原址建造一栋新建筑物。支付给第三方用于拆除该建筑物的总成本为 C1m。土地和新建筑物均符合投资性房地产的定义，且主体 A 采用 IAS 40 下的成本模式。同一区域内空地的公允价值为 C101m。经确定，任何其他收购该土地的市场参与者都会拆除现有建筑物。
本具体示例中的废弃建筑物不符合资产的定义，因为不会有经济利益从该建筑物中流入主体 A。\[IAS 16 第7段\]。该购买交易的经济实质是取得土地，而非取得土地和建筑物。因此，所支付的全部对价（C100m）均应分摊至土地。发生的 C1m 拆除成本属于场地整理成本，应根据 IAS 16 第17(b)段予以资本化。
EX 23.45.1 – 后续支出
准则参考：IAS 40 第16段
主体 D 购入了一项需要翻新的房地产。初始购买价款为 C1m，该价格反映了翻新的需求。随后进行的翻新工程又花费了 C500,000。该投资性房地产的初始确认金额应为多少？
该房地产应按购置成本 C1m 进行初始确认。随后发生的 C500,000 翻新工程支出在发生时应资本化计入该房地产的成本。翻新成本能够带来可可靠计量的额外未来经济利益，符合资产的确认条件，因此也可以予以资本化。作为翻新一部分而被替换的投资性房地产初始成本中的任何组成部分，均需予以终止确认。
EX 23.47.1 – 采用成本模式确认的投资性房地产的资本性改良支出
准则参考：IAS 16 第43、14段
主体 A 于 20X0 年 1 月 1 日购入一项投资性房地产。主体 A 按成本模式对其投资性房地产进行会计处理。20X9 年期间，主体 A 投入大量资金为该房地产安装了现代化的升级玻璃屋顶。主体 A 的管理层认为，为该房地产配备现代化屋顶系统对于吸引和留住租户以及抵御租金下行压力非常重要，同时还能使管理层降低电力成本。
新屋顶应予以资本化，因为屋顶通常在建筑物的使用寿命内会被更换，且建筑物的屋顶属于单独计提折旧的独立组成部分。新屋顶被认为很可能为主体 A 带来未来经济利益。现有屋顶的账面价值应予以终止确认。如果无法得知其原始成本，管理层可以使用估计成本。
FAQ 23.49.1 – 成本模式下公允价值的披露
准则参考：IAS 40 第32、79(e)段
即使主体采用成本模式，准则仍要求其披露投资性房地产的公允价值。这确保了所有投资性房地产主体均能提供公允价值信息。
准则要求披露在多大程度上聘请了持有公认相关专业资格且对所估值投资性房地产的地理位置和类别具有近期经验的独立专业评估师。如果未进行独立估值，则应披露这一事实。
FAQ 23.50.1 – 支持特定负债的投资性房地产
准则参考：IAS 40 第32A、32B、32C段
当主体持有与负债挂钩的投资性房地产时，其可以为以下两类资产分别选择公允价值模式或成本模式：
所有支持特定负债的投资性房地产，且该负债支付的回报直接与包括该投资性房地产在内的特定资产的公允价值或回报挂钩；以及
所有其他投资性房地产，不受前一项选择的影响。
该政策选择主要适用于保险公司和类似主体，其目的是缓解此类主体对资产和负债采用不同计量基础时产生的会计错配。当投资性房地产资产的投资回报与保单持有人负债的回报直接挂钩时，此类主体可以选择对该等投资性房地产按公允价值计量，而无需对所有投资性房地产均按公允价值计量。
部分保险公司和其他主体运营着发行名义份额的内部房地产基金，其中部分份额由挂钩合同的投资者持有，其余份额由主体自身持有。准则不允许主体将基金持有的房地产一部分按成本计量、另一部分按公允价值计量。相反，必须对所有回报与负债直接挂钩的投资性房地产采用一致的会计政策。
在采用不同模式计量的资产池之间出售投资性房地产时，应按公允价值确认，并将公允价值的累计变动计入损益（利润表）。因此，如果一项投资性房地产从采用公允价值模式的资产池出售至采用成本模式的资产池，该房地产在出售日的公允价值即成为其认定成本。
EX 23.58.1 – 公允价值无法可靠计量
准则参考：IAS 40 第53段
主体 A 是一家房地产开发商，正在建造一项投资性房地产。该主体此前一直持有一块土地以备资本增值，随后开始建造一栋用于赚取租金的建筑物。由于未来现金流入存在重大不确定性，该主体无法可靠地确定建筑物的公允价值。然而，土地的公允价值可以根据可观察价格确定。主体 A 对其投资性房地产采用公允价值模式。
该主体有一项会计政策选择：将土地和建筑物作为两个单独的计量单元进行会计处理，或者作为一个单一的计量单元进行会计处理。根据所选择的会计政策，该主体要么：
对土地按公允价值进行会计处理，对建筑物按成本进行会计处理，直至建筑物的公允价值能够可靠确定为止；要么
对土地和建筑物均按成本进行会计处理，直至投资性房地产整体的公允价值能够可靠确定为止。
FAQ 23.58.2 – 在不确定环境下确定投资性房地产的公允价值
准则参考：IAS 40 第53段
IFRS 13 对无法获得可观察输入值的情形作出了规范。
按公允价值持有的投资性房地产的账面价值通常通过聘请外部评估师确定。在不确定的经济环境下，从外部评估师处取得的评估报告可能包含针对估值某些方面的不确定性或保留条款。例如，该不确定性可能涉及缺乏用于确定关键输入值定量估计的经验数据。
尽管如此，IFRS 13 仍要求主体利用当前情况下可获得的最佳信息（可能包括主体自身的数据）来制定不可观察（第三层次）输入值。如果有合理可获得的信息表明其他市场参与者会使用不同的数据，则应对该数据进行调整。然而，主体无需付出过度努力来获取有关市场参与者假设的信息，但应考虑合理可获得的信息。\[IFRS 13 第89段\]。
虽然根据 IFRS 13，主体应一贯地应用估值技术，但如果估值技术或其应用的变更能够得出在当前情况下同等或更具代表性的公允价值计量结果，则该变更是恰当的。市场状况的变化便是此类变更的一个例子。关于处理不确定现金流量的进一步指引载于 FAQ 5.77.3。
最后，IFRS 13 通过向使用者提供恰当的披露来应对第三层次公允价值计量的不确定性——例如，包括对所采用估值技术的描述、如何就估值程序作出决策，以及公允价值计量对重大不可观察输入值的敏感性分析。
EX 23.67.1 – 租赁激励
准则参考：IAS 40 第50(c)段
出租人向投资性房地产的承租人提供了一项现金激励，金额为 C100,000。出租人将其作为租赁付款额的抵减项处理，并初始确认为一项资产。该房地产的估值为 C10m，但该估值包含了承租人将支付的毛租金。为避免出租人重复计算，有必要向下调整估值，以考虑出租人因支付了激励（并将其单独确认为一项资产）而导致实际回报较低这一事实。
EX 23.71.1 – 关于投资性房地产转换的修订
准则参考：IAS 40 第57段
国际会计准则理事会（IASB）发布了关于转换指引的修订，自 2018 年 1 月 1 日起生效。
该修订澄清：要将房地产转入（或转出）投资性房地产，必须发生用途变更。要判断一项房地产是否发生用途变更，应评估该房地产是否符合定义。这种变更必须有证据支持。
理事会确认，孤立来看，仅凭意图的改变不足以支持转换。
该问题源于实务中的困惑：当存在准则未明确列举的用途变更证据时，主体是否应将在建房地产从存货转换为投资性房地产。因此，准则将证据清单重新界定为非穷尽性示例清单，以帮助说明该原则。示例范围也扩大至包括在建和正在开发的资产，而不仅限于已完工房地产的转换。
理事会提供了两种过渡方案：
未来适用法。因房地产重分类产生的任何影响，应作为首次执行日期初留存收益的调整。如果选择该方案，还存在特殊的披露要求。
追溯调整法。仅当无需使用事后判断时，方可以选择该方案。
准则参考：IAS 40 第9(a)段
主体 A 是一家历来在开发完工后即出售房地产的房地产开发商，目前正在建造一栋待售住宅楼。为提高完工后整体出售该房地产的可能性，主体 A 决定在个别公寓完工后即将其出租。租户在整栋房地产全部完工前以及出售前入住。主体 A 应如何对该房地产进行会计处理？
主体 A 应继续将该房地产分类为存货，因为即使在租赁开始后，这仍然与该主体的主营业务及其对该房地产的战略一致。这些租赁旨在提高出售该房地产的可能性，而非持续赚取租金收入，且该房地产并非为资本增值而持有。主体在完工后立即出售该房地产的意图并未改变，因为该房地产继续完全以在正常经营过程中后续处置为目的而持有；因此，该房地产不符合投资性房地产的定义。
准则参考：IAS 40 第57(d)段
主体 B 是一家历来在开发完工后即出售房地产的房地产开发商，目前正在建造一栋待售住宅楼。然而，由于房价处于多年低位，市场上买家和交易寥寥无几，主体 B 决定在市场活跃度改善之前将该房地产出租。主体 B 应如何对该房地产进行会计处理？
主体 B 需要审慎评估该房地产是应继续分类为存货，还是应按照 IAS 40 第57(d)段转换为投资性房地产。如果继续分类为存货与主体 B 对该房地产的战略一致，则应继续将其分类为存货。但是，如果管理层的意图发生改变，转为持有该房地产以赚取未来租金或实现资本增值（例如直至市场价格回升），则应将其转换为投资性房地产。
确定此类房地产的正确分类需要运用判断。与第三方签订租赁本身并不会自动要求重分类为投资性房地产，尽管它可能表明管理层意图发生了变化。
因此，如果该房地产在当前状态下能够以当前市场价格在正常经营过程中立即出售，则可以继续分类为存货。需要考虑的因素包括：
该房地产是否正在积极进行销售推广？
该房地产是否以相对于其当前市场价值而言合理的价格待售？
市场上是否存在带租约（且租期较长）房地产的交易市场，从而使该房地产处于可立即出售的状态？
如果不存在带租约房地产的市场，则任何租约的期限是否短于在当前市场条件下其他类似房地产在正常经营过程中售出通常所需的时间？
如果主体不愿意以当前低迷的市场价格出售该房地产，则该房地产的预期用途很可能已发生变更，从而符合投资性房地产的定义——即为赚取租金收入和资本增值而持有。需要考虑的因素包括：
董事会是否已决定推迟出售该房地产，直至市场价格回升？
商业计划是否已发生变更，将赚取的租金收入和必要的未来维护费用纳入考量？
该商业计划的变更是否已对外公布？
该房地产是否已不再积极进行销售推广？
目前是否不存在类似房地产的活跃市场？
该房地产是否仅以相对于其当前市场价值而言不合理的价格待售？
EX 23.73.1 – 转换的时点
准则参考：IAS 40 第57(b)段
主体 D 从事两项业务：开发房地产用于出售；以及持有投资性房地产用于出租。目前分类为投资性房地产的两项房地产将在不久的将来出售。房地产 X 将在出售前进行重新开发，重新开发将显著改善和提升该房地产。房地产 Y 也将出售，但无需进行重大重新开发（尽管将进行一些基本修缮）。主体 D 希望在开发开始之日将这两项房地产均从投资性房地产转换为存货。主体 D 应如何对这两项房地产进行会计处理？

主体在 20X1 年就建筑物的损失确认 C300,000 的减值损失。土地部分未发生减值，主体继续将该部分作为投资性房地产进行会计处理。截至 20X1 年末，保险公司尚未接受该保险索赔，因此不存在应收补偿，也不能予以确认；彼时收到补偿并非基本确定。20X2 年，C500,000 的补偿成为应收款项，因此计入当年度损益（利润表）。该补偿不得与替代建筑物的成本相抵销；相反，C400,000 的替代建筑物成本应予以资本化，并计入投资性房地产的账面价值。
总体而言，两年利润表合计列示了 C200,000 的净利得（C500,000 的补偿减去 C300,000 的减值）。即使该补偿在 20X1 年即成为应收款项，将减值与补偿相抵销并仅披露 C200,000 的利得也是不可接受的。IAS 40 要求对这两项经济事项分别进行会计处理。

Introduction and scope (paras 24.1-24.24)

24.1 A non-financial asset is impaired if its carrying amount exceeds its recoverable amount. Recoverable amount is the higher of value in use and fair value less costs of disposal. IAS 36 requires annual impairment tests for certain assets and for any non-financial asset where there is an indicator of impairment.
24.2 Where recoverable amount is determined on the basis of fair value less costs of disposal, the measurement guidance in IFRS 13 applies. (See chapter 5 para 140.)
24.3 IAS 36 applies to the impairment of all assets, unless specifically excluded from the standard’s scope. Assets that are excluded are:
- Contract assets and assets arising from costs to obtain or fulfil a contract that are recognised in accordance with IFRS 15.
- Deferred tax assets (IAS 12).

- Financial assets that are included within the scope of IFRS 9. (Examples include cash, debtors and equity investments other than investments in subsidiaries, associates or joint ventures not accounted for under IFRS 9 (IAS 39).)
- Investment property that is measured at fair value (IAS 40).
- Biological assets related to agricultural activity measured at fair value (IAS 41).
- Deferred acquisition costs and intangible assets arising from an insurer’s contractual rights under insurance contracts that are within IFRS 4’s scope.
- Non-current assets (or disposal groups) classified as held for sale under IFRS 5.
- Assets arising from employee benefits under IAS 19.

24.4 IAS 36 applies to financial assets classified as subsidiaries (as defined in IFRS 10 – see chapter 26 para 16), associates (as defined in IAS 28 – see chapter 31 para 9) and joint ventures (as defined in IFRS 11 – see chapter 32 para 25).

24.5 Revalued assets measured at fair value in IAS 16 and IAS 38 are within IAS 36’s scope. The only difference between an asset’s fair value and its fair value less costs of disposal is the direct incremental costs attributable to the asset’s disposal. Costs of disposal could, therefore, cause an impairment if fair value less cost of disposal is higher than value in use.
Basic principles of impairment

24.6 An asset cannot be carried in the balance sheet at more than its recoverable amount. An impairment review compares the asset’s recoverable amount with its carrying value. If the recoverable amount is lower, the asset is impaired and should be written down to the recoverable amount.

24.7 An asset’s carrying amount is the amount at which the asset is recognised on the balance sheet, after deducting any accumulated depreciation or amortisation and accumulated impairment losses thereon.
24.8 An asset’s recoverable amount represents its greatest value to the business in terms of the cash flows that it can generate. That is the higher of:
- fair value less costs of disposal (measured in accordance with IFRS 13); and
- value in use (the present value of the future cash flows that are expected to be derived from the asset).
Identifying assets that might be impaired
24.9 All assets within the standard’s scope are to be tested for impairment where there is an impairment indicator.
24.10 Goodwill, indefinite life intangible assets and intangible assets that are not yet ready for use should also be tested annually for impairment.

24.11 An entity should assess, at each reporting date, whether there is any indication that an asset might be impaired. The term ‘reporting date’ includes the year end date and interim (half-year or quarterly) reporting dates. An entity might be required to complete an impairment test more than once per annum.
24.12 In assessing whether there is any indication that an asset might be impaired, an entity should consider at least the following:
External sources of information, including:

- Observable indications that the asset’s value has declined during the period significantly more than would be expected as a result of the passage of time or normal use. Changes in market values reflect economic conditions, so a significant fall in value could be a symptom of another more pervasive change (for example, change in demand for the asset’s output).
- Significant adverse changes that have taken place (or are expected in the near future) in the technological, market, economic or legal environment in which the entity operates or in its markets.
- Increases in interest rates, or other market rates of return, that might materially affect the discount rate used in calculating the asset’s recoverable amount.
- Where the carrying amount of the entity’s net assets exceeds the entity’s market capitalisation.
Internal sources of information, including:
- Obsolescence or physical damage affecting the asset.

- Significant adverse changes that have taken place (or are expected in the near future) in the extent to which, or in the way that, an asset is used or expected to be used. This includes the asset becoming idle, plans to discontinue or restructure the operation to which the asset belongs, or the asset’s disposal. It also includes reassessing the asset’s useful life from indefinite to finite.
- Deterioration in the expected level of the asset’s performance.
- Where management’s own forecasts of future net cash inflows or operating profits show a significant decline from previous budgets and forecasts.
This list is not exhaustive, and other indicators might be apparent that are relevant to a business’ particular circumstances.

24.13 Evidence from internal reporting, which indicates that an asset might be impaired, includes:
- The actual net cash outflows or operating profit or loss are significantly worse than budgeted.
- Operating losses or net cash outflows are forecasted.
- Cash flows for constructing the asset, or for maintaining or operating it, are significantly higher than those budgeted.

24.14 An increase in market interest rates might not trigger an impairment test in all circumstances. For example, a marginal increase in short-term interest rates is unlikely to lead to an impairment charge where there was significant headroom in the last test.

24.15 Materiality applies in determining whether an impairment review is required. If previous impairment reviews have shown a significant excess of recoverable amount over carrying amount, no review would be necessary in the absence of an event that would eliminate the excess. Previous reviews might also have shown that an asset’s recoverable amount is not sensitive to one or more of the impairment indicators.

24.16 If there is an indication that an asset might be impaired, the useful life, the depreciation method and the residual value for the asset need to be reviewed and adjusted, if necessary, under the appropriate IFRS. This applies, even if no impairment loss is recognised for the asset.
Events after the reporting period

24.17 Events after the reporting period might provide indications that an asset was impaired at the period end. The impairment test should be updated after the period end only if material changes in assumptions provide additional evidence relating to conditions that existed at the balance sheet date. Annual impairment review for goodwill and certain intangibles
24.18 Goodwill and indefinite-lived intangible assets are tested annually for impairment, irrespective of indicators.

24.19 Intangibles that are not yet ready for use should be tested annually, because they are not being amortised. The ability of an intangible asset to generate sufficient future economic benefits to recover its carrying amount is usually more uncertain before it is brought into use.

24.20 The impairment tests on goodwill and intangibles can be performed at any time in the financial year, provided that they are performed at the same time each year. An entity might choose to perform its impairment test at less busy times of the year. Different CGUs might be tested at different times.

24.21 An intangible or goodwill that was recognised during the current financial period should be tested for impairment before the end of the current period. If any assumptions change, or if there is a further impairment trigger before the year end, the calculation should be updated accordingly.

24.22 The annual impairment test requirement for goodwill and intangibles with indefinite useful lives, or that have yet to be brought into use, is in addition to the overriding requirement to test those assets whenever there are indications of impairment. Goodwill and intangible assets might need to be tested for impairment more than once a year where an indicator of impairment exists.

24.23 The same impairment testing, recognition and reversal criteria are applied at interim reporting dates. An entity will not necessarily have to make a detailed impairment calculation at the end of each interim period. An entity should review for indications of impairment, at each interim reporting date, to decide whether such a calculation is needed.

24.24 An entity might be required to recognise an impairment in an interim period but, by the year end, the impairment might have reversed, either in full or partially. An impairment of goodwill recognised in an interim period should not be reversed. See chapter 35 para 29 for more details.

Cash-generating units (paras 24.25 - 24.52)

24.25 Impairment should be identified at the individual asset level, where possible. The recoverable amount should be calculated for the CGU to which the asset belongs only where the recoverable amount for the individual asset cannot be identified.
EX 24.25.1 – Test impairment at the individual asset level where possible

24.26 The recoverable amount of an individual asset cannot be determined if the asset does not generate cash inflows that are largely independent from other assets. Assets should be grouped for an impairment test in these circumstances. The recoverable amount is estimated for the smallest group of assets that generate cash inflows that are largely independent of each other. These are referred to as cash-generating units (CGUs). 24.27 An impairment review of a CGU should cover all of its tangible assets, intangible assets and attributable goodwill. The carrying value of each CGU containing the assets and goodwill being reviewed should be compared with the higher of its value in use and fair value less costs of disposal.

24.28 An impairment test is performed for an individual asset, unless the asset does not generate independent cash inflows. If this is the case the impairment test is performed for the CGU to which the asset belongs unless:
- the asset’s fair value less costs of disposal is higher than its carrying amount; or
- the asset’s value in use can be estimated as being close to its fair value less costs of disposal, and the fair value less costs of disposal can be determined.

24.33 An asset or group of assets is identified as a separate CGU if there is an active market for the output generated by the asset(s), even if the output is used internally.

24.34 An active market is defined as follows: “A market in which transactions for the asset or liability take place with sufficient frequency and volume to provide pricing information on an ongoing basis”.
24.35 Value in use is based on management’s best estimate of future cash flows. Management should use its best estimate of future arm’s length prices for the internal cash flow to:
- estimate the future cash inflows that relate to the sale of the output by the CGU to the entity’s other CGUs; and
- estimate the future cash outflows that relate to the purchase of the output by the other CGUs.

24.36 CGUs should be identified on a consistent basis, from one period to the next for the same assets or types of assets, unless a change is justified. If there is a change, it must be disclosed.

24.37 Assessing the recoverable amount for an individual CGU is difficult where management has multiple assets and has the ability to choose the assets that are used. Determination of what is a CGU can be an area of significant judgement, but it is not an accounting policy choice. Significant judgements should be disclosed.

24.38 IAS 36 is focused on identifying and recognising impairment losses from a group perspective. The whole group is divided into separate CGUs for the purpose of impairment reviews. The CGUs in aggregate cover the whole group and are non-overlapping. The allocation of a group’s activities between separate entities within a group does not necessarily coincide with the way in which the group’s CGUs are defined.
CGU with goodwill or indefinite-lived assets

24.39 Goodwill and indefinite-lived intangible assets are required to be tested annually for impairment. In some circumstances there is an accommodation to carry forward the calculation of recoverable amount made in the previous period, which can be used in the current period if the following conditions are met:
- For goodwill allocated to a CGU and those intangibles that do not generate cash inflows independently of other assets, and so are tested as part of a CGU:
- The CGU’s assets and liabilities, to which such goodwill or intangibles were allocated, have not changed significantly since the last impairment test.
- The most recent impairment test resulted in an amount that exceeded the CGU’s carrying amount by a substantial margin.

- Analysis of events that have occurred and changes in circumstances since the last review indicates that the likelihood that the current CGU’s recoverable amount would be less than its carrying amount is remote.
- If an intangible asset is assessed for impairment as a single asset (that is, it generates cash flows independently of other assets and is not reviewed for impairment as part of a CGU):
- The most recent impairment test resulted in an amount that exceeded the asset’s carrying amount by a substantial margin.

- Analysis of events that have occurred and changes in circumstances since the last review indicates that the likelihood that the asset’s current recoverable amount would be less than its carrying amount is remote.

Measuring recoverable amount (paras 24.53- 24.62)

24.53 Recoverable amount is the higher of an asset’s fair value less costs of disposal and its value in use. This reflects the greatest value of an asset in terms of the cash flows that can be derived from it, either by selling it or by continuing to use it in the business.
FAQ 24.53.1 – Does intention affect recoverable amount? FAQ 24.53.2 – Is it possible for the lower of value in use and fair value less costs of disposal to give a lower impairment charge?

24.55 It is not always necessary to calculate both measures when performing an impairment review. If an asset’s fair value less costs of disposal or its value in use exceeds the asset’s carrying amount, the asset is not impaired and there is no need to estimate the recoverable amount using the other method.
24.56 Estimates, averages or computational shortcuts might provide a reasonable approximation of the detailed computations that would otherwise be required to determine recoverable amount.

24.57 If there is no reason to believe that an asset’s value in use materially exceeds its fair value less costs of disposal, the asset’s recoverable amount can be taken to be its fair value less costs of disposal. This will often be the case for an asset that is held for disposal where the value in use will consist mainly of the net disposal proceeds.
24.58 The recoverable amount should be determined by estimating the asset’s value in use if the fair value cannot be determined.
Fair value less costs of disposal

24.59 Fair value measurement is covered by IFRS 13 (see chapter 5 para 1). This defines fair value of an asset as “the price that would be received to sell the asset in an orderly transaction between market participants at the measurement date”.
24.60 Fair value considers the characteristics of the asset or CGU that a market participant would consider when pricing it. Such characteristics could include:
- the condition and location of the asset or CGU; and
- restrictions, if any, on the sale or use of the asset or CGU.

24.61 Fair value less costs of disposal differs from value in use. Value in use reflects the effect of factors that might be specific to the entity and would not be applicable to entities in general. Fair value reflects the assumptions that market participants would use when pricing the asset.
24.62 Fair value does not reflect any of the following factors to the extent that they would not generally be available to market participants:
- additional value derived from the grouping of assets (such as the creation of a portfolio of investment properties in different locations);
- synergies between the asset being measured and different assets;
- corporate overheads that are specific to the asset's current owner;
- legal rights or legal restrictions that are specific only to the asset’s current owner; and
- tax benefits or tax burdens that are specific to the asset’s current owner.

Value in use (paras 24.63 - 24.138)
24.63 The definition of value in use is “the present value of the future cash flows expected to be derived from an asset or cash-generating unit”.

24.64 Determining value in use involves estimating the future cash flows that are expected to arise from the asset or CGU being tested for impairment. The cash flows consist of those expected to arise from the continued use of the asset or CGU in its current condition and those, if any, expected to result from its ultimate disposal. An appropriate discount rate is then applied to those cash flows, in order to arrive at their present value.
FAQ 24.64.1 – Can dividend discount models be used as a basis for impairment testing?
24.65 Calculating value in use involves the following processes:
- Estimating the future cash flows expected to be derived from the asset in its current condition.
- Estimating the potential variation in the amount and timing of the future cash flows.
- Taking account of the time value of money (discounting), using current market risk-free interest rates.
- Estimating the price for bearing the uncertainty inherent in the asset (for example, whether the asset will perform as intended).
- Taking account of other factors, such as illiquidity, which would be reflected by the market in pricing the future cash flows expected to be derived from the asset.
EX 24.65.1 – Impact of IFRS 16 on value in use

24.66 Risks related to expected variations in the amount or timing of cash flows, uncertainty inherent in the asset and other factors, such as illiquidity, might be reflected in the calculation, either by adjusting the cash flows or by adjusting the discount rate. A risk should be incorporated in either the cash flows or the discount rate, but not both, to avoid double counting.
FAQ 24.66.1 – What factors might influence cash flows?
Basis for estimates of future cash flows
Reasonable and supportable

24.67 Relevant cash flow forecasts should be made on the basis of reasonable and supportable assumptions that represent management’s best estimate of the economic circumstances that will prevail over the asset’s or CGU’s remaining life.

24.68 Management should examine the causes of any differences between actual cash flows and past projections, to assess whether assumptions are reasonable. The current assumptions should be consistent with past actual outcomes, except where circumstances have changed or subsequent events have occurred that make this inappropriate.

24.69 Value in use is an entity-specific measure, but the assumptions used by management should be reasonable and supportable; for example:

- Management assumptions should be consistent with market evidence, such as independent macro-economic forecasts, industry commentators or analysts, brokers' analysis and other third party experts. Greater weight should be given to credible external evidence that is available.

- Any differences between the forecast’s underlying assumptions and market evidence should be analysed and understood. Management might find it helpful to explain these differences in financial statement disclosures or other material accompanying the financial statements.
- Management should understand any differences between fair value less costs of disposal and value in use, and it should ensure that they are supportable.
There should be consistency of assumptions and forecasts where they are in common with impairment tests of different assets required by IAS 36 and other standards.
Based on most up-to-date budget

24.70 The cash flows used for impairment testing be based on the most up-to-date budgets and forecasts that have been formally approved by management, excluding cash inflows and outflows arising from future restructuring or enhancements. If budgets are revised, they should also be approved by management before they can be used in the value in use calculation. Asset in its current condition

24.77 The costs and benefits of a future restructuring should not be recognised in value in use cash flow forecasts, unless the entity is committed to the restructuring, and related provisions have been made. These restrictions could lead to entities using a fair value less costs of disposal basis for the calculation of recoverable amount, because it might be higher.

24.78 A restructuring is a programme that is planned and controlled by management and that materially changes either the scope of the business undertaken by the entity or the manner in which the business is conducted. IAS 37 sets out the conditions that should be complied with before provisions for restructurings can be recognised in financial statements. See chapter 16 para 58.

24.79 Impairment reviews should be based on the most recent budgets and forecasts that have been formally approved by management. These budgets might include costs and benefits of restructuring before they are recognised in the financial statements. If this is the case, the relevant costs and benefits must be removed from the value in use calculation. 24.80 The costs and benefits of future expenditure that is intended to improve or enhance the assets or business should not be taken into account in the cash flow forecasts, because future cash flows are estimated for assets in their current condition.

24.81 Estimates of future cash flows include those cash flows that are necessary to maintain the current level of economic benefits expected to arise from the asset in its current condition. An asset will usually deteriorate through use, or component parts will wear out. Cash outflows for servicing the asset, to maintain its current capability, are taken into account in the estimates.

24.82 Expenditure is included in the cash flows where it is necessary to replace or restore separate components of a single fixed asset that have shorter useful lives than the rest of the asset, such as the lining of a furnace. The expected future cost of replacement or restoration expenditure is treated as if it were part of the day-to-day servicing of the larger asset, and it is included in the cash flows used to assess the larger asset’s recov

24.83 Where a CGU consists of assets with different useful lives, all of which are essential to the ongoing operation of the CGU, the replacement of assets with shorter useful lives is considered to be part of the day-to-day servicing of the CGU when the future cash flows attributable to the CGU are estimated.

Composition of estimates of future cash flows
24.84 The cash flows should include:
- Projections of cash inflows from the continuing use of the asset or the activities of the CGU.

- Projections of cash outflows necessarily incurred to generate the cash inflows from continuing use of the asset or CGU (including cash outflows to prepare the asset for use), and that are directly attributable to the asset or CGU.
- Projections of such cash outflows that are indirectly attributable (such as those relating to central overheads), but that can be allocated on a reasonable and consistent basis to the asset or CGU.
- Net cash flows expected to be received (or paid) for the disposal of assets or CGUs at the end of their useful lives.
- Cash outflows to maintain the operating capacity of existing assets, including, for example, cash flows for day-to-day servicing.
- Cash outflows for expected future variable rents and short-term and low value leases that are not included in the lease liabilities per IFRS 16.

- Cash outflows to replace leased assets at the end of the lease term which are essential to maintaining the operations. This can be included as a capital expenditure or a perpetual payment (representing the ongoing payments post the lease term).

Asset not available for use

24.85 Cash flows that are to be incurred before an asset or CGU is ready for use or sale should be estimated and included in the forecast provided that the project is already in progress. Examples might be future cash flows relating to a building under construction or a development project that is not yet completed. For consistency, the expected cash inflows once the asset is complete should also be included.

24.86 The cash flows should exclude cash flows relating to financing (which include interest payments), since the related liabilities are excluded from the carrying amount and because the cost of capital is taken into account by discounting the cash flows.

24.87 Tax cash flows should also be excluded, because value in use is calculated on the basis of discounting pre-tax cash flows at a pre-tax discount rate. However, observable market rates of return are generally post-tax rates; so, in practice, value in use is typically calculated by discounting post-tax cash flows at a post-tax discount rate as a proxy for discounting pre-tax cash flows with a pre-tax discount rate. 24.88 Cash flows relating to assets that generate cash flows independently from the asset under review are excluded from the forecasts (because they are also excluded from the carrying amount of a CGU). Examples would include financial assets such as receivables, except for trade debtors included in the CGU for practical reasons (see para 24.45).

24.89 Cash outflows relating to obligations that have already been recognised as liabilities would be excluded, because the related liability is excluded from the CGU, unless included as part of working capital (see para 24.45). This ensures the comparison of like with like. Examples of such liabilities include payables, pensions or provisions.

If the pension liability is excluded from the CGU’s carrying amount, the cash flows relating to settling the recognised liability should be excluded from the value in use calculation. 24.91 The cash outflows attributable to a CGU should include sensible allocations of corporate overheads, in the same way that the carrying values of CGUs should, where practicable, include apportionments of corporate assets.

24.92 The estimate of cash flows expected to be received (or paid) for the disposal of assets or CGUs at the end of their useful lives should be the amount of the expected disposal proceeds in an arm’s length transaction between knowledgeable, willing parties, reduced by the estimated costs of disposal.
24.93 The estimate of cash flows from the disposal of an asset at the end of its useful life is determined in a similar way to its fair value less costs of disposal, except that:

- The entity uses prices prevailing at the date of the estimate for similar assets or CGUs that have reached the end of their useful lives and that have operated under similar conditions to those in which the asset or CGU will be used.

- Those estimated selling prices are adjusted both for future inflation and for expected specific future price increases. (However, if the effect of future inflation is excluded from the estimates of future cash flows and from the discount rate, it is also excluded from the estimate of net cash flows on disposal.)
24.94 Assumptions about inflation can be dealt with in one of two ways:

- One method is to forecast cash flows in current prices and not forecast future inflation. The cash flows are then discounted at a real discount rate (that is, a rate of return that excludes inflation).

- The second method is to forecast cash flows to include estimates of inflation in revenues and costs. The cash flows are then discounted at a nominal discount rate (that is, a rate of return that includes inflation).
It is important that inflation is treated consistently in the cash flow projections and the choice of discount rate.

24.95 Where future cash flows are expected to be denominated in a foreign currency, they should be estimated in that currency and then discounted at a rate appropriate for that currency. The entity then translates the present value (expressed in the foreign currency) at the spot rate of exchange at the date of the value in use calculation.
24.96 Forecasting future foreign cash flows and translating them at estimated spot exchange rates at future dates is prohibited, because such estimates cannot be reliably made.

24.97 Internal transfer pricing directly affects the cash inflows and operating cash outflows relating to separate CGUs – for example, a vertically integrated group where one CGU transfers part of its output to another CGU in the same group at a price that is lower than the market price for its output. 24.98 Estimated cash flows or discount rates should reflect the range of possible outcomes rather than a single, most likely, minimum or maximum possible amount. Risk must be incorporated into the cash flow model, to reflect uncertainty. Risks include variations in amount and timing of cash flows, and uncertainty inherent in the asset. This can be reflected either in the discount rate or in the cash flows. An expected cash flow approach incorpora
‘Traditional’ and ‘expected cash flow’ approaches to present value

24.99 There are two approaches to estimating cash flows: the traditional approach, and the expected cash flow approach. The traditional approach uses a single set of cash flows and a single discount rate. It assumes that a single discount rate can incorporate all of the expectations about the future cash flows and the appropriate risk premium, and so it places more emphasis on the selection of the discount rate.

24.100 The expected cash flow approach starts with cash flows that reflect the risks that management anticipates (for example, cash flows based on probability). Risk-adjusted probability cash flow projections are not certain, and so it is not appropriate to use a risk-free rate to discount such cash flows. The discount rate will be lower than the rate used in a traditional approach, but it will not be risk-free.

24.101 Projected future cash flows are discounted at a pre-tax rate that reflects both current market assessments of the time value of money and the risks specific to the asset for which the future cash flow estimates have not been adjusted. This means that an asset is regarded as impaired if it is not expected to earn a current market-related rate of return on its carrying value.

24.102 The rate of return expected by the market is the return that investors would require if they chose an investment that would generate cash flows of the same amounts, timing and risk profile as those that the entity expects from the asset or CGU under review. The rate is independent of the way in which the asset is financed. It is estimated from current market transactions for similar assets or from the weighted average cost of capital (WACC
24.103 If an asset-specific rate is not available directly from the market, an entity should estimate an appropriate discount rate that reflects, as far as possible, a market assessment of:
- The time value of money to the end of the asset’s useful life.
- The risks that the future cash flows will differ in amount or timing from estimates.
- The price for bearing the uncertainty inherent in the asset.
- Other factors that market participants would reflect in the rate, such as illiquidity.
24.104 The entity might take into account the following factors in determining this rate:
- The WACC for the entity, determined using techniques such as the capital asset pricing model.
- The entity’s incremental borrowing rate.
- Other market borrowing rates.

24.105 The rates are adjusted to take into account the way in which the market would assess the specific risks associated with the estimated cash flows and to exclude risks that are not relevant to the estimated cash flows or for which the estimated cash flows have been adjusted. Factors to consider might include:
- Country risk, such as the risk of political unrest.
- Currency risk, such as the risk of devaluation.
- The nature of the asset being tested; intangible assets are higher risk.
- Whether the cash flows are optimistic or stretch targets.
- Price risk, such as the risk that prices might be forced down by competitive pressures.

24.106 The discount rate is independent of the entity’s capital structure and the way in which the purchase of the asset or CGU was financed. The future cash flows from the asset do not depend on how the asset was purchased.

24.107 The discount rate should not reflect risks for which the estimates of future cash flows have already been adjusted, to avoid double counting. Discount rates should reflect assumptions that are consistent with those inherent in the estimated cash flows.

24.108 An entity normally uses a single discount rate for estimating an asset’s value in use. Separate discount rates are used for different future periods if the value in use is sensitive to risks for different periods or to the structure of interest rates over the asset’s life.

24.109 Inflation should also be treated consistently in the present value calculations. The discount rate is a real rate (inflation should be excluded) if the future cash flows are estimated at current values. The discount rate is a nominal rate (including inflation) if the estimated future cash flows include inflation.
24.110 The discount rate for value in use calculations should be calculated on a pre-tax basis.

24.111 Observable market rates of return are generally post-tax rates (for example, an entity’s WACC). A post-tax rate should be adjusted to a pre-tax rate. The pre-tax discount rate is not always the post-tax discount rate grossed up by a standard rate of tax.

24.112 Discounting post-tax cash flows at a post-tax discount rate should lead to the same result as discounting pre-tax cash flows with a pre-tax discount rate, and so it can be used as a proxy. This only works if the pre-tax discount rate is the post-tax discount rate adjusted to reflect the specific amount and timing of the future tax cash flows. Significant deferred tax balances can cause discrepancies in this calculation.

24.113 Goodwill acquired in a business combination represents future economic benefits arising from assets that are not capable of being individually identified and separately recognised, such as a skilled workforce.

24.114 Goodwill does not generate cash inflows independently from other assets or groups of assets, and so the recoverable amount of goodwill as an individual asset cannot be determined. Goodwill acquired in a business combination should be allocated, from the acquisition date, to each of the acquirer’s CGUs or groups of CGUs that are expected to benefit from the synergies of the business combination. This is done irrespective of where the other

24.116 Goodwill sometimes cannot be allocated on a non-arbitrary basis to individual CGUs, and so it is allocated to groups of CGUs. Each CGU (or group of CGUs) to which goodwill is allocated from the date of acquisition should:
- represent the lowest level within the entity at which management monitors goodwill for internal purposes; and
- not be larger than an operating segment (as defined by para 5 of IFRS 8) before aggregation.

Goodwill can then be monitored and tested for impairment in a way that is consistent with management’s internal management systems, thus avoiding development of additional systems specifically to deal with goodwill.

Reallocation should be based on a relative value approach, as for disposal. Relative values should be adopted, unless the entity can demonstrate that some other method better reflects the goodwill attributable to the reorganised CGUs.

24.122 Restructuring of an operation is an impairment indicator if it has an adverse effect on the entity. An impairment review should be performed prior to any restructuring, to ensure that the reallocation process does not mask any pre-existing impairments.

24.123 Goodwill might be allocated to a group of CGUs. So, individual CGUs within the group might not have goodwill directly allocated to them. A CGU with no goodwill allocated is tested where there is an indication of impairment. The impairment test compares the unit’s carrying amount (excluding any goodwill) with its recoverable amount, and any impairment loss is recognised.

24.124 Goodwill might be allocated to individual CGUs or to groups of CGUs. Any CGU or group of CGUs to which goodwill has been allocated should be tested for impairment annually. It should also be tested where there is an indication of impairment. The impairment test compares the carrying amount of the CGU or group of CGUs, including the allocated goodwill, with the recoverable amount of the CGU or group of CGUs. FAQ 24.124.1 – Do you need to keep a record of goodwill and its allocation to CGUs?

24.125 The annual impairment test for CGUs containing goodwill can be carried out at any time in the financial year, but it should be done at the same time each year. Different CGUs can be tested for impairment at different times in the year. However, if some or all of the goodwill allocated to a CGU was acquired in the current financial year, the CGU should be tested for impairment before the end of that financial year.

24.126 There might be an indication of impairment of an asset within a CGU to which goodwill has been allocated. The asset should be tested for impairment before the CGU is tested. This also applies to a CGU within a group of CGUs to which goodwill has been allocated. The impairment test is a two-step process:

- Step 1: Test the individual asset, or related CGU if the recoverable amount for the individual asset cannot be determined. Any impairment should be recognised at this step, to reduce the carrying amount to the recoverable amount. Testing performed at the CGU level would include goodwill to the extent that goodwill is monitored at this level.
- Step 2: Test the CGU or group of CGUs including goodwill. This second stage is a comparison of the recoverable amount with the restated carrying amount after the step 1 impairment test.

The two-stage approach ensures that, where there are indicators of impairment, assets and CGUs within a group of CGUs are tested separately for impairment first, with any impairment recognised before the larger group, including goodwill, is tested.

Due to the different levels of impairment testing required, it is important that CGUs are correctly identified as the smallest group of assets that generate cash inflows that are largely independent of each other. Impairments should not be masked by incorporating additional assets and cash flows from the same operating segment.
