Entities need to consider whether the de-recognition criteria are met each time a receivable is sold – that is, the analysis of a factoring or similar program is not static and needs to be re assessed each time a new sale occurs.

This is particularly relevant when applying the ‘risks and rewards test’ in paragraph 3.2.6 of IFRS 9 / paragraph 21 of IAS 39 (that is, in assessing whether an entity has transferred significantly all risks and rewards, has retained significantly all risks and rewards, or falls somewhere in between).

As a result of COVID-19, certain exposures to risks and rewards and the relative size of each kind of risk might have changed. For example, late payment risk and/or credit risk might have become more significant as compared to other risks, and the relative size of the late payment risk as compared to the credit risk might have changed. Historical trends in risk factors might no longer be representative of expected exposure to risks at the time wh

Reference to standard: IAS 39 para 30; IFRS 9 para 3.2.16 Reference to standing text: 44.49

The continuing involvement includes both obligations to support the risks arising from the asset’s cash flows (for example, if a guarantee has been provided) and the right to receive benefits from these cash flows. A related liability is recognised if continuing involvement includes obligations, such as guarantees, as well as part of the original asset.
Warranties, contractual credit notes and two-party offset arrangements are not taken into account in measuring an entity’s continuing involvement. This is because:
- Such arrangements do not prevent a transfer of contractual rights to receive cash flows from an asset.

- Warranties relate to the asset’s condition at the date of sale and to whether a valid receivable exists (business risk of the underlying transaction), rather than to risks and benefits in relation to its future performance (financial risk associated with the asset).
- Contractual credit notes relate to the overall contractual relationship between the seller and its customer, rather than the specific contract which creates the receivable.
- Two-party offset arrangements merely transfer to the transferee the value that the transferor obtained when its receivable from the debtor was extinguished.

On the other hand, options or commitments to repurchase the transferred assets on a change in circumstances should be taken into account in measuring the entity’s continuing involvement. An example of a change in circumstance is a change in tax law or regulation.

A factoring transaction involves a transferor transferring its rights to some or all of the cash collected from some financial asset (usually receivables) to a third party (the factor) in exchange for a cash payment.

In a non-recourse factoring arrangement, the transferor does not provide any guarantee about the receivables’ performance. In other words, the transferor assumes no obligations whatsoever to repay any sums received from the factor regardless of the timing or the level of collections from the underlying debts. - a put option by the factor for any defaulted assets; or

EX 44.61.4 – Securitisations
Reference to standard: IAS 39 paras 30, BC 63; IFRS 9 paras 3.2.16, BCZ3.24 Reference to standing text: 44.61

Securitisation is a method of raising finance. Securitisations were first used by originators of mortgage loans through a sale of a block or pool of loans. These sales are typically to a subsidiary or a thinly capitalised vehicle specially set up for the purpose – a special purpose entity (SPE). The SPE finances the purchase by issuing loan notes or other marketable debt instruments to outside investors that are often secured on the SPE’s assets.

In addition to pools of loans, other pools of debts are securitised in a similar way to mortgages. Examples include credit card receivables, leases, hire purchase loans and trade debtors. An SPE structure isolates the assets legally from the transferor and its creditors (‘ring-fence’). This helps to avoid any consequences from bankruptcy and enables the originator to raise funds at competitive rates. The following outlines a typical securitisatio
- The assets to be securitised are transferred by an originator/transferor to an SPE for an immediate cash payment.

- The SPE finances the transfer by issuing loan notes to investors. The SPE’s shares or residual beneficial interests, if any, are usually held by a party other than the originator (charitable trusts have often been used for this purpose). In addition, the major financial and operating policies are usually pre-determined, to a greater or lesser extent, by the agreements that establish the securitisation (in other words, the SPE operates on so-cal

- Because the SPE’s business activities are constrained and its ability to incur debt is limited, it faces the risk of a shortfall of cash below what it is obligated to pay to investors. Arrangements are, therefore, made to protect the investors from losses occurring on the assets by a process termed ‘credit enhancement’.

A commonly used form of credit enhancement occurs via the issue of subordinated debt (perhaps to the transferor) and other forms of equity-like claims that have the effect of dividing the risk of loss on the underlying assets (‘tranching’).

Credit enhancement might take a variety of other forms, including over-collateralisation (the aggregate value of assets transferred exceeds the consideration provided by the SPE), third-party guarantee of the issuer’s obligations (securities backed by a letter of credit) or third-party credit insurance. All of the arrangements provide a cushion against losses up to some limit.

- The transferor is often granted rights to cash remaining from the transferred assets, after payment of amounts due on the loan notes and other expenses of the issuer. These rights are generally intended, at least in part, to compensate the transferor for assuming some of the risk of credit or other losses. The mechanisms used to achieve this include servicing or other fees, deferred sale consideration, ‘super interest’ on amounts owed to the tr

- Cash accumulation from the assets (for example, from mortgage redemptions) is either used to redeem the loan notes or it is reinvested in other more liquid assets until the loan notes are repaid. Any surplus cash usually accrues to the transferor, as noted above.

- The transferor might continue to service the assets (for example, collecting amounts from the borrower, and setting interest rates) for which it might receive a ‘servicing fee’. Often, the surplus cash mentioned above is extracted by an adjustment to the service fee.
In many situations, the SPE will be no more than an extension of the originator, rather than an economic entity in its own right, and so it will be consolidated under IFRS.

Depending on the structure of the transaction, the sale of the financial assets by the originator to the SPE might also fail to qualify for de-recognition. Most commonly, sales fail to qualify for de-recognition either because the pass-through conditions are not met (for example, if the securitisation is a ‘revolving structure’) or the selling entity has retained substantially all of the risks and rewards of ownership of the financial assets.

EX 44.78.1 – Servicing assets and liabilities
Reference to standard: IAS 39 para 24; IFRS 9 para 3.2.10 Reference to standing text: 44.78

Servicing is inherent in all loans and receivables. Servicing of mortgage loans, credit card receivables or other financial assets commonly includes collecting payments as they fall due, accounting for and remitting principal and interest payments to the transferee, monitoring non-performing loans/debtors, executing foreclosure if necessary and performing other administrative tasks. The service provider incurs the costs of servicing the assets, o

Servicing rights do not meet the definition of a financial instrument, because they represent a commitment to supply a service and can only be settled by the service delivery. Servicing rights are essentially an expected stream of cash flows that results from a contractual agreement. Therefore, they are so similar to financial instruments that they are recognised and initially measured on the same basis as financial assets and liabilities.
Where the benefits of servicing exactly compensate the service provider for its servicing responsibilities, there is no servicing asset or liability and the service contract’s fair value is zero.

Servicing assets and liabilities are subject to the measurement requirements of IFRS 13 when initially recognised. Servicing assets or liabilities are subsequently amortised over the period of estimated net servicing income or net servicing loss. Subsequent measurement at fair value through profit or loss is precluded, because the fair value option is applicable only to financial items and, therefore, it cannot be applied to servicing rights.

There are no SPEs involved. Entity P has sold the loans directly to the bank.

The financial instruments being transferred have similar characteristics. They are all fixed-rate loans to similar counterparties that mature at approximately the same time (five years). They can be assessed as a group of similar financial assets in their entirety.
Step 3 - Have the rights to the cash flows expired?
No, the portfolio of loans has not yet reached maturity, so the rights to the cash flows still exist.
Step 4 - Is there a transfer?

Yes, entity P has assigned the loans to the bank. In addition, although the debtors have not been notified that their loans have been transferred, this does not preclude this transaction from meeting the definition of a transfer, because entity P is only servicing the loans and has no rights to cash flows (other than the servicing fee of 13bp).
Step 5 - Risks and rewards analysis

Entity P has retained one-third of any credit losses that are incurred by the bank on these loans. Entity P has not retained any other risk on these loans. Therefore, entity P has retained some risks and rewards, since credit risk is the only significant risk, but not substantially all risks and rewards, and should ask the control question.

The bank does not have the ability to sell the loans unilaterally. There is no market in the loans and, because the loans are subject to the guarantee, the bank would want to also sell the loans subject to that guarantee. That additional restriction means that entity P still controls the loans. Therefore, entity P will continue to recognise the loans to the extent of its continuing involvement.

Entity P has neither retained nor transferred substantially all of the risks and rewards relating to the loans and has retained control; it should therefore account for the transfer using continuing involvement. The continuing involvement is the lower of (a) the amount of the asset, and (b) the maximum amount of the consideration received that the entity could be required to repay (‘the guarantee amount’):
- The amount of the asset equals C10 million.

- The maximum amount of the consideration received (C10.1 million) that the entity could be required to repay – the guaranteed amount – is one-third of the principal balance and amounts to C3,333,333.
The continuing involvement asset is therefore C3,333,333 (the lower of (a) and (b)).

The associated liability is measured in such a way that the net carrying amount of the transferred asset and the associated liability is equal to the fair value of the rights and obligations retained by the entity when measured on a stand-alone basis, in accordance with paragraph 31(b) of IAS 39 / paragraph 3.2.17 of IFRS 9.

The entity has the obligation to provide a guarantee for one-third of credit losses. The fair value of the guarantee obligation is C100,000. Accordingly, the liability is C3,433,333, being the aggregate of the amount of the continuing involvement asset above (C3,333,333) and the guarantee amount (C100,000).

FAQ 44.109.1 – Why do entities exchange or modify debt instruments?

Entities frequently negotiate with lenders to re-structure their existing debt obligations. There might be a variety of reasons for doing so, not necessarily when the entity is in financial difficulties. Such re-structuring might result in a modification or an exchange of debt instruments with the lender, that could be carried out in a number of ways. Examples include:

- An entity might decide to take advantage of falling interest rates by cancelling its exposure to high-interest fixed-rate debt, pay a fee or penalty on cancellation and replace it with debt at a lower interest rate. This is an exchange of old debt with new debt.

Whether a modification or exchange of debt instruments represents a settlement of the original debt, or merely a renegotiation of that debt, determines the accounting treatment that should be applied by the borrower.

FAQ 44.110.1 – What qualitative and/or quantitative tests are required to determine whether terms are ‘substantially different’?
Reference to standard: IAS 39 paras 40, AG62; IFRS 9 paras 3.3.2, B3.3.6 Reference to standing text: 44.110

Paragraph B3.3.6 of IFRS 9 requires an entity to determine whether the present value of the new cash flows under the new terms is at least 10% different from the present value of the remaining cash flows of the original liability, using the original effective interest rate. If the difference is 10% or greater, the existing liability is de-recognised and a new financial liability is recognised.

The standard is not clear whether the quantitative analysis (described above) is the definition of ‘substantially different’, or whether it is only an example such that a broader analysis that considers qualitative factors can also be performed. We believe that an entity has an accounting policy choice: either it can apply only the quantitative 10% test (described above); or, if the 10% test is passed, it could choose to also perform a qualitativ
The chosen accounting policy should be applied consistently and disclosed.
Determining whether the terms are substantially different, from a qualitative perspective, is judgemental and will depend on the specific facts and circumstances of each case.

Changes to the terms of the liability might be significant, on a qualitative basis, if they significantly affect the economic risks of the liability. Alternatively, the substance of the modification might be that the existing liability is prepaid/settled and a new liability has been issued.
Qualitative factors include, but are not limited to, the following:
- A change in the currency in which the liability is denominated.
- A change in the interest basis (such as a change from fixed rate to floating rate, or vice versa).
- A change in any conversion features in the instrument.
- A substantial change in covenants.

- The liability was prepayable at par, with no significant penalty at the date of the renegotiation, which results in the renegotiated rate approximating the current market rate of interest for the new terms and conditions.

- The liability was close to its maturity date at the date of the renegotiation and was extended for a significant additional period, which results in the renegotiated rate approximating the current market rate of interest for the new terms and conditions (including the new maturity date).
FAQ 44.110.2 – Who is the ‘existing lender’ where lending is via a syndicate of banks?
Reference to standard: IAS 39 paras 40, AG62; IFRS 9 paras 3.3.2, B3.3.6 Reference to standing text: 44.110

There is no guidance in the standard that assists in interpreting the terms ‘existing borrower’ and ‘existing lender’ when looking at transactions where lending is via a syndicate of banks. In such cases, the borrower should determine, in the first instance, whether it has borrowed under one loan or under multiple loans. Sometimes, syndicated loans are structured with one ‘lead lender’ signing the loan agreement. The agreement’s substance rather
Presented below are a number of factors that, individually or in combination, would tend to indicate that the borrower has borrowed under multiple loans (this is not an exhaustive list):

- The borrower has the ability to selectively repay amounts on the loan to different members of the syndicate. In other words, any payments made by the borrowers are not always split on a pro rata basis amongst all the syndicate members.
- The terms of the loan are not homogeneous for various syndicate members.
- The borrower has the ability to selectively renegotiate portions of the loan with individual syndicate members or subsets of all of the syndicate members.
- Individual syndicate members have the ability to negotiate their loan directly with the borrower, without the approval of other syndicate members.
Example 1 – Change of loan terms and change in interests within syndicate (single loan)

An entity signs a loan agreement that was negotiated with a syndicate of 20 banks that each have a 5% interest in the total amount borrowed. The entity has determined that it has borrowed under a single loan.

A year later, the borrower and the syndicate members agree to a change in the contract terms that has an impact on future cash flows: an extension of the maturity of the loan. In addition, three banks sell their interest back to one of the existing syndicate members (bank A), so that bank A now has a 20% stake.

From the borrower’s perspective, the loan is a single loan. Accordingly, since the modification is between an existing borrower and lender (the syndicate), the change to the terms of the loan would be evaluated on an aggregate basis to determine whether the modification is an extinguishment. The transfer between syndicate members has no impact on the accounting by the borrower.
Example 2 – Multiple loans

An entity has a loan agreement signed by 20 banks, which are each determined to have granted separate loans to the borrower. Each of the 20 banks has a 5% stake in the total face amount of the loan. If new creditors join the group, they must individually sign a new contract with the borrower. From the borrower’s perspective, these are multiple loans and are accounted for as such.

Four of the banks transfer their 20% combined stake to another bank, without any other change in the terms of the loan. It is necessary to determine whether the transfer is undertaken in a manner that results in the borrower being legally released from primary responsibility for the liability by the existing bank lender. In this example, the new lender has to individually sign a new contract with the borrower, and the borrower is legally released

Bank A (a current syndicate member) might sell a participation in its loan to bank B. In such a case, there would be no effect on the entity (borrower), unless the entity has been legally released from primary responsibility by bank A. Bank A is still a creditor of the entity and bank B is a creditor of bank A.

Alternatively, five of the banks in the syndicate agree to extend the maturity of their loans. The remaining 15 institutions did not agree to the extension. The loans with the banks that agreed to the modification would be evaluated individually, to determine if they were modified or extinguished. The loans to the banks that did not agree to the modification are unchanged. They therefore do not need to be evaluated for modification or extinguishm

If all of the lenders agree to change terms of the loan that have an impact on its future cash flows, then, in principle, loans with each lender should be evaluated separately to determine if they have been extinguished or modified. If all of the loans have homogeneous terms, practically the same answer will be achieved if the loans are evaluated on an aggregate basis.
EX 44.110.3 – Exchange or modification of only one component
Reference to standard: IAS 39 paras 40, AG62; IFRS 9 paras 3.3.2, B3.3.6 Reference to standing text: 44.110

The liability being exchanged or modified might be only one component of a financial instrument. Where two or more components of a financial instrument are interdependent, a change to the terms of one component is likely to have repercussions on the others.
Example 1 – Extension of the term of a convertible bond where the conversion option is accounted for as an embedded derivative

Entity B issues a convertible bond in which the conversion option is accounted for as an embedded derivative (because it violates the fixed for fixed rule in IAS 32, see chapter 43). Some time after issuance, the issuer and the holder renegotiate the terms of the convertible bond. The revised terms include extending the bond’s maturity and increasing the conversion ratio: more ordinary shares of the issuer are to be delivered.

From the issuer’s perspective, the modification of the host contract and the derivative should be assessed together when applying the 10% test. This is because the cash flows relating to the host debt and embedded derivative are interdependent.
The term ‘cash flow’ in the 10% test includes the impact of settlement in a variable number of shares. One possible way of applying it is to assess the estimated cash flow as being the higher of:
- the fair value of the share settlement at the date of the modification (using the current market share price); and
- the present value of cash flows attributable to the host.

This approach reflects the optionality, from the holder’s perspective, to choose the more valuable settlement option. Another way of determining the fair value of the share settlement in this approach is to use the forward price(s) of the entity’s shares as at the estimated conversion date, and to discount to the modification date. Where the expected conversion date cannot be estimated reliably under this alternative, the contractual maturity dat
Example 2 – Exchange of a convertible instrument for debt

Entity A has issued two-year convertible debt for C100, in which the conversion option meets the ‘fixed for fixed’ test in IAS 32 (see chapter 43). It is therefore accounted for as an equity component, with a liability recognised for the debt component. At the end of year 1, the convertible debt has a fair value of C90 and the host debt component has a fair value of C85. Entity A agrees with the convertible debt holders to exchange their instrume

Entity A has a policy choice as to whether a qualitative test is applied in addition to the 10% quantitative test when de-recognising financial liabilities. If entity A considers both qualitative factors and the 10% quantitative test, either of the two approaches (A and B) could be applied, to determine whether the liability component of the convertible bond should be de-recognised. However, if entity A has a policy of only de-recognising financi
Approach A – qualitative assessment: extinguished in its entirety

From a qualitative perspective, provided the original conversion option was substantial (that is, its worth is not insignificant to the holder) at the date of the exchange, the new non-convertible debt instrument is substantially different from the convertible debt. This is by virtue of it not being convertible. The risk profile and related returns arising from the original conversion option are effectively terminated. The existing convertible de

A gain or loss is recognised on the extinguishment of the convertible bond in accordance with IAS 32. This gain or loss is the difference between the carrying amount of the debt component and the allocated consideration paid to redeem it. The full consideration paid (in this case, the C90 new debt issued) is allocated to the debt and equity components of the existing convertible instrument. This is done at the date of the transaction. The allocat

The new debt allocated to extinguishing the equity conversion option of C5 (C90 × 5/90) does not result in a gain or loss. Rather, the difference between this amount and the carrying value of the conversion option is taken directly to equity.
Approach B – quantitative assessment: debt component subject to 10% test, equity component extinguished

Under this approach, the de-recognition requirements are viewed as applying to financial liabilities only. Part of the new debt instrument replaces the debt component of the convertible instrument, and part replaces the equity component of the original instrument. The new debt instrument is, therefore, allocated to the debt and equity elements of the convertible instrument for the purpose of their separate de-recognition assessments. The allocati

The de-recognition test should be applied to the debt component only. Applying the 10% test on this basis results in the entity continuing to recognise the old debt component. Equally, the terms of the debt component are not considered to be substantially modified, from a qualitative perspective. The revision of the terms of the debt component is, therefore, treated as a modification in this example.

Under IAS 39, where a financial liability measured at amortised cost is modified without this resulting in de-recognition, the difference due to the change in terms (using the same effective rate) is either adjusted for by applying paragraph AG8 of IAS 39, or it is spread over the remaining life of the new debt.

Under IFRS 9, where a financial liability measured at amortised cost is modified without this resulting in de-recognition, a gain or loss should be recognised immediately in profit or loss. This means that the difference cannot be spread over the remaining life of the instrument. For further guidance on accounting for modifications that do not result in de-recognition under IFRS 9, see chapter 42 para 121.

The remaining part of the new debt instrument extinguishes the conversion option, which does not give rise to a gain or loss (IAS 32 para 33). The difference between the amount of the new debt that extinguishes the conversion option and the previous carrying value of the conversion option is taken directly to equity.

The combined result of the two elements means that, at the date of the exchange, part of the new debt is measured at its fair value (being the part that replaces the equity component). Where there is no de-recognition of the old debt component, part of the debt is measured at the amortised cost of the old debt component (the part that replaces the debt component of the original convertible).

If applying the de-recognition criteria to the debt component results in de-recognition of the existing old debt component, the gain or loss on de-recognition is calculated in the same way as discussed under approach A.
FAQ 44.110.4 – How should the restructuring of an undrawn revolving credit facility be accounted for?
Reference to standard: IAS 39 para AG 62; IFRS 9 para B3.3.6 Reference to standing text: 44.110

Entities with undrawn revolving credit facilities (RCFs) might renegotiate the terms of their borrowing facilities with the existing lender (for example, by extending the maturity or renegotiating the interest rate payable).
Although loan commitments are generally outside the scope of IFRS 9 and IAS 39, they are subject to the de-recognition requirements. [IFRS 9 para 2.1(g)]. [IAS 39 para 2(h)].

How should an entity apply the ‘10% test’ for financial liabilities (in para B3.3.6 of IFRS 9 and para AG 62 of IAS 39) in this situation, to determine whether or not the original undrawn RCF has been substantially modified and should be de-recognised, along with any associated deferred fees?
Note that, as well as the quantitative ‘10% test’, an entity might also, as a policy choice, consider qualitative factors (see FAQ 44.110.1).
Judgement is required when applying the 10% test to undrawn RCFs, because there is no explicit guidance in either IFRS 9 or IAS 39 as to how the ‘10% test’ should be applied to undrawn RCFs.

If management is able to reliably estimate the future cash flows of the facility, a reasonable approach could be to use these estimated future cash flows as the basis for the ‘10% test’. If it is not possible to reliably estimate future cash flows, a reasonable approach would be to assume that the facility will be fully drawn. EX 44.117.2 – Renegotiation of debt under IFRS 9
Reference to standard: IFRS 9 para B3.3.6 Reference to standing text: 44.117
This example assumes that the entity applies the amendment described in paragraph 44.110.1.

Where the modification of a financial liability is not accounted for as an extinguishment, the fees paid to third parties and some of the fees paid to the lender (see FAQ 44.117.1) are adjusted against the existing liability’s carrying value and spread forward by adjusting the effective interest rate in accordance with paragraph B3.3.6A of IFRS 9.

A company borrowed C1 million on 1 January 20X0 at a fixed rate of 9% per annum for ten years. The company incurred issue costs of C100,000. Interest on the loan is payable yearly in arrears. As a result of deteriorating financial conditions during 20X5, the company approached its lender for a modification of the loan’s terms. The following terms were agreed with effect from 1 January 20X6 (all interest paid to date):
- The interest rate is reduced to 7.5% payable yearly in arrears.
- The original amount payable on maturity is reduced to C950,000.
- The maturity of the loan is extended by two years to 31 December 20Y1.
- Renegotiation fees of C30,000 and compensation for legal costs of the lender amounting to C10,000 are payable to the lender on 1 January 20X6.

The renegotiation fees were paid to the lender, and the entity assessed that they relate to compensation paid to the lender in return for the reduction in interest rate, a reduced final amount payable on maturity, as well as the extension of the term of the loan. The additional amount paid to reimburse the lender for its cost related to legal services does not reflect any kind of compensation for the change in the terms of the instrument. The len
The loan would be recorded initially at 1 January 20X0 at net proceeds of C900,000 and would be amortised using the effective interest rate (EIR) method. The EIR is 10.6749%.

At 1 January 20X6, the remaining cash flows on the old debt comprise four annual interest payments of C90,000 and the C1 million of principal payable at redemption. The present value of these remaining cash flows on that date amounts to C947,674, as shown above.

Paragraph B3.3.6 of IFRS 9 addresses which fees should be included in the 10% test. All payments between borrower and lender are included, irrespective of whether they compensate the lender for a change in the terms of the contract (in this example, C30,000) or for any costs incurred (in this example, C10,000).

Step 1 – Scope exception from the general model: simplified approach for trade and lease receivables

45.12 The model includes some operational simplifications for trade receivables, contract assets and lease receivables, because they are often held by entities that do not have sophisticated credit risk management systems. These simplifications eliminate the need to calculate 12-month ECL and to assess when a significant increase in credit risk has occurred.

45.13 For trade receivables or contract assets that do not contain a significant financing component, the loss allowance should be measured at initial recognition and throughout its life at an amount equal to lifetime ECL. As a practical expedient, a provision matrix can be used to estimate ECL for these financial instruments.

45.14 An entity has an accounting policy choice for lease receivables, and trade receivables and contract assets which contain a significant financing component in accordance with IFRS 15. It can either apply the simplified approach (that is, to measure the loss allowance at an amount equal to lifetime ECL at initial recognition and throughout its life) or it can apply the general model.
45.15 An entity can apply the policy election for trade receivables, contract assets and lease receivables independently of each other, but it must apply the policy choice consistently.
Step 2 – Scope exception from the general model: purchased or originated credit-impaired assets

45.16 The general impairment model does not apply to purchased or originated credit-impaired assets. A financial asset is considered credit-impaired on purchase or origination if there is evidence of impairment at the point of initial recognition (for instance, if it is acquired at a deep discount). IFRS 9 includes a list of factors that would provide evidence that a financial asset is credit-impaired:
- significant financial difficulty of the issuer or the borrower;
- a breach of contract, such as a default or past due event;

- the lender(s) of the borrower, for economic or contractual reasons relating to the borrower’s financial difficulty, having granted to the borrower a concession(s) that the lender(s) would not otherwise consider;
- it is becoming probable that the borrower will enter bankruptcy or other financial reorganisation;
- the disappearance of an active market for that financial asset because of financial difficulties; or
- the purchase or origination of a financial asset at a deep discount that reflects the incurred credit losses.
The standard clarifies that it might not be possible to identify a single discrete event, so the combined effect of several events should be analysed.

Lifetime ECL are included in the estimated cash flows when calculating the effective interest rate on initial recognition. Step 3 – Practical expedient for financial assets with low credit risk

45.19 As an exception to the general model, if the credit risk of a financial instrument is low at the reporting date, the entity can measure impairment using 12-month ECL, and so it does not have to assess whether a significant increase in credit risk has occurred. The use of this practical expedient is optional; the entity can also choose to apply the general model for those assets.
45.20 The financial instrument has to meet the following requirements, in order for this practical expedient to apply:
- it has a low risk of default;
- the borrower is considered, in the short term, to have a strong capacity to meet its obligations in the near term; and
- the lender expects, in the longer term, that adverse changes in economic and business conditions might, but will not necessarily, reduce the ability of the borrower to fulfil its obligations.
[IFRS 9 App B para B5.5.22].

45.21 The credit risk of the instrument needs to be evaluated without consideration of collateral. Financial instruments are not considered to have low credit risk because that risk is mitigated by collateral. Financial instruments are also not considered to have low credit risk simply because they have a lower risk of default than the entity’s other financial instruments or relative to the credit risk of the jurisdiction within which the entity
[IFRS 9 App B para B5.5.22].
45.22 Financial instruments are not required to be externally rated. An entity can use internal credit ratings that are consistent with a global credit rating definition of ‘investment grade’.
[IFRS 9 App B para B5.5.23].

45.23 The low credit risk simplification is not meant to be a bright-line trigger for the recognition of lifetime ECL. Instead, when credit risk is no longer low, the entity should assess whether there has been a significant increase in credit risk to determine whether lifetime ECL should be recognised. This means that, if an instrument’s credit risk has increased such that it no longer qualifies as low credit risk, it is not automatically includ
[IFRS 9 App B para B5.5.24].
Step 4 – Exploring the general model: assessing a significant increase in credit risk

45.24 The entity looks at the change in the risk of a default occurring over the expected life of the financial instrument, rather than the change in the ECL, when assessing whether the credit risk on a financial instrument has increased significantly since initial recognition. An entity should compare the risk of a default at the reporting date with the risk of a default at the date of initial recognition.

45.31 All reasonable and supportable information available without undue cost or effort should be taken into account to perform the assessment of changes in credit risk.

45.32 The standard provides a non-exhaustive list of information that might be relevant in assessing changes in credit risk:

- Significant changes in internal price indicators of credit risk as a result of a change in credit risk since inception, including, but not limited to, the credit spread that would result if a particular financial instrument or similar financial instrument with the same terms and the same counterparty were newly originated or issued at the reporting date.

- Other changes in the rates or terms of an existing financial instrument that would be significantly different if the instrument was newly originated or issued at the reporting date (such as more stringent covenants, increased amounts of collateral or guarantees, or higher income coverage) because of changes in the credit risk of the financial instrument since initial recognition.

- Significant changes in external market indicators of credit risk for a particular financial instrument or similar financial instruments with the same expected life. Changes in market indicators of credit risk include, but are not limited to:
- the credit default swap prices for the borrower;
- the length of time for which, or the extent to which, the fair value of a financial asset has been less than its amortised cost; and
- other market information related to the borrower, such as changes in the price of a borrower’s debt and equity instruments.
- An actual or expected significant change in the financial instrument’s external credit rating.

- An actual or expected internal credit rating downgrade for the borrower or decrease in behavioural scoring used to assess credit risk internally. Internal credit ratings and internal behavioural scoring are more reliable when they are mapped to external ratings or supported by default studies.

- Existing or forecast adverse changes in business, financial or economic conditions that are expected to cause a significant change in the borrower’s ability to meet its debt obligations, such as an actual or expected increase in interest rates or an actual or expected significant increase in unemployment rates.

- An actual or expected significant change in the operating results of the borrower. Examples include actual or expected declining revenues or margins, increasing operating risks, working capital deficiencies, decreasing asset quality, increased balance sheet leverage, liquidity, management problems or changes in the scope of business or organisational structure (such as the discontinuance of a segment of the business) that result in a significan
- Significant increases in credit risk on other financial instruments of the same borrower.

- An actual or expected significant adverse change in the regulatory, economic or technological environment of the borrower that results in a significant change in the borrower’s ability to meet its debt obligations, such as a decline in the demand for the borrower’s sales product because of a shift in technology.

- Significant changes in the value of the collateral supporting the obligation or in the quality of third-party guarantees or credit enhancements, which are expected to reduce the borrower’s economic incentive to make scheduled contractual payments or to otherwise have an effect on the probability of a default occurring. For example, if the value of collateral declines because house prices decline, borrowers in some jurisdictions have a greater i

- A significant change in the quality of the guarantee provided by a shareholder (or an individual’s parents) if the shareholder (or parents) have an incentive and financial ability to prevent default by capital or cash infusion.

- Significant changes, such as reductions in financial support from a parent entity or other affiliate or an actual or expected significant change in the quality of credit enhancement, that are expected to reduce the borrower’s economic incentive to make scheduled contractual payments. Credit quality enhancements or support include the consideration of the financial condition of the guarantor and/or, for interests issued in securitisations, wheth

- Expected changes in the loan documentation, including an expected breach of contract that might lead to covenant waivers or amendments, interest payment holidays, interest rate step-ups, requiring additional collateral or guarantees, or other changes to the contractual framework of the instrument.

- Significant changes in the expected performance and behaviour of the borrower, including changes in the payment status of borrowers in the group (for example, an increase in the expected number or extent of delayed contractual payments or significant increases in the expected number of credit card borrowers who are expected to approach or exceed their credit limit or who are expected to be paying the minimum monthly amount).

- Changes in the entity’s credit management approach in relation to the financial instrument; that is, based on emerging indicators of changes in the credit risk of the financial instrument, the entity’s credit risk management practice is expected to become more active or to be focused on managing the instrument, including the instrument becoming more closely monitored or controlled, or the entity specifically intervening with the borrower.
[IFRS 9 App B para B5.5.17].

45.44 If the entity determines that there has not been a significant increase in credit risk, it measures the loss allowance for the particular asset or group of assets at an amount equal to 12-month ECL.

45.49 ECL are a probability-weighted estimate of credit losses. A credit loss is the difference between the cash flows that are due to an entity in accordance with the contract and the cash flows that the entity expects to receive discounted at the original effective interest rate. ECL consider the amount and timing of payments, thus a credit loss arises even if the entity expects to be paid in full but later than when contractually due.

45 - 减值（IFRS 9）
引言和范围（第45.1段至第45.10段）
45.1 IFRS 9 概述了一种基于自初始确认后信用质量变化的“三阶段”减值模型（“一般模型”）：
![](assets/158.png)
关于购买或源生的已发生信用减值的金融资产，有专门的指引（见下文第45.16段及以后段落）。

45.2 第一阶段包括自初始确认后信用风险未显著增加的金融工具，或（由企业选择）在报告日具有较低信用风险的金融工具。对于此类资产，应确认未来12个月内预期信用损失（ECL），且利息收入按资产的账面余额（即不扣除信用损失准备）计算。未来12个月内预期信用损失是指因报告日后12个月内可能发生的违约事件而导致的预期信用损失。它并非12个月期间内的预期现金流量短缺，而是资产的全部信用损失，并按未来12个月内发生该损失的概率进行加权。
45.3 第二阶段包括自初始确认后信用风险已显著增加（除非其在报告日具有较低信用风险且企业选择了该选项）但尚无减值客观证据的金融工具。对于此类资产，应确认整个存续期预期信用损失，但利息收入仍按资产的账面余额计算。整个存续期预期信用损失是指在企业面临信用风险的最长合同期间内，因所有可能发生的违约事件而导致的预期信用损失。预期信用损失是信用损失的加权平均值，权重为发生相应违约的风险。
45.4 第三阶段包括在报告日有减值客观证据的金融资产。对于此类资产，应确认整个存续期预期信用损失，且利息收入按账面净额（即扣除信用损失准备后的金额）计算。
FAQ 45.4.1 – 第三阶段已发生信用减值的金融资产的利息收入列报及预期信用损失折现转回 FAQ 45.4.2 – IFRS 9下的“第三阶段”预期信用损失准备是否与IAS 39下的已发生损失准备相同？ FAQ 45.4.3 – 金融资产发生信用减值（或不再发生信用减值）时利息收入计算方式变更的日期 FAQ 45.4.4 – 融资租赁应收款的利息收入列报
45.5 企业在确定金融工具的信用风险是否已显著增加时，应考虑可获得的合理且有依据的信息，以将报告日发生违约的风险与初始确认该金融工具时发生违约的风险进行比较。
45.6 在实务中应用这些要求可能较为复杂。本章提供了如何应用该模型的指引。

45.7 国际会计准则理事会（IASB）设立了国际财务报告准则金融工具减值过渡资源小组（“ITG”），作为一个讨论平台，就新减值要求所引发的实施问题向利益相关方提供支持。总体而言，ITG 的宗旨是：征集、分析并讨论利益相关方在实施新减值要求过程中产生的问题；向 IASB 通报这些实施问题，帮助 IASB 确定是否需要以及需要采取何种行动来解决这些问题；并为利益相关方提供一个公开平台，使其能够向参与实施的其他各方学习新减值要求。在会议期间，ITG 成员就相关问题分享了各自的观点。ITG 并不发布指引。IASB 决定就每个问题采取何种行动（如有）。我们在本章相关之处纳入了对 ITG 讨论的索引。
45.8 此外，巴塞尔银行监管委员会发布了关于银行信用风险及预期信用损失模型实施与应用的指引。本章不涉及该指引，仅聚焦于 IASB 发布的 IFRS 9。企业应参考巴塞尔委员会或其他监管机构发布的对其产生影响的任何相关补充指引。
45.9 该模型应适用于：
- 以摊余成本计量的债务工具投资；
- 以公允价值计量且其变动计入其他综合收益（FVOCI）的债务工具投资；
- 所有未以公允价值计量且其变动计入当期损益的贷款承诺；
- 适用 IFRS 9 且未以公允价值计量且其变动计入当期损益进行会计处理的财务担保合同；以及
- 属于 IFRS 16 范围内的租赁应收款，以及属于 IFRS 15 范围内并产生收取对价的有条件权利的应收账款和合同资产。
该模型不适用于权益工具投资。
[IFRS 9 第5.5.1段]。
45.10 贷款承诺的签发方应对所有贷款承诺应用 IFRS 9 的减值要求，包括原本不属于本准则范围内的贷款承诺（除非该贷款承诺以公允价值计量且其变动计入当期损益）。

步骤1——一般模型的范围例外：应收账款和租赁应收款的简化方法
45.12 该模型为应收账款、合同资产和租赁应收款包含了一些操作上的简化处理，因为持有这些资产的企业通常不具备复杂的信用风险管理系统。这些简化处理免除了计算未来12个月内预期信用损失以及评估信用风险何时显著增加的需要。

45.13 对于不含重大融资成分的应收账款或合同资产，应在初始确认时及整个存续期内按照相当于整个存续期预期信用损失的金额计量损失准备。作为一项实务权宜措施，可以使用减值准备矩阵来估计这些金融工具的预期信用损失。
![](assets/160.png)

45.14 对于租赁应收款，以及根据 IFRS 15 包含重大融资成分的应收账款和合同资产，企业拥有会计政策选择权。企业既可以采用简化方法（即在初始确认时及整个存续期内均按照相当于整个存续期预期信用损失的金额计量损失准备），也可以采用一般模型。
45.15 企业可以针对应收账款、合同资产和租赁应收款相互独立地作出会计政策选择，但必须一贯地应用所选的会计政策。
![](assets/161.png)
步骤2——一般模型的范围例外：购买或源生的已发生信用减值的金融资产
45.16 一般减值模型不适用于购买或源生的已发生信用减值的金融资产。如果在初始确认时点即存在减值证据（例如，以大幅折价购入），则该金融资产被视为在购买或源生时即已发生信用减值。IFRS 9 列举了一系列可为金融资产已发生信用减值提供证据的因素：
- 发行方或借款人发生重大财务困难；
- 违反合同，如违约或逾期事件；
- 借款人的贷款人出于与借款人财务困难有关的经济或合同考虑，给予借款人在任何其他情况下都不会做出的让步；
- 借款人很可能破产或进行其他财务重组；
- 发行方或债务人财务困难导致该金融资产的活跃市场消失；或
- 以大幅折扣购买或源生一项金融资产，该折扣反映了发生信用损失的事实。
准则明确指出，可能无法识别单一的离散事件，因此应当分析若干事件的综合影响。
[IFRS 9 附录A]。

45.17 对于购买或源生的已发生信用减值的金融资产，减值在初始确认时即基于全部整个存续期预期信用损失确定。在初始确认时计算实际利率时，整个存续期预期信用损失包含在估计现金流量中。在资产的整个存续期内用于确认利息的实际利率是经信用调整的实际利率。因此，在初始确认时不确认损失准备。

45.18 整个存续期预期信用损失的任何后续变动（无论是有利变动还是不利变动），都将立即计入利润表，即使整个存续期预期信用损失小于初始确认时包含在估计现金流量中的预期信用损失金额。

步骤3——具有较低信用风险的金融资产的实务权宜措施
45.19 作为一般模型的例外，如果金融工具在报告日的信用风险较低，企业可以使用未来12个月内预期信用损失来计量减值，从而无需评估信用风险是否已显著增加。使用该实务权宜措施是可选的；企业也可以选择对这些资产应用一般模型。
45.20 为适用该实务权宜措施，金融工具必须满足以下要求：
- 借款人在短期内履行其合同现金流量义务的能力很强；以及
- 贷款人预期，从较长时期来看，经济和商业状况的不利变化可能会（但未必会）降低借款人履行其义务的能力。
[IFRS 9 附录B第B5.5.22段]。
45.21 评估金融工具的信用风险时不得考虑担保物。金融工具不会因为其信用风险因担保物而降低就被视为具有较低信用风险。金融工具也不会仅仅因为其违约风险低于企业的其他金融工具，或者相对于企业经营所在司法管辖区的信用风险较低，就被视为具有较低信用风险。
[IFRS 9 附录B第B5.5.22段]。
45.22 并不要求金融工具具有外部评级。企业可以使用与全球通用的“投资级”信用评级定义一致的内部信用评级。
[IFRS 9 附录B第B5.5.23段]。
45.23 低信用风险简化处理并非旨在成为确认整个存续期预期信用损失的绝对分界线触发条件。相反，当信用风险不再较低时，企业应评估信用风险是否已显著增加，以确定是否应确认整个存续期预期信用损失。这意味着，如果一项工具的信用风险增加致使其不再符合低信用风险条件，该工具并不会自动进入第二阶段。企业在为该工具计算整个存续期预期信用损失之前，需要评估信用风险是否已显著增加。
[IFRS 9 附录B第B5.5.24段]。
步骤4——探索一般模型：评估信用风险显著增加
45.24 企业在评估自初始确认后金融工具的信用风险是否已显著增加时，应关注金融工具预计存续期内发生违约的风险的变化，而非预期信用损失的变化。企业应将报告日发生违约的风险与初始确认日发生违约的风险进行比较。
[IFRS 9 第5.5.9段]。

45.25 对于贷款承诺，企业应考虑与该贷款承诺相关的贷款发生违约的风险的变化。对于财务担保合同，企业应考虑特定债务人就该合同发生违约的风险的变化。就对贷款承诺和财务担保合同应用减值要求而言，企业成为不可撤销承诺一方的日期应被视为初始确认日。
[IFRS 9 附录B第B5.5.8段]。[IFRS 9 第5.5.6段]。
FAQ 45.25.1 – 用于确定信用风险显著增加的初始确认日能否“重置”为贷款承诺或信贷额度大幅增加之日？
45.26 企业应采用与针对相关金融工具进行内部信用风险管理所采用的违约定义一致的“违约”定义，并在适当情况下考虑定性指标（例如财务契约）。但是，存在一项可推翻的推定，即违约的发生不晚于金融资产逾期90日，除非企业有合理且有依据的信息表明采用更滞后的违约标准更为恰当。用于此目的的违约定义应一贯地应用于所有金融工具，除非有可获得的信息表明另一违约定义对特定金融工具更为恰当。
[IFRS 9 附录B第B5.5.37段]。

45.28 未来12个月违约概率并非始终是使用整个存续期违约概率的合理近似值。例外情况包括：
- 到期一次性还本贷款，即债务人在贷款授信的前12个月内的付款义务不重大；
- 信用相关因素的变化仅在12个月之后才对金融工具的信用风险产生影响的贷款；以及
- 相关宏观经济或其他信用相关因素发生变化，而这些变化未充分反映在未来12个月内发生违约的风险中的情况。

45.30 简单地或绝对地比较初始确认日和报告日的违约概率（PD）是不恰当的。金融工具的违约概率通常会随着时间的推移而降低。因此，企业在比较违约概率时，需要考虑金融工具在初始确认时和在报告日的相对剩余期限。这意味着，报告日金融资产剩余存续期的违约概率（例如，一项五年期工具已过三年，则剩余期限为两年），应当与初始确认时预期的该工具最后两年（即第4年和第5年）的违约概率进行比较。企业可能会发现这一要求在操作上具有挑战性。

45.32 准则提供了一份在评估信用风险变化时可能相关的非穷尽信息清单：
- 由于自初始确认后信用风险发生变化而导致的信用风险内部价格指标的显著变化，包括但不限于：如果在报告日新源生或新发行具有相同条款和相同交易对手的特定金融工具或类似金融工具所产生的信用利差。
- 由于自初始确认后金融工具信用风险发生变化，导致现有金融工具的利率或条款发生其他变化，如果该工具是在报告日新源生或新发行的，这些利率或条款将会显著不同（例如更严格的限制性条款、增加担保物或担保金额，或更高的收益覆盖率）。
- 特定金融工具或具有相同预计存续期的类似金融工具的信用风险外部市场指标的显著变化。信用风险市场指标的变化包括但不限于：
- 针对借款人的信用违约互换（CDS）价格；
- 金融资产的公允价值小于其摊余成本的时间长短和程度；以及
- 与借款人有关的其他市场信息，例如借款人债务工具和权益工具的价格变化。
- 金融工具外部信用评级的实际或预期显著变化。
- 借款人内部信用评级的实际或预期下调，或用于内部评估信用风险的行为评分下降。当内部信用评级和内部行为评分与外部评级相映射或得到违约研究的支持时，它们会更加可靠。
- 预期将导致借款人履行其偿债义务的能力发生显著变化的商业、财务或经济状况的现有或预测的不利变化，例如利率的实际或预期上升，或失业率的实际或预期显著上升。
- 借款人经营成果的实际或预期显著变化。示例包括实际或预期的收入或利润率下降、经营风险增加、营运资金不足、资产质量下降、资产负债表杠杆率上升、流动性问题、管理问题，或导致借款人履行偿债义务的能力发生显著变化的业务范围或组织结构变化（例如终止某一业务分部）。
- 同一借款人的其他金融工具的信用风险显著增加。
- 借款人所处的监管、经济或技术环境的实际或预期显著不利变化，导致借款人履行偿债义务的能力发生显著变化，例如由于技术变革导致市场对借款人销售产品的需求下降。
- 作为债务抵押的担保物价值或第三方提供的担保或信用增级质量的显著变化，这些变化预期将降低借款人按合同规定期限还款的经济动机，或以其他方式对发生违约的概率产生影响。例如，如果房价下跌导致担保物价值下降，某些司法管辖区的借款人可能会有更大的动机对其抵押贷款违约。
- 如果股东（或个人的父母）有动机且有财务能力通过注资或提供现金来防止违约，则股东（或父母）提供的担保质量的显著变化。
- 预期将降低借款人按合同规定期限还款的经济动机的显著变化，例如母公司或其他关联方提供的财务支持减少，或信用增级质量的实际或预期显著变化。信用质量增级或支持包括考虑担保人的财务状况，和/或就证券化中发行的权益而言，考虑次级权益预期是否能够吸收预期信用损失（例如证券所对应的基础贷款的预期信用损失）。
- 贷款文件的预期变更，包括可能导致豁免或修订限制性条款、免息期、利率上调、要求追加担保物或担保，或对工具合同框架作出其他变更的预期违约。
- 借款人预期表现和行为的显著变化，包括组内借款人付款状况的变化（例如，预期延迟合同付款的次数或程度增加，或预期接近或超过信用额度的信用卡借款人人数或预期仅支付每月最低还款额的信用卡借款人人数显著增加）。
- 企业与该金融工具相关的信用管理方法的变化；即基于新出现的金融工具信用风险变化指标，企业的信用风险管理实务预计将变得更加积极或专注于管理该工具，包括对该工具进行更密切的监控或控制，或企业专门对借款人进行干预。
[IFRS 9 附录B第B5.5.17段]。

45.33 即使担保物价值的变动可以被视为信用风险变动的指标，企业在评估信用风险是否显著增加时也不应考虑担保物。但是，在计算预期信用损失时，应当考虑从担保物中预期可收回的金额。
[IFRS 9 附录B第B5.5.55段]。[IFRS 9 附录B第B5.5.12段]。
EX 45.33.1 – 评估有担保贷款的信用风险显著增加 FAQ 45.33.2 – 全额担保贷款能否符合已发生信用减值的条件？
逾期30日的可推翻的推定
45.34 确定信用风险是否已显著增加时，需同时使用前瞻性信息和历史信息。通常预期应在金融工具逾期之前即确认整个存续期预期信用损失。一般而言，在金融工具逾期或观察到其他滞后的借款人特定因素（例如合同修改或重组）之前，信用风险即已显著增加。在评估信用风险的变化时，必须使用比逾期信息更具前瞻性且无需付出不必要的额外成本或努力即可获得的合理且有依据的信息。
[IFRS 9 附录B第B5.5.2段]。
45.35 企业在确定自初始确认后信用风险是否已显著增加时，不能仅依赖拖欠信息；还需考虑合理可得的前瞻性信息，其中包括组合层面的信息。如果无法获得前瞻性信息，企业可以使用逾期信息来确定自初始确认后信用风险是否已显著增加；在此情况下，也应考虑组合层面的信息。存在一项可推翻的推定，即当合同付款逾期超过30日时，信用风险自初始确认后已显著增加。
45.36 如果有合理且有依据的证据表明信用风险并未显著增加（例如，未付款系行政管理疏忽所致，而非源于借款人的财务困难），则该推定可以被推翻。另一个例子是，企业能够获得历史证据，证明违约发生风险的显著增加与付款逾期超过30日的金融资产之间不存在相关性，但该证据确实识别出当付款逾期超过60日时存在此类相关性。
[IFRS 9 附录B第B5.5.20段]。
45.37 如果在合同付款逾期超过30日之前信用风险即已显著增加，则该可推翻的推定不适用。
45.38 一般而言，信用风险的显著增加会随着时间推移逐步发生，并早于金融资产已发生信用减值或处于违约状态。应当在金融资产被视为已发生信用减值或违约之前确认整个存续期预期信用损失。
[IFRS 9 附录B第B5.5.7段]。

45.39 可获得的定性信息和非统计定量信息可能足以确定某项金融工具已满足按相当于整个存续期预期信用损失的金额确认损失准备的标准。也就是说，相关信息无需经过统计模型或信用评级流程，即可确定金融工具的信用风险是否已显著增加。但是，在其他情况下，企业可能需要考虑定性信息，包括来自其统计模型或信用评级流程的信息。或者，如果两类信息均相关，企业可以同时基于两类信息（即内部评级流程未捕获的定性因素以及报告日的信用风险特征）进行评估。
[IFRS 9 附录B第B5.5.18段]。
FAQ 45.39.1 – 信用风险显著增加的定性与定量评估
应当在何种层级上执行信用风险增加的评估

45.40 企业可能无法在金融工具逾期之前识别单项金融工具信用风险的显著变化。零售贷款就可能属于这种情况，因为在客户违反合同条款之前，企业通常很少或根本不会就单项工具例行获取和监控更新的信用风险信息。如果在单项金融工具逾期之前未捕获其信用风险的变化，则仅基于单项金融工具层面信用信息计量的损失准备将无法如实反映自初始确认以来的信用风险变化。企业应当着眼于组合层面的信息来执行评估。如果组合层面可获得的信息表明该组合中包含的工具的信用风险已经增加，企业不能通过仅在单项资产层面进行评估来避免计算整个存续期预期信用损失。
[IFRS 9 附录B第B5.5.3段]。
45.41 企业可以基于共同信用风险特征对金融工具进行分组，目的是便于开展分析，以及时识别信用风险显著增加并确认损失准备。企业不应将具有不同风险特征的金融工具归为一组，从而掩盖该信息。共同信用风险特征的示例可能包括但不限于：
- 借款人所处地理位置；以及
- 担保物相对于金融资产的价值（如果其对发生违约的概率产生影响，例如某些司法管辖区的无追索权贷款或贷款价值比）。
[IFRS 9 附录B第B5.5.5段]。
FAQ 45.41.1 – 有担保债务工具的信用风险显著增加评估
45.42 IFRS 9 提供了一些如何执行组合分析的示例。准则规定，可以基于共同的借款人特定特征（例如地理位置或邮政编码、源生时的还款缓冲空间/负担能力或行为评分）将单项风险敞口划分为子组合（即“自下而上”方法）。或者，企业可以使用一般信息估计组合中信用风险已显著增加的比例，并在此基础上计算预期信用损失（即“自上而下”方法）。
[IFRS 9 附录B第B5.5.6段]。

- 取消合同的合同能力在金融工具的日常正常管理中并不执行，仅当企业在授信额度层面察觉信用风险增加时才可能取消合同；以及

- 类似金融工具在信用风险增加后发生相关违约所需的时间长度；以及
- 一旦金融工具的信用风险增加，企业预期将采取的信用风险管理措施，例如削减或取消未提取额度。

- 通过评价一系列可能的结果而确定的无偏概率加权平均金额；
- 在报告日关于过去事项、当前状况以及未来事项和经济状况预测的合理且有依据的信息。

45.65 企业可以使用各种内部和外部数据来源来计量预期信用损失。可能的数据来源包括历史信用损失经验、内部评级、其他企业的信用损失经验，以及外部评级、报告和统计数据。但是，企业应当考虑关于特定金融工具或类似金融工具信用风险的可观察市场信息。
[IFRS 9 附录B第B5.5.51段]。

45.66 历史数据可作为计量预期信用损失的基础。应对此类数据进行调整，以反映并未影响历史数据所基于期间的当前状况和对未来状况的预测，并消除历史期间中与未来合同现金流量不相关状况的影响。根据历史信息的性质和计算时间，并与报告日的情况以及所考虑金融工具的特征相比较，最佳的合理且有依据的信息可能是未经调整的历史信息。对预期信用损失变动的估计应当反映各期间相关可观察数据的变化（例如失业率、房地产价格和大宗商品价格的变化），并在方向上与之保持一致。企业应定期复核用于估计预期信用损失的方法论和假设，以减少估计值与实际信用损失经验之间的任何差异。
[IFRS 9 附录B第B5.5.52段]。
FAQ 45.66.1 – 在新冠肺炎疫情（COVID-19）和预期信用损失的背景下，哪些信息属于“合理且有依据的”？ FAQ 45.66.2 – 在气候变化和预期信用损失的背景下，哪些信息被视为“合理且有依据的”？
45.67 关于历史信用损失率的信息，应应用于其界定方式与观察到该历史信用损失率的组别相一致的组别。用于估计预期信用损失的方法，应使每组金融资产能够与相似的风险特征以及反映当前状况的相关可观察数据相联系。
[IFRS 9 附录B第B5.5.53段]。
45.68 企业还应考虑可获得的预测信息，例如包含在商业计划中的信息（“内部信息”）或市场提供的信息——例如表明信用评级预期变化的价格变动（“外部信息”）。
45.69 预期信用损失的估计并不要求对遥远未来的期间作出详细估计。对于此类期间，企业可以根据可获得的详细信息外推预测。对于超出“合理且有依据的预测”的期间，企业应通过考虑报告日关于当前状况的信息以及对未来事项和经济状况的预测，来考量如何最佳地反映其预期。
[IFRS 9 附录B第B5.5.50段]。
45.70 准则并未具体规定如何根据可获得的信息外推预测。可以采用不同的外推方法。例如，企业可以在剩余期间内应用平均预期信用损失，或者基于最后一项可获得的预测使用稳定的预期信用损失率。这些仅为示例，也可能适用其他方法。企业应选择一种方法并一贯应用；如果重大，则应根据 IFRS 7 第35(g) a)段披露所选择的方法。这是一个高度依赖判断的领域，可能对减值准备产生重大影响。
[IFRS 7 第35(g)段]。
45.71 预期信用损失的估计应反映通过评价一系列可能的结果而确定的无偏概率加权平均金额。至少应考虑两种结果。特别是，企业应考虑发生信用损失的可能性以及不发生信用损失的可能性。
[IFRS 9 附录B第B5.5.41段]。

45.72 用于估计预期信用损失的方法应适合组合的具体情况和性质。在某些情况下，相对简单的建模可能已足够。例如，具有共同风险特征的一大组金融工具的平均信用损失，可能是对概率加权金额的合理估计。在其他情况下，可能需要使用多个情景，明确特定结果的现金流量金额和时间以及这些结果的估计概率。
[IFRS 9 附录B第B5.5.42段]。

45.73 在计量预期信用损失时，对预期现金流量短缺的估计应反映预期来自属于合同条款组成部分且企业未单独确认的担保物及其他信用增级的现金流量。
[IFRS 9 附录B第B5.5.55段]。
FAQ 45.73.1 – 计量有担保贷款或附有其他信用增级（如信用违约互换）贷款的预期信用损失 FAQ 45.73.2 – 当财务担保并非所担保债务的组成部分时，持有人应如何确认、计量和列报财务担保 FAQ 45.73.3 – 就应收账款或租赁应收款持有的现金担保物：确认及对预期信用损失计量的影响

45.74 对有担保金融工具预期现金流量短缺的估计，应反映预期从取消担保物赎回权（处置担保物）中获得的现金流量金额和时间，减去取得和出售担保物的成本。无论取消担保物赎回权是否很可能发生，均应如此（即对预期现金流量的估计需考虑取消担保物赎回权的概率以及由此产生的现金流量）。因此，预期在合同到期日之后通过变现担保物而产生的任何现金流量，均应纳入此项分析。因取消担保物赎回权而取得的任何担保物，不应作为独立于有担保金融工具的资产予以确认，除非其满足资产的相关确认标准。
[IFRS 9 附录B第B5.5.55段]。
45.75 金融资产合同现金流量的修改可能导致现有金融工具终止确认（见第44章第32段）。如果修改导致现有金融资产终止确认并随后确认一项经修改的金融资产，则该经修改的资产被视为一项“新”金融资产。在应用减值要求时，修改日即为该金融资产的初始确认日。这通常意味着在满足确认整个存续期预期信用损失的要求之前，按相当于未来12个月内预期信用损失的金额计量损失准备。
[IFRS 9 附录B第B5.5.25段]。
45.76 然而，在某些不寻常的情况下，可能有证据表明经修改的金融资产在初始确认时即已发生信用减值，因此应确认为一项源生的已发生信用减值的金融资产。例如，当对不良资产进行实质性修改并导致原金融资产终止确认时，就可能出现这种情况。
[IFRS 9 附录B第B5.5.26段]。
45.77 合同修改可能不会导致终止确认。在此情况下，应调整经修改资产的账面余额，以反映修订后的合同现金流量。新的账面余额按经修改的估计未来合同现金流量以该资产原实际利率折现的现值确定。由此产生的调整应作为修改利得或损失计入利润表。
45.78 经修改的资产应采用与任何其他金融工具相同的方式进行评估，以确定是否发生了信用风险显著增加。企业应考虑资产在经修改的合同条款下于报告日的信用风险，并将其与该金融资产在原未修改合同条款下于初始确认日的信用风险进行比较。如果该比较未显示信用风险显著增加，则损失准备应按未来12个月内预期信用损失计量。
[IFRS 9 附录B第B5.5.27段]。

45.79 经修改但未终止确认的金融资产不会自动被视为具有较低的信用风险。企业应基于无需付出不必要的额外成本或努力即可获得的所有合理且有依据的信息，评估自初始确认后信用风险是否已显著增加。这包括历史和前瞻性信息，以及对金融资产预计存续期内信用风险的评估，其中包含有关导致修改之情况的信息。表明不再满足确认整个存续期预期信用损失标准的证据，可能包括按照经修改的合同条款保持最新且按时付款的履约记录。通常，客户需要在一段时间内持续表现出良好的付款行为，信用风险才会被视为有所降低。例如，在合同条款修改后，仅按时付款一次通常不足以消除过去漏付或未足额付款的记录。
[IFRS 9 附录B第B5.5.27段]。

Reference to standard: IFRS 9 para 5.4.1 Reference to standing text: 45.4 Banking & capital markets

In which line item in the income statement should an entity recognise the unwinding of the discount (at the effective interest rate (EIR)) on the loss allowance for expected credit losses (ECL) for a stage 3 financial asset?
A stage 3 financial asset is a credit-impaired financial asset that is not a purchased or originated credit-impaired asset.

For a stage 3 financial asset, the unwinding of the discount on the lifetime ECL is debited to interest revenue in the income statement. In addition the unwinding of the discount on the gross carrying amount of the asset at the EIR is credited to interest revenue. Thus, interest revenue for a stage 3 asset will represent the EIR applied to the amortised cost of the asset, in accordance with paragraph 5.4.1(b) of IFRS 9.
This is illustrated in the following simplified example, which was discussed by the Transition Resource Group for Impairment of Financial Instruments (ITG) at its meeting in December 2015.

An entity holds a stage 3 financial asset measured at amortised cost. The EIR is 10%. At 31 December 20X1, the gross carrying amount of the asset (before deducting the loss allowance) is CU100, and the amortised cost (after deducting the loss allowance) is CU40. Accordingly, the lifetime ECL at 31 December 20X1 is CU60.

Between 31 December 20X1 and 31 December 20X2, there were no contractual cash flows, cash settlements and no change in the expected timing or amount of cash flows on the asset. (For the purposes of this illustration, the effects of compound interest have been ignored.)
The table below summarises the application of the EIR in 20X2 and the carrying amounts at 31 December 20X2.
At 31 December 20X1 (A) CU Application of EIR in 20X2 (B) = (EIR × (A)) CU At 31 December 20X2 (A+ B) CU Gross carrying amount 100 10 110 Expected credit loss (60) (6) (66) Amortised cost 40 4 44

Interest revenue for the 12 months to 31 December 20X2 is CU4, being the application of the EIR to the amortised cost of the asset. This comprises the unwinding of the discount (at the EIR) on the gross carrying amount (CU10 = CU100 × 10%) less the unwinding of the discount (at the EIR) on the ECL (CU6 = CU60 × 10%).

FAQ 45.10.2 – What is a loan commitment for the purposes of applying IFRS 9’s impairment requirements?
Reference to standard: IFRS 9 para 2.1(g) Reference to standing text: 45.10

The issuer of a loan commitment (except those loan commitments measured at fair value through profit or loss as described in paragraph 2.3 of IFRS 9) shall apply IFRS 9’s impairment requirements. While IFRS 9 does not contain a definition of a loan commitment, paragraph BCZ2.2 of IFRS 9 states that loan commitments are firm commitments to provide credit under pre-specified terms and conditions.

A bank commits to providing a loan where the price is to be determined on draw-down at the discretion of the bank. However, the price must be set in good faith and in line with general market conditions on the date of draw-down – that is, the bank is not able to set defensively or unreasonably high interest rates to avoid making the loan. Yes. If the terms and conditions of the arrangement give rise to an enforceable contract to extend credit, a loan commitment within the scope of IFRS 9’s impairment requirements will exist. It is not necessary that the price of the loan to be provided is fixed at the date of entering into the loan commitment.

FAQ 45.13.1 – Use of an impairment provision matrix
Reference to standard: IFRS 9 para 5.5.15 Reference to standing text: 45.13

A non-financial entity holds trade receivables that do not have a significant financing component. The entity would like to use a provision matrix to determine lifetime expected credit losses (ECL). What are the key factors to consider in developing a provision matrix that is compliant with IFRS 9?
IFRS 9 allows a provision matrix to be used for recognising ECL on trade receivables. Factors to consider in developing such a provision matrix include:

- Appropriately grouping receivables if historical (or forecast) credit loss experience shows significantly different loss patterns for different customer segments. For example, receivables could be grouped by geographical region, product type, customer rating, collateral or trade credit insurance, or type of customer.

- Adjusting historical credit loss experience to incorporate relevant, current and more forward-looking information that is reasonable and supportable, and available without undue cost or effort at the reporting date.
- Determining different loss rates for the different ageing ‘buckets’ of trade receivables. For example, older receivables would be expected to have a higher loss rate than more current receivables.

In order to determine the amount of ECL to be recognised in the financial statements, the entity could set up a provision matrix, based on its historical observed default rates, which is adjusted for forward-looking information. See EX 45.13.2 for an illustrative example.

Reference to standard: IFRS 9 para B5.5.35 Reference to standing text: 45.13
IFRS 9’s impairment model is an ‘expected credit loss’ (ECL) approach.

Given the complexity of implementing an expected loss model, IFRS 9 mandates a simplified approach for trade receivables without a significant financing component (and permits entities to use the same simplified approach for trade receivables with a significant financing component). Generally, normal trade receivables with terms of one year or less would not have a significant financing component. The simplification requires an entity to use life

IFRS 9 allows a provision matrix to be used to determine the ECL for trade receivables. IFRS 9 is not prescriptive about how to develop a provision matrix. One approach is illustrated below. However, other approaches might also be appropriate, provided that they are consistent with the principles in IFRS 9.
The impact of COVID-19 on the provision matrix approach is highlighted for each step in the boxes below.
COVID-19 impact – Overall

- COVID-19 has had a significant impact on economies and has caused disruption to many companies’ operations. The economic environment has changed dramatically, and the impact on ECLs cannot be ignored.
- As a result, assumptions and simplifications used previously in provision matrices might no longer hold in a COVID-19 environment, and they might need to be revisited.
- The key pre-COVID-19 assumptions that need to be revisited include the following:
- groupings of receivables that share similar credit risk characteristics; and
- the inclusion of forward-looking information into the loss rates and use of multiple scenarios.
How does a provision matrix work?

A provision matrix uses past data and forward-looking information to calculate the ECL. A provision matrix essentially applies an expected loss rate to every ageing category of receivables, including the current category. Illustrative Example 12 in IFRS 9 provides the following simple example:
Current 1–30 days past due 31–60 days past due 61–90 days past due More than 90 days past due Expected loss rate 0.3% 1.6% 3.6% 6.6% 10.6%

Gross carrying amount of receivable Lifetime expected credit loss allowance (Gross carrying amount × lifetime expected credit loss rate) Current & accrued unbilled receivables CU15,000,000 CU45,000 1–30 days past due CU7,500,000 CU120,000 31–60 days past due CU4,000,000 CU144,000 61–90 days past due CU2,500,000 CU165,000 More than 90 days past due CU1,000,000 CU106,000 Total CU30,000,000 CU580,000
ECL rates are developed for each ageing category, and they are applied to the outstanding balances to determine the ECLs and, ultimately, the ECL provision to be recognised.

It is important to note that each ageing category, including those receivables that are not past due, have an ECL rate. This is because, even for sales that have just occurred, there is a possibility that the debtor will not pay for credit reasons.

The term ‘expected’ is often used in everyday parlance to mean ‘more likely than not to occur’. However, in the context of ECL, ‘expected’ is used to refer to a probability-weighted amount calculated by multiplying various possible outcomes by the likelihood that each outcome will occur, and then adding up all of those values.

The outcome of the model looks very simple, but determining the ECL rate to apply often requires significant judgements to be made. We discuss some of the key considerations in establishing a provision matrix below, and we highlight the impact of COVID-19 on them.
What data and information are required to produce a provision matrix?
In its simplest form, a provision matrix requires history of past sales, the time from sale until payment receipt, and the amounts written off for the equivalent period.
Only those losses that are due to credit risk are within the scope of the ECL. This could include the losses from credit notes issued to debtors who do not have the ability to pay.

Other pricing adjustments or concessions (for example, due to disputes / discounts / inefficiencies) are subject to guidance in IFRS 15, ‘Revenue from contracts with customers’. The guidance in IFRS 15 should be applied prior to determining the amount of the credit loss allowance under IFRS 9.

As a result of COVID-19, a company might expect to give customers a discount, because goods or services could not be completed in the manner that was initially agreed in the contract. Such discounts would not be considered credit losses, and so they should not be incorporated into the estimates of ECL, as discussed further in FAQ 45.49.9. However, the entity would need to determine how such estimated discounts impact the amount of revenue recogni

Depending on the availability of internal data, management might have to supplement the internal data with external data and analysis to the extent necessary. For example, data regarding the impact of COVID-19 on the expected default rates of companies in particular industries or geographies might be available from credit rating agencies or other market information providers.
Step 1: Define the portfolio

- Depending on the diversity of its customer base, the entity should use different provision matrices for different groups of receivables on the basis of shared credit risk characteristics. FAQ 45.24.6 – How do changes in impairment methodology such as a change in definition of default, impact the assessment of whether a significant increase in credit risk has occurred?
Reference to standard: IFRS 9 para 5.5.9 Reference to standing text: 45.24 Banking and capital markets
How do changes in impairment methodology, such as a change in definition of default (DoD), impact the assessment of whether a significant increase in credit risk (SICR) has occurred?

An entity changes the DoD that it uses in estimating IFRS 9 expected credit losses (ECL). This change could occur for a number of different reasons (for example, changes in regulatory requirements or in internal risk management policies and procedures).

The entity uses probability of default (PD), loss given default (LGD) and exposure at default (EAD) as inputs to its model used to estimate ECL. The DoD is one of the key inputs to this model. Moreover, the entity uses an increase in an instrument’s lifetime probability of default as one of the criteria to determine whether an SICR has occurred.
Question 1: Does the change meet the definition of a change in estimate or change in policy as defined under IAS 8?
Question 2: How should the entity consider the change in DoD for the purpose of assessing whether an SICR has occurred?

Please note: This FAQ assumes that the change is not the correction of a prior period error under IAS 8 and that, where the change is following a change in regulatory requirements, it is appropriate to update the DoD as discussed in FAQ 45.26.1 'Aligning the definition of default: Regulatory versus Accounting'.
Solution 1: Change in policy versus change in estimate

A change in ECL resulting from using an updated DoD, which is an input into the ECL estimation methodology, is a change in an estimate under the definition in IAS 8 and not a change in accounting policy.

Paragraph 5 of IAS 8 defines a change in accounting estimate as “an adjustment of the carrying amount of an asset or a liability … that results from new information or new developments and, accordingly, are not corrections of errors”.
In contrast, accounting policies are the specific principles, bases, conventions, rules and practices applied by an entity in preparing and presenting financial statements.

The DoD is an element of the ECL estimation methodology and the updated DoD reflects a change in the circumstances on which the estimate is based. In other words, it is a component of the measurement technique used to calculate ECL. It follows that changes to the ECL estimate that result from revising the DoD are accounted for as changes in accounting estimates under IAS 8. This is similar to revisions resulting from a change in a valuation techn
The effect of a change in an accounting estimate does not result in the restatement of prior year comparative amounts. [IAS 8 para 34]. [IAS 8 para 36].

If an entity considers using changes in the risk of default occurring over the next 12 months (such as changes in the 12-month PD) as a reasonable approximation to changes in lifetime risk of default occurring (for example, changes in lifetime PD), it needs to complete a robust analysis before first use of the approximation, to support that conclusion. The level of initial analysis required would depend on the specific type of financial instrumen
As indicated in paragraph B5.5.14 of IFRS 9, in some circumstances changes in the 12-month risk of a default occurring may not be an appropriate proxy for a lifetime assessment, for example when:
- the financial instrument only has significant payment obligations beyond the next 12 months;
- changes in relevant macroeconomic or other credit-related factors occur that are not adequately reflected in the risk of a default occurring in the next 12 months; or
- changes in credit-related factors only have an impact on the credit risk of the financial instrument (or have a more pronounced effect) beyond 12 months.

An entity needs to be satisfied on an ongoing basis that the use of changes in the 12-month risk of a default occurring continues to be a reasonable approximation for changes in the lifetime risk of a default occurring. This need not be a full analysis, such as that undertaken on initial use of the approximation for a particular financial instrument or portfolio. - identify the key factors that would affect the appropriateness of using changes in the 12-month risk of a default occurring as an approximation of changes in the lifetime risk of default occurring;
- monitor these factors on an ongoing basis as part of a qualitative review of circumstances; and

- consider whether any changes in those factors indicate that changes in the 12-month risk of a default occurring is no longer an appropriate proxy for changes in a lifetime risk of default occurring.

If it was determined that changes in the 12-month risk of a default occurring were no longer a reasonable approximation for the assessment of changes in the lifetime risk of a default occurring, an entity would be required to determine an appropriate approach to assess significant increases in credit risk that captures changes in the lifetime risk of a default occurring.
What else should an entity consider when using changes in 12-month risk of default occurring as an approximation to changes in lifetime risk of default occurring?
Entities are required to disclose how they make the assessment of significant increases in credit risk in accordance with paragraph 35G of IFRS 7.

An entity sells a machine to a customer for a price that consists of fixed and variable consideration. The fixed consideration is CU100, and the variable consideration is dependent on the machine’s quality (for example, measured by a percentage of defective output during the first six months of operating the machine) and may be between CU0 and CU30. At 1 November 20X5 (the delivery date) and 31 December 20X5 (the reporting date), the entity expects to have a right to receive CU25 from the customer resulting from the variable consideration. However it estimates that only CU20 is highly probable in terms of paragraph 56 of IFRS 15. As the amount of variable consideration is conditional on the future percentage of defective output of the machine, the entity recognises a contract asset of CU20 i
At the reporting date the entity expects to receive only CU2 with respect to the contract asset due to a decrease in the customer’s credit-worthiness after the delivery date.
In accordance with paragraph B5.5.29 of IFRS 9, a credit loss is the present value of the difference between:
- the contractual cash flows that are due to an entity under the contract; and
- the cash flows that the entity expects to receive.

The contractual cash flows used for determining ECL should be consistent with the cash flows used in measuring the recognised contract asset in accordance with IFRS 15 (that is, the highly probable cash flows of CU20). This is consistent with the determination of ECL for lease receivables in accordance with paragraph B5.5.34 of IFRS 9.
In this case (ignoring the time value of money for simplicity), the ECL for the contract asset will be CU18 (contractual cash flows of CU20 less expected cash flows of CU2).

An entity sells a machine to a customer for a price that consists of fixed and variable consideration. The fixed consideration is CU100, and the variable consideration is dependent on the machine’s quality (for example, measured by a percentage of defective output during the first six months of operating the machine) and may be between CU0 and CU30. The machine is delivered on 1 November 20X5 and is put into operation directly after delivery. The
The entity recognises a trade receivable of CU100 in respect of the fixed consideration, as it has an unconditional right to receive that amount three months after delivery.

The estimated amount is constrained byparagraph 56 of IFRS 15, which states that the entity shall recognise some or all of an amount of variable consideration estimated only to the extent that it is highly probable that a significant reversal will not occur when the uncertainty associated with the variabl

At 1 November 20X5 (the delivery date) and 31 December 20X5 (the reporting date), the entity recognises a contract asset of CU20 in respect of the variable consideration. This is because this amount is expected to be highly probable in accordance with paragraph 56 of IFRS 15 and is conditional on the future percentage of defective output of the machine.
At the reporting date (31 December 20X5), the entity expects to receive only CU117 of the total consideration, due to the credit risk of the customer.
How should the entity determine the loss allowance for the trade receivable and the contract asset respectively?

The ECL should be determined separately for the trade receivable and the contract asset. That is, the entity should determine the risk of default and credit loss for the respective due dates for the trade receivable and contract asset separately and use them to calculate the ECL for each asset.

If however the trade receivable and contract asset had the same due date, this approach would result in the overall ECL being allocated on a proportionate basis between the trade receivable and contract asset.

An entity sells a machine together with 12 months of maintenance services. The machine is delivered to the customer on 1 February 20X1, and the purchase price is payable 6 months after delivery. The maintenance fee is due at the end of each month. The total consideration is allocated between the machine and the maintenance in accordance with IFRS 15 based on their relative stand-alone selling price. This is because in scenario B the entity considers that it is probable that it will collect the consideration in respect of future maintenance services, as the financial difficulties of the customer are expected to be only temporary.

Accordingly the entity cannot enforce recoverability of the contract asset and therefore has no reasonable expectation of recovering the contract asset. As a result the contract asset should be fully written off in accordance with paragraph 5.4.4 of IFRS

FAQ 45.52.2 – Factors to consider in assessing the expected credit loss (ECL) on jointly and severally liable financial guarantee contracts
Reference to standard: Reference to standing text: 45.52

Group X consists of parent A and its 5 wholly owned subsidiaries (B, C, D, E and F). Subsidiary B borrows CU100m from bank Y. The loan benefits from a cross-company guarantee where all the group entities are jointly and severally liable for any losses that bank Y incurs on its loan to subsidiary B, but is otherwise unsecured.

Where entities are jointly and severally liable, it is possible for the lender to call upon a single guarantor to settle the complete obligation arising from the financial guarantee contract (‘FGC’), exposing the guarantor to the maximum amount payable under the FGC. However, it is also possible for the lender to call upon multiple guarantors to settle proportions of the amounts due, or for a single guarantor that was called upon to settle the am

Assume that the cross-company guarantee meets the IFRS 9 definition of an FGC, is accounted for under IFRS 9 and is not measured at FVTPL. Paragraph 4.2.1(c) of IFRS 9 would require each group entity to estimate the expected credit loss (ECL) as part of the subsequent measurement of the FGC in its separate financial statements.
When estimating the ECL for use in the subsequent measurement of the FGC in the separate financial statements of each of the individual guarantors, what factors should be considered?

In line with the general ECL measurement principles of IFRS 9, the ECL on an FGC is a probability-weighted estimate of the cash shortfalls based on reasonable and supportable information. The cash shortfalls arising from an FGC are the expected payments to reimburse the holder for a credit loss that it incurs, less any amounts that the entity expects to receive from the holder, the debtor or any other party (that is, the net cash outflow expected

Since there are inherent differences between being the sole guarantor and being jointly and severally liable with others, the ECL measurement should consider all the facts and circumstances and existing arrangements between the parties within the group.

In estimating the net cash outflow, consideration should first be given to any legal agreements that exist between the co-guarantors, for example that specify the order in which the co-guarantors would be called upon or subsequent reimbursement by fellow guarantors. The FGC might also provide for a guarantor’s right of recovery against the guaranteed entity in the event of a guarantee being called upon. Where such agreements exist, they should be
In the absence of such legal agreements, the following factors may be relevant in estimating the net cash outflow:
- The relative credit ratings of each of the guarantors. In certain instances, it might be more likely for a lender to call against an entity with a relatively higher credit rating.
- The extent of correlation between the credit risks of the individual guarantors and the guaranteed entity, that is, the default correlation. For example:

- If a guarantor is in the same industry or has the same success drivers as the guaranteed entity, resulting in both the entities being subject to similar risk and to a high degree of correlation, there might be less likelihood of that guarantor being called upon. That is because there is greater likelihood that the specific guarantor would also be in financial difficulty at that time. In this scenario, it would be more likely for the lender to s

- If subsidiary B defaults it could indicate insufficient resources elsewhere in the group, or contagion risk. In this scenario, customers stop dealing with apparently healthy entities in the same group due to uncertainties. This might result in cases where all the guarantors would be unable to fulfill their obligations to a certain extent in the event of default by subsidiary B. In such a scenario, each guarantor might be called upon for only a

- The value and liquidity of the assets held by each of the guarantors. It might be more likely for a lender to call against an entity with more assets or assets that are more liquid and so could be monetised more easily. For example, an operating entity may have more liquid assets than an intermediate holding company whose only asset is its investment in an unlisted subsidiary.
- Legal jurisdiction. For example, it might be easier for the lender to claim against entities which are in the same legal jurisdiction, compared to entities that are not.

- Legal provisions in the relevant territory, such as Common Law. These might provide a guarantor with a right of recovery against its co-guarantors in the event of a guarantee being called upon. However, in practice it might be less likely for group entities to initiate legal proceedings against each other, and depending on the legal framework, it might also be challenging to estimate the outcome of such proceedings.

These considerations could result in different financial guarantee liability amounts being estimated and recognised by the individual guarantors and might require a significant level of judgement. Entities should therefore also consider as appropriate:
- IAS 1 disclosures around significant estimates and judgements;
- Disclosure requirements of the related party arrangements per IAS 24; and
- IFRS 7 disclosures relevant to financial guarantees including the requirement in paragraph 35G to disclose assumptions used in estimating ECL.
